chapters.title: Chapter 1: Audata
chapters.html:
It was like waking up from a dream.

Sometime, somewhere, Audata of Aedes Elysiae woke up from a very long, very fuzzy nightmare.

A chill clung to her shoulders, like a heavy coat made of frost. Her hands, always as warm as the hearth, were now cold and stiff as she twitched her fingers against a familiar wooden floor.

It took her a long moment to return – return? – to the present. When she did, she found herself lying on the ground, wood hard against her back and head aching. Her tongue felt heavy and dry, like a cloth abandoned outside in the fields for days. Her eyelids stuck together, so she had to rub her eyes to finally – finally – pry them open and look around.

She was… at home. Where else would she be? Another option would have been the fields, but–

Wait.

Why was she on the ground, then? Did she pass out? … That had only happened during her pregnancy. Why did she pass out? Why–?

With a low grunt, she rolled on the floor and managed to use the table as leverage to stand up. The world tilted around her, so she raised a hand and rubbed her temples, cursing under her breath. She sure hoped Phainon wasn’t around to hear her and internalize her cursing – not that he needed any help with Hieronymus around, anyway – but then hit another blank when she realized that… her home seemed terribly quiet.

And that was weird, wasn’t it? If she had actually passed out, then someone – Hieronymus, at least – should have noticed and made a fuss about it. He would have probably dragged Phainon away from his classes or adventures and–

Why couldn’t she remember? Her mind was a mess, with too many questions and a persistent ache at the back of her head, as if someone was hammering away against her skull, over and over again.

Where was everyone? Why was she alone, here, unconscious, with no memories about what had happened last?

She remembered… what was the last thing she remembered? Making dinner? Working on that challenging quilt she had wanted to finish before Phainon made up his mind about leaving? Checking on the kids? Helping Hieronymus with the repairs?

She drew a blank, and that… that was scary. It was really scary, because she had the nagging feeling that something bad had happened, and yet…

“Audata!” Before she could become overwhelmed by her own thoughts, she was snapped back to the real world by a loud yell and the front door slamming into the wall. In no time at all, there were hands grasping at her arms, her shoulders, her face. She came face to face with her husband, who searched her face and eyes for– something. “Audata, are you okay?”

For a moment, she didn’t remember how her mouth worked – weird, that for a single second she had been surprised at having a mouth at all – and the words died on her tongue. Her confused mind struggled to understand everything that was going on, trying to make sense of her scattered memories that made no sense. And yet, instinct took over and her hands clutched at Hieronymus’ shoulders too, shaking, desperate for something to anchor her to the present.

Really, what happened?

“I… think so?” she managed to stutter out. Hearing her own voice grounded her a bit more, until she could finally feel Hieronymus’ solid grip around her arms, feel his calloused fingers, see his worried blue eyes stare at her as if she would fly away otherwise. She swallowed, and nearly cringed when the saliva felt more dense and metallic than usual for a short second. “... You?”

“I woke up in the middle of the field, and I got worried when I rushed over and saw more people unconscious and… I just– I got so worried.” And finally, Hieronymus hugged her tightly, letting out a long sigh of relief. She clutched him back, and only then did she realize that her hands were shaking as much as his. “Do you… remember anything?”

“From just before I passed out?” asked Audata, even though she was quite sure that they were thinking the same thing. At Hieronymus’ slight nod, she shook her head. “... No. Nothing.”

And then, they both– froze.

Her heart cold again, just like her hands, she stepped back from Hieronymus’ embrace and her fingers dug like claws on his arms, eyes wide and absolutely terrified.

“Dear… where’s Phainon?” she asked, breathless and feeling cold dread climb up her chest until she was sure that whatever air was coming out of her mouth was actually ice.

“... I haven’t seen him,” breathed her husband, and immediately, they both turned to the opened front door, almost expecting their dear child to waltz inside, completely fine, with a self-conscious grin, a hand behind his head, hair messy–

“Let’s go,” urged Audata, and she didn’t need to tell him twice, because Hieronymus quickly took her hand and the both of them rushed out of their home, eyes roving over the dirt paths.

Nothing.

Audata saw Galba rub his head, clutching the stone fence around his home with a scratched hand. She saw the other man look around, a spark of worry in his eyes that turned into confused panic when he saw no sign of his own son Piso. She saw Pythias rushing through the dirt paths, calling out the name of her daughter Livia.

The cold in Audata’s chest spread. She could see no hint of white hair, no children running down the path with panicked yells – not even a hint of rosy pink hair.

She clutched at Hieronymus’ arm as the parents of their little group crossed glances and came together in the middle of the crossroads.

“Does anyone know anything?” asked Pythias, voice breathless and hands shaky as she clutched her precious necklace from her late husband in her hands. “Livia…”

“I haven’t seen any of the kids,” shook his head Galba, lips thin. “But then again, they usually run off by themselves. They could just be– out there.”

Audata clung to that possibility with shaky hands and tried to take a deep breath to calm herself down. It would do no one any favors if they lost their minds and panicked like headless chickens before they could get any answers. The kids would be okay – Phainon and Cyrene were already older, they were smart, they knew how to take care of themselves. They just had to find them.

Because they should still be in the village… right?

Audata grabbed Hieronymus’ arm again to stop him from running off like the rest of their little group and looked him right in the eye.

“Could Phainon have left already?” she asked, even though she knew that it couldn't be possible. “I mean, the last thing I remember was him telling us that he had everything packed and–”

“He wouldn't,” was Hieronymus’ firm answer. He took her shaking hands, squeezing them and– grounding her, again. “He wouldn't have left without telling us. We said we would see him off.”

And that– was true. Phainon wouldn't have run off without a word, especially knowing how worried they always got when he missed a meal or when he didn't answer their calls. When he told them that he had decided to leave their little village to pursue his goal of mastering the sword, he had seemed nervous and a bit embarrassed, but he had stood firm and he knew that his parents would support him, no matter what. He had no reason to disappear like this, and so–

“You're right,” nodded Audata, finally taking a deep breath. It didn't really help quell her worry, but it shifted her perspective enough to have faith in her own son, anyway. “You’re right, of course you are. Let's go.”

And so, they scattered. 

Some rushed to the pier, some rushed to the Sacrament Courtyard with other neighbors. Audata and Hieronymus hurried to the riverside, hoping to find the little group of children simply playing amongst themselves, none the wiser.

Instead, they found Livia and Piso crying beneath a tree, hands shaky and clothes absolutely drenched.

“We can’t find Phainon and Cyrene!” cried Piso, devastated, clutching at Audata’s tunic with dirt-stainned hands.

“We’re sorry! We don’t know what happened!” cried Livia from where Hieronymus was trying to get her sandal out of the mud by the river.

“It’s okay. Your parents are very worried about you, so we’ll take you back to them for now,” she tried to comfort them, trying for a smile but falling short as her own worry took root in her heart.

“Phainon and Cyrene will be fine. They’re big kids, now,” tried to cheer them up Hieronymus, but his own grin wavered.  

Their eyes met – both crushed by worry, panicked, and not knowing what to do. Sure, disappearing kids weren't uncommon, and they usually knew better than to leave the little area around the village to avoid any bandits – not that there were many to start with, but merchants talked – and most of the time, the kids were just playing in the forest, but… The fact that no one could remember what had happened moments – moments? – before was… worrying. Very, very worrying.

They regrouped at the pier, where families reunited and cried in relief.

In contrast, Audata and Hieronymus hung back, sticking close to each other to avoid crumbling down like a house of cards.

“They’ll be fine,” was muttering Hieronymus, but Audata didn’t know if it was to convince her, or if it was to convince himself. Maybe both. “Cyrene is the smartest girl I know. And Phainon is now much better with a sword, he can protect the two of them, no problem.”

And yet, the other villagers regarded them with pity, with worry, placing gentle hands on their shoulders and inviting them to dinner, with promises to comb the fields as soon as possible to search for the couple of kids that had always been the heart of their little community.

Audata clasped Hieronymus’ hand between her own, trying to ignore just how cold she felt. Just like ice.

—

There was no sign of Phainon or Cyrene anywhere near the village.

Audata had even resorted to wandering the forest and riverbed and dirt paths around the village and windmills, calling out the name ‘Khaslana’, hoping that the use of his full name would make her kid run back home with the tail between his legs, just like Snowy would.

But he never did.

And that only worried them more and more because, as mischievous and rambunctious as Phainon could be, he was too well-behaved to make his parents and the rest of the village worry unnecessarily.

The fact that they couldn't find Cyrene either was also troubling.

Chances were that the two kids were together, which usually meant that they were safe and sound. However, in this case, when apparently everyone had passed out and woken up with no memories of what had happened before their unwilling nap, their absence covered their little village in a heavy cloak of paranoid worry and uneasiness. And, of course, the two most affected by it were… Audata and Hieronymus.

“I’m sorry, we haven’t found any clues today either,” was Galba’s predictable answer when their search party returned that night – because nights existed, now, which had been another fright they had to panic through, hiding in their homes immediately before they figured out that they were safe.

Audata managed to force a smile for her dear neighbor, hoping to alleviate the clear guilt weighting on his shoulders. She wasn’t sure if she succeeded, guessing from how he dragged his feet back home.

But she couldn’t really bring herself to hope for the best – not anymore, not when nearly an entire week’s worth of search parties all over their little village and surrounding forest and hills amounted to… nothing. No clues; not about their unexpected ‘nap’, and not about their missing children.

“We can always… venture further,” commented Hieronymus one night, when both of them had been staring listlessly at the walls of their little home, silence heavy and uncommon in a house as lively as theirs had always been.

What should have been Phainon’s share of dinner sat untouched on the other side of the table, now cold.

“How much further?” asked Audata, clutching his hand tightly.

“As much as it’s needed,” was his answer, and even though the hesitation in his voice was as clear as their new mornings, his determination was still firm like bedrock.

Audata hummed, unconvinced, but she knew that time would ground her hesitation to dust and push her forward.

And so, when a messenger from a neighboring village rushed into their disheartened meeting after another failed search, Audata and Hieronymus crossed a glance and braced themselves for whatever twist destiny threw at them.

“The Era Nova has come!” was yelling the man, waving a long parchment decorated with gold that shined too brightly under the sun to be fake. “Amphoreus is saved! There is no more Black Tide! No more monsters! No more mad Titans! We’re free!”

As the man rambled on and on about the true dawn that a prophecy promised, Audata hugged herself with her arms, eyes sharp and jaw tense, because, as out-of-the-way as Aedes Elysiae had always been, rumors still reached them all the same. Merchants were few and far between, but for a long time, most of them brought with them countless news of felled cities, of refugees in need of protection, of mad Titans wanting to crush their little dreams to dust and ashes. 

When Phainon had started mentioning his interest in going out and exploring the world and forging himself into a warrior, Audata and her husband had been… worried, to say the least. They hadn’t let Phainon see their worry, of course, but it was still there. He was free to follow whatever path he wanted, after all – they wouldn’t stand in his way, not like how Hieronymus’ father had done, back in the day. And if that meant that Phainon had decided to plunge himself into a world of wars and suffering, then… then they just had to hope that the golden fields of home would be able to guide him back to their embrace.

Could Phainon be out there? But how could that be? Last she knew, he had been playing with the other children out in the fields, leading the way with the sword Hieronymus made for him not long ago. A last adventure before he set off.

(How long had they been asleep? They hadn’t aged a day– they couldn’t–)

And then the messenger started revering golden-blooded heroes, those who had sacrificed themselves to grant them all a dawn with no shadows, a future with no strings, freedom from a doomed fate, and Audata– froze.

She remembered, clear as yesterday, how she had panicked when Phainon had bled gold, how Cyrene had bled gold, how the village chief at the time had raised their hands to the sky and called these two children sacred, saviors, chosen of the Titans, before singing praises to the statue of Oronyx and kneeling before the two toddlers, too young to understand, too innocent, too–

“Hieronymus,” she called, voice trembling, her hand clutching at her husband’s arm desperately, because she was connecting the dots and the picture they painted was anything but hopeful. Hieronymus grabbed her hand with just as much desperation as her. “What are we going to do?”

And Hieronymus, with that firm resolve of his, set his jaw, looked to the path leading out of their little village, their little world, and–

“Simple,” he said, mind already made up. He looked down at Audata and his eyes were shining with resolve – just like Phainon’s. “We set off.”

chapters.title: Chapter 2: Hieronymus
chapters.html:
“Are you sure about this?” asked Pythias, lingering by the door as both Audata and Hieronymus hurried from one corner of their little house to the other, stuffing clothes, food, anything they might need into a worn bag, their eyes just short of manic. “I mean… from what the messenger told us, Amphoreus is still dangerous. You don’t have guards to protect you, you’re not trained in combat–”

“Pythias,” interrupted Hieronymus, placing both hands on her shoulders and staring at her right in the eye. “We have to do this. Phainon is out there– I know he is. We need to find him and bring him home.”

“We’re very thankful for all your hard work these past few days, Pythias,” added Audata, smiling up at her, a glint of ruefulness in her eye. “But… I think we all know that those two are not here anymore. Staying here… we’d be like sitting ducks.”

“And I don’t know about you, but I definitely don’t have a duck face,” nodded Hieronymus, terribly serious, before he sighed and released Pythias’ shoulders. “Don’t misunderstand. We know how dangerous this is, but– it’s Phainon. And Cyrene.”

Pythias, predictably, took a deep breath and let it out, shaking her head with a sad little smile. Hieronymus had known her for so long that he could see just how much she actually wanted to look at this situation with hope, but she had been in most of those search parties, knew that the chances of her two star students being anywhere near Aedes Elysiae were nearly null.

“I’ll pray to Oronyx everyday for you,” she said, and that was that.

Hieronymus nodded and smiled and wondered if there was even a Titan that would hear her prayers, now that the so-called Era Nova had washed over Amphoreus. They didn’t know enough to say, didn’t know enough to understand. They would plunge themselves into a different world, a world they hadn’t even seen before it became something new. But– Phainon was their son. And he was worth it, every time.

So, early the very next day, both of them left their little village behind, bags slung over their shoulders and hearts beating fast as a rabbit in their chest.

—

Hieronymus felt like a teenager again, curious about the outside world and willing to go out and have countless adventures – only to be stopped by his strict father, over and over again.

“The outside world is dangerous, full of senseless wars. Do you want to be dragged into one of those conflicts, son?” had asked his father once, pointing his old sickle at him and glaring down with a mighty frown.

“I wouldn’t!” had replied young Hieronymus, inexperienced, naive, full of hope and hungry for adventure – like those stories that talked of honorable heroes, wielding sun-like swords and shooting lightning-like arrows.

His father had scoffed, before turning back to his work in the fields.

“You would. Everyone does, willing or not,” he had grumbled, words heavy with something Hieronymus hadn’t been able to name, and that was that.

And when Phainon, so similar to Hieronymus in that regard, had listened to the same stories and came to the same conclusion, the same choice, the same wish for adventure, Hieronymus had found himself in the same position as his father all those years before. And while Hieronymus’ father had predictably scolded Phainon for the same lofty ideas that Hieronymus had entertained all those years ago, he… came to realize that he couldn’t follow in his own father’s footsteps. 

And so, he had told Phainon to follow his heart, to see the world with his own eyes, to exchange his sickle for a mighty sword if he so wished, before coming back home. 

Had he made a mistake?

Now that he could see what laid beyond the hills of gold, he found that, even if his naive choice and guidance were the culprit that had dragged them all into this unpleasant situation, he… couldn’t let himself regret it.

If Phainon had gotten to see this world with his own eyes, experienced what laid beyond, lived through even half of the adventures that those heroes of legend went through, then… Then it was worth it.

(Was it, though? Those heroes had never changed, had never dealt with the consequences of their ferocious battles, but would a normal person react like that?)

They wandered around the area near their village for a few days, but when that didn’t get them many – new – answers, they decided to broaden their search. Further. And further.

They passed by Janusopolis, saw the Grove in the distance, visited numerous villages and settlements where people whispered countless rumors about the Era Nova and how it came about, about the heroes beyond the sky, about the Chrysos Heirs, about the demigods, about how Amphoreus had been reforged.

But weren't the Chrysos Heirs… a simple myth? Hieronymus still remembered how the old priests of the village wove complicated stories about these legendary individuals, singing praises to the Titans and their chosen ones. Hieronymus' parents had scoffed, back in the day, calling the priests crazy. When Phainon was born, and they learned of his golden blood, everyone had become suspiciously quiet. And when Cyrene appeared – Oronyx’ chosen they called her – the words left unsaid were loud.

Still– Hieronymus had tried not to think too much about it. They were just legends, after all. Phainon and Cyrene were normal human kids, with normal human bad ideas and a mischievous streak that kept them all on their toes.

And yet, everyone now said that the Chrysos Heirs were real, that they could ascend to Titans or that they already had, that they were the very example of mighty and honorable heroes, capable of saving their world through their strong wills.

When Hieronymus tried to reconcile that image with the two laughing children he knew… He felt cold.

For the first time since they left Aedes Elysiae, Hieronymus felt actual fear for whatever they would find when they – hopefully – found their son and the girl adopted by the entire village.

Still, they continued their little self-imposed mission, noting down most of the rumors that floated their way, even the seemingly sketchy ones, just in case. They spent nights upon nights trying to make sense of them, of the long list of names, digging into all variations of the same story.

Every day, after Parting Hour, they bundled around their cheap notebook and tried to make sense of all the words they had recorded throughout the day. Not that they made much leeway on it, when a lot of the rumors contradicted each other – how could there be two Deliverers, sharing a single role? 

It reminded Hieronymus of Phainon’s destined card, and that thought was chilling when added to the fact that the Chrysos Heirs were apparently real, so he buried it under piles of question marks and worry. In any case, a lot of the rumors about the revered Deliverer were about a gray-haired traveler from beyond the sky fighting with a flaming lance or something called a– bat?

“So, Amphoreus now has days and nights, because there is no more Kephale holding up the dawn,” recited Hieronymus, frowning down at the notebook. Audata, checking on their dwindling supplies, nodded absent-mindedly. “And there are no more Titans, because they're dead. And the world is now in the process of settling down after the Era Nova… whatever that means.” Hieronymus sighed and leaned back against the only rickety chair in their room. “This sounds like one of Cyrene's stories.”

“It does, doesn't it?” mumbled Audata. She smiled softly, a hint of sadness bleeding through the perpetual worry in her eyes. “She was fond of happy endings.”

Hieronymus hoped that preference was the reality in this case, too.

By the time they left the fifth village, their little notebook was overflowing with notes and half-formed theories and yet– they were no closer to finding any leads that would point them towards where Phainon could be.

It was weighing on both of them, by this point. Hieronymus tried to get Audata to cheer up, pointing out any and all interesting landmarks they passed through as their long journey pulled them further and further away from their little home by the seaside. He wasn’t sure if he succeeded, but it was better than nothing.

He only wished he had Phainon’s as-always ready support, with his witty ideas and boundless energy. And yet… that was the problem.

Hieronymus’ hand still reached out to his side sometimes, expecting to find someone that wasn’t there. He had seen Audata almost call for Phainon countless times, eyes searching for him in the streets, until she remembered that he wasn’t with them.

And every single time, it was like something sharp had stabbed through his heart, like the ground had crumbled beneath his feet.

And still, they didn’t give up and continued on their search, their notebook filling with more and more rumors, their bags becoming lighter and lighter as they had to eat the food they packed and their savings dwindled.

—

“The Era Nova was brought by a Deliverer from beyond the stars!”

“No, they say it was the demigod of Worldbearing, Kephale’s successor!”

“It’s the same person, dumbass!”

“No, it’s not! Look, there are twelve Titans, but thirteen demigods–”

“The Deliverer is not a demigod, though.”

“They have to be, if they are the Worldbearer.”

“You’re spouting nonsense!”

“No, no, let him talk! I’ve heard they’re two people, but they look similar – only, one of them has gray hair and the other has white hair.”

Hieronymus stopped so suddenly Audata – who had been walking behind him, frowning down at their messy notebook full of scribbles and questions marks – inevitably ran into his back with a yelp. He ignored her soft apology and grabbed her arm, hurrying after the arguing trio, a million questions on his tongue.

White hair. It wasn’t uncommon to see people with white hair, but– but what if– And Phainon was probably one of those they called Chrysos Heirs, too, and–

“Wait, do you mean there are two Worldbearers now?” 

“That’s a stupid explanation, even for you.”

“Ugh, did you even listen to the official message? Three travelers from beyond the stars, the three of them took the positions of three demigods. And so–”

“Excuse me!” interrupted Hieronymus, finally catching up to the three men that were now glaring at each other. All of them turned their heated gazes to him, so Hieronymus tried to calm his breathing and smile assuredly at them, waving a hand. “I’m sorry, I just wanted to ask– you mentioned a white-haired Chrysos Heir, right?”

“I’m still not sure that Heir exists, actually–” grumbled one of them, frown deep and offended, only to be cut off by another, who nodded encouragingly at Hieronymus.

“Yes, I did. Did you want to hear more rumors about him?” he asked, an excited glint in his eyes.

“Actually– I just wanted to ask for his name?” said Hieronymus, and he had to bite his tongue to stop himself from asking for more – after all, these men couldn't even agree on whether or not this mysterious Heir even existed, any and all information they could have would be wrong or far from the truth. “If you know of it, of course.”

“I’ve already told you, it makes no sense–” tried again the same man, raising his hands to the sky, as if some benevolent Titan – that didn’t exist anymore – would be willing to give him patience to deal with his companion.

“He has various names, but the one I’ve heard the most is… yes, it should be something like ‘Phainon’.” And even though the name felt foreign and slightly different when said in an accent not their own, it was clear that it was– it was–

Hieronymus felt his breath leave his lungs at once and he felt Audata claw at his arm, a desperate and shaky grasp that ended up being the only anchor to reality he had, as his mind drowned in a cacophony of rumors and information and an echo of his son’s name, over and over again.

With a gasp, he grasped at Audata’s hand in turn.

“Thank you,” he managed to get out to the now-confused group of men in front of him, before he turned and dragged Audata after him, forward, forward, until they could both hide in an alley and– breathe.

“Hieronymus,” was mumbling Audata, voice breathless, clutching at his shoulders now, hands cold like icy claws. “Hieronymus, they called him Phainon– and he has white hair–”

“What are the chances that they meant another Phainon, who has white hair and incidentally has golden blood?” gasps Hieronymus, because suddenly, breathing feels way too difficult for his overwhelmed mind.

Audata, instead of answering, lets out a slightly-unhinged laugh and falls to her knees.

—

With a tangible lead, they got their final destination easily: Okhema, the Holy City.

They had already heard much about the biggest city in Amphoreus, the one where legends themselves were born and where unlimited riches and power shone like the dawn on Kephale’s back.

And so, it was quite understandable that two humble farmers from the outskirts of the world felt… pretty nervous when the overbearing silhouette of said city started peeking from behind mountains and hills, like a glittering mirage. Countless people followed the winding paths, whispering amongst themselves, talking about rumors and news and their plans in the city.

Hieronymus was quite surprised to realize that they were only two more in the endless wave of people that came to the Holy City seeking answers. When conversing with a  large family on the road, they soon learned that they were not alone in their mysterious ‘nap’ and the following amnesia. It put everyone on edge, apparently, which was… not surprising, either.

“We’re going to the city to seek an audience with Lady Goldweaver,” said one merchant, gesturing to his own family. His smile was wry as his gesture moved to encompass everyone around them. “As I’m sure the rest of these travelers plan to do, as well.”

So, they were merely two more travelers in a long procession of confused citizens seeking answers from the so-called demigods and heroes.

Or, well– answers would be nice, yes, but Audata and Hieronymus’ actual objective was and would always be finding their son. Finding their son’s dear friend.

It would probably be more difficult than they had thought, however, as they soon found out when they finally stepped foot in Okhema, the Holy City, the now-called city of refugees, the last bastion of the Flame-Chase and Amphorean civilization itself.

(Which was weird, because as far as Hieronymus knew – which was probably less than most people, seeing as they didn’t really leave their small village and merchants and messengers were few and far between –  Amphoreus hadn’t fallen. Yet. There were more city states still standing… right?)

The city was beautiful, a marvell, a masterpiece, a perfect balance between gold and white, riches and humility, brimming with people, guards stationed at each corner, their eyes sharp and careful but willing to lend a hand to whoever needed it.

They were led – as the rest of the travelers by their side – to temporal inns and offered rooms in people’s houses in one part of the city, their guides apologizing profusely for the lackluster attention they could offer them all. Too many people at once, they said. Understandable, they said, with what had happened.

Hieronymus wondered what had actually happened.

Still, they soon realized their newest problem.

“How are we going to find Phainon in such a big city?” asked Audata, rubbing her eyes, sitting on their temporary bed, looking that much older. The worry that had weighed on her all these days had made the first vestiges of wrinkles around her eyes to become more pronounced, had made her paler, had made her frown a lot more than usual.

“Well… they mentioned that he was a Chrysos Heir, right?” he mentioned – as if they didn’t already know as soon as he bled gold. “He’s… probably with the rest of the Chrysos Heirs? They are pretty important, so… I don’t think he’ll be that difficult to find. Now, getting to him, on the other hand…”

“Oh, right. They don’t… know us. Probably.” And Audata frowned, again, and Hieronymus had this urge to smooth her frown away with a finger, like he always tended to do when Phainon got frustrated with an assignment from school. “We still don’t know what happened. Nobody knows.”

“They mentioned that Lady Goldweaver would make an announcement about that, didn’t they?” he thought outloud, thinking back to the whispering grandma’s that had lagged behind them while they walked through Okhema. Then he paused and tried to grin, like so many times in the past, when everything seemed much more simple, when they were still in Aedes Elysiae’s gentle gold embrace. “Who knows, maybe we can ask her directly.”

And that– finally managed to get a small smile from Audata. After days and weeks of traveling, of worry, of listening to unfounded rumors that could be true or false, but that always painted a worrisome situation and past – past? – for their kid… A small smile felt like a blessing. It made Hieronymus long for that moment when their little family could come together once again, and they would get to go back home.

(Even if there was a paranoid voice at the back of his mind that reminded him that maybe, just maybe, the Phainon they’d find was… different from the smiling and bright child they remembered.)

“For now… I think we’d best ask around for more information. About what happened, about these heroes everyone keeps mentioning, about…” and he trailed off, feeling more of that doubt sneak up on him and clutch his heart with icy claws.

Audata grabbed his hand tightly, anchoring herself or maybe anchoring him.

Hieronymus didn’t hesitate to cling to her just as tightly.

Chapter End Notes

Holy shit??? I didn't expect this many people. At least, not with only one chapter. Thank you so so much for the support!!
I'm a bit sick so sorry if something sounds weird. Also (I don't remember if I've said it before??) English is not my first language. Constructive criticism is welcome, but only if you're not being a dick about it.

chapters.title: Chapter 3: Audata
chapters.html:
They got to work the very next day.

They had saved plenty of money over the years, but when all is said and done, farmers weren’t usually that rich. They had to hurry.

Easier said than done, though.

Okhema was a bustling city that seemingly had no end. To two country bumpkins, the Holy City seemed to spread farther than even their golden fields of wheat, an infinite forest of white houses and elegant tapestries and bridges and people and more people–

It was overwhelming.

Hieronymus and Audata stuck close together, afraid that the never-ending waves of people rushing through the city would drag them away from each other like stray boats in the middle of the sea. 

Things being what they were, trying to find information in this manner was less than ideal. The city was chaotic after days and weeks of confused people flooding into it, seeking answers and aid for their respective towns and villages. Most city states had sent their own representatives – who didn’t hesitate to announce themselves as such, elbowing the ‘poor farmers’ out of the way – but smaller towns and isolated villages had sent their own people, with their families, because how could they even think of separating them when no one knew what had happened?

Alas, real and concise information was hard to come by, and the rumors they could catch were similar to what they had already heard on the road: that the Chrysos Heirs of Okhema had fought for Amphoreus and won, that a Deliverer – or was it two Deliverers? – had ushered in the dawn, that suddenly there was a sun over their heads and night approached with different stars.

No names, no timelines, nothing concrete that would help them understand what was happening and what would happen from here on out. In any other moment, Audata would have felt nervous and worried, but knowing that her son wasn’t by her side anymore, she could only feel a deep sense of frustration and impatience. It was a mother’s instinct, after all – she needed to see him, make sure he was alive and okay.

Hieronymus and her split off at some point, trying to cover more ground.

Audata talked to the kind grandma that always watched the horizon with a wistful smile and so she learned of Kephale’s sudden disappearance.

“We could see the towering silhouette of the Titan all the way from here,” she said, pointing to a suspiciously empty horizon with her crooked finger. “He protected us until the very end. Right now, that’s where the sun rises.”

Audata talked to the guards loitering around the area where most of the visitors from all around Amphoreus were made to stay.

“We know as much as you do,” sighed one of them, terribly young. Audata tried to imagine Phainon this young, with the same uniform, wielding a real weapon, and then regretted it almost immediately. “We’re also hoping for the Council to make some sort of announcement, or something.”

Audata talked to the kind-eyed man who usually handed out free food for the more humble visitors with his wife.

“I’ve heard that Marmoreal Palace is a bit overwhelmed by the situation right now. Why, they’ve even closed the baths. Everyone loves the baths! They only closed them once before, when–” And then the man closed his mouth, a strangely confused look passing through his eyes, as if he had forgotten what he was about to say. “Mm, I don’t seem to remember when the last time was. But, what I can say is that they better get a hold of themselves and tell the people what is going on, before they start breaking into the Palace. If the Chrysos Heirs really did save Amphoreus, the last thing they deserve is for crazy people to disturb their rest!”

Audata accepted the warm bread the man offered her with a trembling smile, before she hurried off.

They didn’t know much, but what they did know made her heart squeeze painfully and her mind conjure up possibilities she didn’t like to dwell too much on.

“Please, Titans, I know I’m not your fiercest and most loyal believer, but if you still exist right now… Please, let our son be okay.”

After another day of little to no progress, Audata felt tired and discouraged.

“There are just… too many people,” she said, her voice a small mumble, really, leaning against a building as she fidgeted with the simple bowl of broth the usual couple had handed out to everyone in the agora. “We can't possibly ask everyone in this city.”

“No, that would be a lost battle,” sighed Hieronymus, standing over her, his own food ignored in his hand as he looked around at the numerous families strewn around the agora, under the tall arches of the buildings and colorful fabrics hanging over their heads. 

From what she could see, most of these families were feeling the same; a few of the groups were arguing with each other, frustration clear in the way they frowned and gestured around at the mess of people stuck in here with no answers. Some of the families were talking of going back to their homes. Others pointed out that they were there to ask for help with the rebuilding of their towns and villages in the first place. Everyone was lost, with no answers, no explanation, no help and no guidance.

They were all in the same boat, thought Audata, though their aims were different.

Not for the first time, she turned to look at the towering silhouette of Marmoreal Palace. Even in the orange tones of dusk, it stood firm and untouchable in the horizon, watching over Okhema, just like a guardian would.

If what the people of Okhema said was true, then the revered Chrysos Heirs lived there. Which meant that it was likely for Phainon to be there as well.

Audata sighed – so close, and yet so far.

If they were younger and more reckless, they would have shaken off all hesitation to rush to the Palace and force their way in, as far as they could, in search of their son. And if they were stopped in the way, they would have fought back and demanded to see Phainon, anyway. But– what could two farmers even do, against the most powerful army in Amphoreus? No, they had to be smart about this.

Even if it meant living with this anguish, this worry, for another day. And another. And another. Until they could reunite under this new sun.

“Audata,” called Hieronymus, tapping her shoulder lightly. Audata blinked, finally looking away from the Palace to frown at her husband. Hieronymus nodded to the other side of the agora, shoulders tense. “Look.”

Audata followed his gaze until she saw a weathered soldier waving a hand in the air to get everyone's attention. He was flanked by other warriors, all of whom bore red and blue colors, and who garnered suspicious glances from the travelers closest to them, as if they expected the guards to up and arrest or attack them. Most of these people were from the countryside, remembered Audata; they probably weren't used to seeing so many armed warriors without the subsequent trouble associated with them.

“Silence, please. I will only say this once,” said the man, and his voice projected all around the agora, commanding and firm.

Immediately, everyone fell quiet – though a few children whispered amongst themselves and a baby wailed, before the mother hurried to shush them – and looked at him, waiting. 

The man made sure that he wouldn't be interrupted with a heavy glance around the agora before he continued.

“Lady Aglaea, the Goldweaver, will speak at Marmoreal Palace tomorrow at Entry Hour Hour. She will explain everything that has happened and what the plan going forward will be. We are aware that a lot of you have come here seeking aid and answers. But please understand that Amphoreus has just gone through a world-ending crisis and that, now that we're safe, there are other priorities that must be addressed first.” He paused for a moment, letting his words sink in. “After Lady Aglaea’s speech, we'll open proper channels for communication and aid, but I must emphasize – we no longer have the Titans’ blessings and Amphoreus finds itself at the start of a new era. Therefore, empathy, cooperation and patience will be our most useful tools from now on.”

The plaza remained silent and shocked, even as the man nodded in a clear gesture of farewell, before he turned around and left, followed by his soldiers.

Audata found herself speechless, too. So did Hieronymus. They stared at the place the man had just been in, eyes distant, numerous puzzle pieces finally slotting together to form a complicated picture that was still too hard to understand and believe.

Slowly, the whispers started again, and then the conversations, and then the conjectures and theories and worry. Audata heard some angry words here and there, mostly frustrated, worried that the aid they needed would come too late.

Hieronymus placed a hand on her shoulder, and when she looked up at him, she saw a new glint in his eyes - determination, a new objective.

“We can get answers,” he said, pointed, almost excited. He grinned down at her. “Now, then. We should go rest. We have to get up early, if we want to get good seats.”

A new objective. A new hope. Answers.

Audata took Hieronymus' hand, finished off her food and nodded.

—

Even arriving hours early, they still found a pretty sizable crowd outside the Palace’s waterfall-like gates. 

Once again, it was overwhelming how many people there were everywhere, compared to their little village where smaller groups of people were the norm. They stood to the side because of that reason alone, staying close to the sides while still being able to see the top of the stairs, where most of the gazes lingered, waiting for the Lady Goldweaver to appear.

“She would be… like Phainon, right?” she mumbled, mostly to herself, as she fidgeted with her worn sleeves, feeling inadequate, not for the first time. There were more people like them, of course – humble, wearing clothes of lower quality, with the hardened hands of laborers – but a good portion of the crowd was clearly from the city, with their colorful and expensive clothes and accessories and cared-for hair and beards. “A Chrysos Heir.”

“That’s what they say,” mumbled back Hieronymus, stretching his neck so he could see over the guards stationed by the stairs, guarding the Palace with their heavy stares and sheathed weapons. “Though, it’s a bit difficult to imagine someone this important looking like… Phainon.”

Audata knew what he meant. It was unlikely that someone with the reputation of the Lady Goldweaver would look even remotely similar to how they remembered their child – clothes in disarray, with wheat in his messy hair, hands always dirty from his adventures in the fields, crooked smile on his face.

And that only reminded Audata that their dear child would probably look very different from what they remembered. The shock she had felt when looking at a calendar weeks before they came to Ohema had been cruel and sudden, like a bucket of cold water. More than ten years, just like that. A long, long nap, and suddenly, their son was away in the richest city of Amphoreus, revered as– a Deliverer? Like Cyrene’s cards? Audata still couldn’t wrap her mind around it, and neither could a lot of people, because they kept arguing about it in the streets, in the inns, in the bars.

Answers. They were there for answers. And a chance.

So, Audata tried to keep herself still and waited for a flash of gold to finally appear from the Palace.

Slowly, the area filled to the brim with countless Amphoreans who whispered among themselves, who looked around with nervous glances, who waited.

Audata tried to take a grounding breath. Hieronymus grabbed her hand and squeezed, trying to calm them both down. Audata didn’t know if that accomplished anything, but all thoughts soon came to a halt as all soldiers suddenly straightened, firm and unshakable.

Something gold glittered under Amphoreus’ new sun, thin and flowing. Audata frowned, trying to get a better look at it – was that a thread? – but then Hieronymus pushed against her with a sudden breath and Audata’s eyes moved immediately to the waters parting and– to the silhouette that stepped outside.

Lady Aglaea, the Goldweaver, was draped in finery and gold. She stood proud and firm at the top of the stairs, and her mere appearance was enough to make everyone present fall silent. Her dress was adorned with jewels, her head was crowned in gold. And yet, when she looked down, Audata had the sudden thought that her eyes weren’t really seeing them. They were distant, slightly unfocused and, most of all, exhausted.

Lady Aglaea was a golden mirage, but beneath the golden splendor, Autodata couldn’t help but glimpse loud echoes of struggle and exhaustion. She carried it all with grace, and even though Audata didn't know her personally, she couldn’t help but wish for Aglaea to take a moment to rest, even as Amphoreus drowned under chaos and confusion.

“Amphoreus, I stand here, today, as the spokesperson for the Chrysos Heirs.” Her voice carried, cutting off everyone that even dared open their mouth to complain and yell their displeasure at her – they never got to, as her heavy and sharp gaze rove over them like a sharp sword. “First of all, I’m sure most of you are here seeking answers about what has happened. I’ll be brief – Amphoreus has ushered in the Era Nova, and thus, a new dawn opens before us. But this dawn didn’t come without sacrifice and loss. Even though we stand here today, Amphoreus still has a long road ahead until everything is as it once was centuries ago, when this land was unmarred by the Black Tide.”

At this, whispers spread around the people – everyone knew of the Black Tide and how merciless it could be, the wars it brought and the devastation it left behind.

Hieronymus’ hand clenched around Audata’s.

“I know all of you would like nothing more than to return to your past lives, but I must ask for your patience and collaboration. Amphoreus can’t stand back up on its feet if its people aren’t ready to support each other and work together to reach that tomorrow that is now so close to our hands.” Aglaea’s words fell on them like heavy weights – and yet, some of the richer people grimaced. “Therefore, let’s all join hands. We’re working on the necessary plans for rebuilding Amphoreus to its past splendor, so, please, from tomorrow onwards, if you have any inquiries or requests that demand our attention, you can head to a special branch of the Palace to state your needs.” Lady Aglaea paused, before she took a step back and gestured for someone else to come forward. “Castorice, if you would.”

“Yes, Lady Aglaea,” came the soft voice of another girl, and for a moment, Audata’s heart stopped when she saw a flash of something similar to pink behind Lady Goldweaver, before her hope shattered into pieces. That was not Cyrene – her hair was violet, her face was too fine, her eyes too different from blue. “Starting tomorrow, we’ll–”

After that scare, Audata found herself drifting away from her words, instead taking note of the finely-made dress this girl – Castorice – wore, her neatly folded hands. She had a heavy presence, she thought. Softer than Lady Aglaea’s, but just as imposing. As if they were looking at… gods.

But Phainon was also one of them, right? And Cyrene? And they were human, too. They weren’t gods. They laughed, they cried, they had bad ideas that usually backfired on them.

So, Audata looked closer, because if these people were truly gods, then Phainon would be too, and somehow, that image was too alienating, too wrong for her to accept it just like that. There had to be something more, something…

Human.

And then, Audata finally saw Lady Castorice’s folded hands shaking, the soft blush on her cheeks, the slight hesitation each time she took a breath and had to continue her speech. The poor girl was nervous, speaking in front of so many people.

Somehow, that made Audata let out a sigh of– relief. And she smiled, because now that she had started seeing signs that maybe, just maybe, the untouchable Chrysos Heirs that everyone in this city treated like gods, something other, were in the end just as human as the rest of them, she could finally breathe easy.

Audata saw Lady Aglaea cross her arms on her chest, before she seemingly found a loose thread and didn’t have quite the time to hide her displeasure. She snapped it off and then looked at Lady Castorice with a glance that Audata was quite sure was fond and full of encouragement.

The Chrysos Heirs were just as human as the rest of them, she realized.

Somehow, that simple confirmation came with relief and happiness and...

“Audata?” called Hieronymus, a bit worried. 

Audata shook her head with a small smile.

Maybe it was because she felt lighter after that speech - that didn’t really shed much light, at least for them – but after the two Chrysos Heirs were done, Audata dragged Hieronymus after her as she rushed forward, elbowing her way through the crowd until they could reach the stairs. The guards were pushing people away, annoyed by their attempts to reach the Palace and yelling that it was still off-limits for everyone.

That lightness she felt faded a bit at that, replaced by frustration once again, coupled with more bitterness. Hieronymus grabbed her shoulder, yelling at her over the crowd, telling her that they should leave before they were trampled to the ground or arrested.

Audata huffed, annoyed, and looked up– just in time to meet the thoughtful gaze of Lady Castorice.

Their eyes met and something passed through Lady Castorice’s eyes – something that could have been surprise or intrigue.

Audata didn’t have time to dwell more on it or react, because Hieronymus dragged her off, yelling angrily at another man that pushed against them.

Still, those eyes, a soft pink, stuck in her mind for the rest of the day – gentle, so gentle.

—

(“Is something wrong, Castorice?” asked Aglaea when they were safely inside Marmoreal Palace's peace and quiet once again. 

“Oh– no, it’s nothing, Lady Aglaea. It’s just…” Castorice trailed off, feeling a bit silly. After all, it had just been a strange feeling, like looking at someone you knew a long time ago, but whose name she couldn’t remember anymore. “It’s nothing.” It was probably the fault of their still-overwhelmed memories, probably, so Castorice smiled and gestured for Aglaea to lead the way. “Let’s just focus on what matters now. There’s much work to be done.”

“Indeed,” agreed Aglaea, but her gaze lingered on Castorice as she walked off to continue her duties, considering and thoughtful.)

—

Lady Aglaea’s speech didn’t really give them any new information, but it did confirm the myriad of rumors that they had been hearing everywhere in Amphoreus.

Era Nova… it sounded hopeful and brilliant, but in reality, it seemed to be a bureaucratic nightmare for the ones in charge. Audata didn’t envy them at all, especially after seeing people’s reaction – the yells, the frustration, the threats – until the Chrysos Heirs’ words were finally understood in their entirety.

Hieronymus and Audata hurried away from the Palace before the crowd dispersed, making their escape to the city of Okhema proper, now visibly more empty. That simple fact was a welcomed development, thought Audata, taking a deep breath and letting herself be led by Hieronymus’ firm hand as they wandered the streets without the overwhelming chatter and pushes of dozens of other people around them.

“So… we don’t really have that many answers yet, right?” she sighed, mostly to herself, but Hieronymus heard her anyway and hummed.

“Well, I’d say that ‘not many’ is better than nothing,” he said in the end, turning to smile at her. “If it comes a day when we can’t wait anymore, well– we know where they live.”

“If it comes a day, he says… as if that day wasn’t a few weeks ago,” she replied, smiling slightly in return. Then, she sighed again and stopped in the middle of the half-empty plaza to run her hand through her hair. “What should we do now? Continue asking around? Try to get in contact with some Chrysos Heir so we can ask them about… about Phainon?”

Hieronymus hummed again, thoughtful. He turned to look at her and place a hand in her arm, gaze looking around them as if the people lingering by the streets would give him a sign, guide them to their son, no questions asked.

And then he froze, eyes widening in what could only be shock.

Audata felt worry climb up her throat once again, grabbing her husband’s arm with her own cold hands.

“Hieronymus? Dear? What’s–?” she asked, trying – and maybe failing – to sound as calm as she could, because, while Hieronymus looked shocked, he didn’t look fearful.

Hieronymus cut her question off turning her around to follow his gaze, still locked on one of the walls surrounding the plaza, the only one which glowed a warm gold–

It was a mural.

Audata could feel her breath catch in her chest, cold like frost, as her eyes trailed the golden lines and struggled to make sense of them, finding faces, weapons, long capes and–

She recognized Lady Aglaea’s golden wreath in her curly hair, the cascade of gold that was her dress, hands pointing a sharp sword to the side in clear defense of the other silhouettes by her sides.

She recognized Lady Castorice, hair long and bone-like, stance graceful, dress turning into a swarm of butterflies as it flowed behind her and her scythe.

She found other silhouettes, then, people she didn’t recognize. And yet, it was clear as day that they were other Chrysos Heirs: a lion-manned man brandishing sharp claws and ferocious roars at invisible enemies, another man embraced by tree roots and one starry eye, a girl with curly hair who raised her hands to hug the skies, a cat-like woman in the middle of her sprint behind a glittery coin, a man with Dromas-like horns standing protectively with a lance, a girl seeking cover under an umbrella, a small woman ready to place the last chess piece on the board, a woman who played music with her blades, three young children with joined hands.

But in the middle of it all–

A traveler from afar, brandishing a feather against destiny.

And–

A woman with long hair, bow ready to shoot the sky, a halo of laurel around her head and a too-familiar feather in her hair.

A man, with immense wings at his back and a halo of jagged light behind his head, hair as messy as always, pointing a broadsword to victory.

“That’s…” she whispered, but her voice failed her and so she could do nothing but stare and stare and feel cold.

“It must be,” mumbled Hieronymus, and his hands on her shoulders clenched until it was more painful and it all became real.

Those had to be both Phainon and Cyrene.

Those– those were the children that had disappeared from home and who they had been trying to find all this time and who were now– adults. 

Heroes. 

Changed. 

Because they had clearly changed. A lot. And maybe Audata had been naive, thinking that Phainon wouldn’t… wouldn’t have changed that much? She had been naive and stupid, then, because of course he would have changed after years apart, where time stopped for them but continued on for Phainon and Cyrene, unrelenting and merciless.

It was stifling, because now she had very real and very concise confirmation that, indeed, whoever they would find when they next met their son wouldn’t be the innocent and dreamy child they remembered. And that– hurt. It hurt in a deep and consuming way, because with every rumor that passed by them, with every trace they found, it became more and more real. And what was more terrifying, if not reality itself?

And yet, she needed to look past it. She needed to accept it. She had already known that her child would be different, now this was just another nail in the coffin. Cruel and heavy, but it was the truth nonetheless.

So, she walked slowly to the mural, dragging Hieronymus with her, and looked at the face of who was definitely her son.

He still had those rebellious strands of hair that always stuck up on the top of his head, she noted with a trembling smile. She still remembered it like it was yesterday – because for her, it was – how she used to fight with his hair every morning before Phainon rushed off to school, Cyrene laughing in tow, only for those strands of hair to be back to normal when he returned for dinner.

She choked on a teary laugh, raising a hand to caress the sharp angles of the painted-Phainon’s cheek.

And it hit her, then, eyes moving from his vaguely drawn face, eyes alight with determination, to the thorned halo, the pair of wings – just how much had he been through?

“What happened to you, my sweet child?” she whispered to the wind, looking for more familiar details from his childhood and finding... none.

And that was just another sword stabbing her heart.

She turned to Cyrene, then, and though the young girl didn’t have something as outlandish as wings, Audata still found strangeness and a weird sense of otherworldliness in her, as if this Cyrene was just a reflection of herself.

“What have you lived through?” she mumbled, then, and somehow, that made it all heavier, even more real. It gave sound to her worry and sadness and–

Oh.

They had lost so much time, hadn’t they? Time where they could have been together, time where they could have seen these children grow up and–

And Audata crumbled under it all, after weeks of blind faith and hope, finding only a stark and cruel truth – her children were all grown up, they had lived through something they could never even begin to understand.

All alone.

They had been all alone.

And so, Audata sank to her knees and wept.

She wept for her son, she wept for her son’s kind-hearted best friend.

And she wept for the time they would never get back.

Chapter End Notes

Audata: *sees that fuckass ahoge* that's my son???
Also, just in case: the reunion is still a bit... far away. Because apparently I can't stop yapping. I'll need to change the chapter count soon *long sigh*.

chapters.title: Chapter 4: Hieronymus
chapters.html:
Chapter Notes

Holy shit I didn't expect this much support for this little fic?? Thank you!!! *discreetly ups the chapter count*

It took them a pretty long time to calm down and get a hold of themselves. 

Audata kept crying on-and-off for nearly an entire hour, and Hieronymus could admit quite readily that he had been too shocked and in denial to actually process much of what he was seeing, before it all crashed down on him at once like a pile of wood and threatened to suffocate him.

Because suddenly, the mural that had depicted a stranger turned into a mural that depicted his son.

And that was crushing, because it took the image he had of his son and ripped it to shreds mercilessly, it plunged him into the cold sea that was reality until it drowned him, it stabbed his heart like a sword made of ice.

The Phainon he remembered was a young teen with a wide smile and a mischievous streak that looked at the future with trepidation but also excitement and curiosity. A child of the golden wheat fields, who spent his days helping out on the field, playing and practicing with his sword.

This Phainon was– he was a stranger. 

And he knew that it was a bit unfair, maybe even stupid, to judge from a simple mural, an interpretation that someone that might not have known Phainon had made, but–

Wings. A halo. Firm and strong, pointing his sword at the sky, gaze made of steel. The last time Hieronymus had seen his son, Phainon hadn't even been able to keep his sword stable for longer than half a minute!

And Cyrene- she had a bow now, and a halo, and long hair and she was taller. Hieronymus had been able to pick her up without throwing his back only a few days before- only, it was longer than that. It was years. Of course she had finally grown up. She was probably a priestess, just like the priests in the village had wanted, right? But also a Chrysos Heir, apparently, and how did that even work?

(They were heroes, now. But not those from the hero stories Hieronymus was used to. He didn't know those heroes, but he did know these children... that were now adults. And heroes.

... Oh, Titans.)

After the first hour of quiet panic and crying, more people started flowing into the plaza, so Hieronymus tried to gather his wits and grabbed Audata’s hand to drag them back to their temporary abode, back to the southern part of the Holy City. People ignored them, mostly, too busy complaining and whispering about Lady Aglaea's speech and the measures to kick-start the rebuilding process she had announced. It was probably for the best, he thought distantly – after all, it would have been quite strange to see two humble farmers run through the streets, panicked and teary. Or maybe not. What would he know about what was or wasn't normal in a city as large as this?

Even when they were finally in the refuge of their temporary room at the inn, they remained quiet and lost in thought. Hieronymus was sure that Audata was struggling with the same revelations as him, but neither said anything. Maybe it was because, again, it would make it all more real. And more real, right now, meant more cruel.

“Should we even be here, Hieronymus?” asked Audata moments later, sitting on the bed with her hands clasped tightly on her lap. Her eyes, red from crying, were distant as she stared at a vague spot on the floor.

Hieronymus’ heart hurt.

“What do you mean?” he asked, as soft as he could make it, almost afraid of his wife’s answer.

“I mean– he has a different life, now,” she explained, voice so terribly empty it sent spikes of pain through Hieronymus’ chest. “I don't know what happened, but– we were gone. Probably. And he– he probably moved on, right? Without us.” And when Audata looked up, eyes heavy and yet desperate, Hieronymus left his post by the hobbling desk to hurry to her side and grab her shoulders as they shook under her sheer heartbreak. “What if he– what if we make things worse? What if he doesn't want to see us? What if–?”

“Audata,” he cut her off, firm and yet so very gentle. When her gaze finally caught his, as present as she could be under the circumstances, Hieronymus forced himself to smile through his own pain and worry. “You know our son better than that.”

And Audata's face– crumbled.

With a choked gasp, she folded forward, digging her fists against her face, jaw clenched tight and shoulders raised, and Hieronymus held her up as she gasped through the newest wave of emotions that threatened to drag her away.

It had always been like this. It was what had made Hieronymus fall head over heels for her, at first – how much she felt every emotion, how she embraced the sea of feelings in her chest. She was deeply connected with the world around her, all the people she came in contact with, and yet that fact dragged her under the waves countless times. Phainon was – had been? – like that, too. They both had people skills, where Hieronymus struggled not to put his foot in his mouth most of the time. They both felt deeply for this world.

So now, as Audata rode wave after wave of conflicting emotions, Hieronymus held her. And waited for the storm to pass, trying to gather his own thoughts.

It wasn't easy. After all, he had the same doubts as his wife.

Should they have left their humble village to embark on such a reckless and maybe even naive journey? Should they continue pursuing their son, even while ignorant of his story? Should they dig into whatever truth the Chrysos Heirs wanted to keep from the populace? 

Hieronymus didn't know about all of that, but– the only thing he was sure about was that they wanted to see their son and make sure that he was okay.

And that would have to be enough.

—

“We are going to find Phainon.”

“We are going to talk to him.”

“And we'll leave all the choices to him.”

They looked each other in the eye and laid their objectives on the table, making a promise out of them. As always, saying it all out loud made it more real, binding. It helped them stay focused as the world seemed to shift and change around them, leaving them abandoned somewhere in the way.

There was something that Hieronymus wanted to check, because the more he thought about it, the more it bothered him.

Their last memories were dated more than a decade ago. That brought to light a very… uncomfortable possibility, but a very real one. And if that possibility was the truth, then a myriad of other questions appeared. And if that possibility was the truth, then… their reunion with Phainon and maybe Cyrene would be– 

Hieronymus just needed to be sure, before they made a mistake that would hurt their son.

So, after spending much of the night thinking and overthinking this matter, he left Audata sleeping peacefully in their room and slipped away, as the sky bloomed into pinks and oranges and the streets came alive slowly. He left a short note on the door for Audata and then just– plunged himself into this new and unfamiliar world.

This early in the Entry Hour, there weren’t as many people up and about, so Hieronymus took the time to actually look around and admire just how grand and different the Holy City was, compared to their tiny village by the sea. The golden fields he was used to were replaced by white buildings and colorful banners, glittering gold decorations and tall mountains. 

It was difficult to get used to all of this, he thought, and then he wondered if Phainon had managed to become accustomed to this parallel world.

And then– he sighed and continued on his way.

He had set off early to gather more clues about the entire situation, and yet, there he was, lost in thought and longing for a past that should have felt more distant than it did. 

As it were, it was no surprise when he ran into someone and inevitably sent all the scrolls in her arms to the ground.

“Oh, I’m so sorry,” he apologized immediately, feeling all his blood rush up to his cheeks and ears. It was in these moments when he was grateful that, at least, he didn’t have his wife and son’s pure white hair that would make his embarrassment all the more obvious. He crouched down, looking at the various scrolls strewn all over the ground, clearly of very good quality. “Let me help you.”

“Don’t worry. I wasn’t paying attention while running, so it was probably my fault,” said the girl, a bit embarrassed as well but gracious enough to laugh about the accident. “Thanks for the help, anyway.”

They both gathered the scrolls silently, Hieronymus taking note of the weathered pages and detailed borders. For a moment, he wondered who this girl was, to be carrying such scrolls – they looked like they would belong in a museum, maybe, or at the very least, a library. She looked young, with pink and teal hair tied up in twin-tails and a very expensive-looking dress, but her smile was gentle and warm, nothing like those rich assholes that had insulted everything that moved up at the Marmoreal Palace the previous day.

He knew not to make an enemy of important-looking people, though.

“I’m sorry, again. I wasn’t looking where I was going,” he said, trying for a smile and probably falling into a grimace.

“Oh, don’t worry! You’re a guest, right?” asked the girl, eyes too sharp for her youthful appearance.

“Ah… am I that obvious?” he said with a small laugh and a rueful smile.

A strange look passed through the girl’s face at that, something like confusion or recognition, before it was swept away by another smile and a slight nod.

“A bit, yes. But– ah! Don’t worry, it’s nothing bad. It’s just– this look that people always have when they first see Okhema,” she explained good-naturedly.

“It is certainly… something,” he said, because he couldn’t quite come up with just a single word to describe this place and how it made him feel.

The girl’s smile widened at that and, with a short moment of balancing the scrolls in her arms, she offered her hand.

“I’m Hyacine, healer of the Twilight Courtyard and– Chrysos Heirs, technically,” she said, stumbling in the middle for some reason, and definitely leaving Hieronymus’ mind reeling at the revelation. Her smile didn’t falter as Hieronymus took her hand, mind blank. “If you ever need help with anything, you can come to me or any of my companions.”

Well, thought Hieronymus’ struggling mind, this was as good a chance as any.

“Actually… I did have a small inquiry,” he said, and then hit a blank when he found himself in the middle of a crossroads

He could either ask about this suspicion that had been festering in his mind for probably too long, a dark possibility that loomed over them, or he could simply ask… about Phainon. About where he was or how to get in contact with him or– or simply if he was–?

Hyacine’s smile dimmed slightly when he trailed off, her eyes taking on a glint that Hieronymus couldn’t quite place – it could be sadness, it could be realization, it could be numerous things, but none of them seemed to be good.

“You… are missing memories from these past years, aren’t you?” she asked, soft like a mumble.

Hieronymus startled, turning his wide eyes to her face and staring.

“How did you…?” he whispered back, but when Hyacine’s smile dimmed even more until it was very clearly something tinted by sadness, he trailed off again, feeling weightless with the realization that this girl, this Chrysos Heir, definitely had answers to one of his most-pressing questions.

“Come with me for a moment,” said Hyacine, nodding to the side, where they would be hidden by a small patio between streets. Hieronymus followed her, trying to breathe through the nervousness and worry. The next time Hyacine turned to him, she looked incredibly serious. “How many years are missing from your memories?”

For a moment, Hieronymus felt tongue-tied. For a moment, he couldn’t even remember the shock he had felt when looking at the current calendar, the year carved on the top, laughing at them from how impossible it felt. 

But now, seeing what he had seen, he was starting to realize that this was reality. 

It was time they faced it – and they were, with all the hurt and worry and pain it brought. It would be worth it, he decided, if it led them to a well-deserved reunion.

So, he licked his dry lips, tried to take a deep breath and–

“More than ten years,” he answered, his own voice feeling distant, but real enough as it passed through his throat and mouth.

Hyacine closed her eyes for just a second, controlled and yet empathetic.

“That must have been… hard,” she said, and the words felt heavy in her tongue, in the air between them.

“You know what happened, right?” he asked, voice low and careful. He saw the hesitation in Hyacine’s eyes, the words she wanted to say, but that she didn’t know if Hieronymus would be able to bear. So– “Tell me.”

Hyacine took a deep breath and left the scrolls on a nearby bench. Only then did she move closer to him to put a hand on his arm, steady and grounding.

“More than a decade ago... you died.” And those words felt like a punch to the gut, a rock falling on his head, the sea dragging him under the waves– “You were consumed by the Black Tide, then. When Amphoreus managed to complete the Era Nova not long ago, everyone that was once consumed by it was restored to their last moments, give or take a few hours or days.”

It was only because Hyacine’s hand still grabbed his arm that he didn’t immediately topple over to the ground – no, she hurriedly led him to the bench and sat him down heavily. Her hand grounded him, but not much. Even a Chrysos Heir could not make a miracle.

Dead. They were – had been? – dead. And now– revived. The Black Tide. Then that meant– merchants always talked about consumed villages, about monsters, about people lost to the tide that turned into– but–

“Breathe, sir.” And now there were two hands on his shoulders, pressing down firmly but not painfully.

Hieronymus tried to breathe. 

At first, the only thing he could smell and taste was ash and fire, and it hurt, but then it was as if his mind was fighting against the fire until all that was left was ice, freezing, unrelenting and all-cleansing.

(It reminded him slightly of Cyrene, of the strange dream that had rendered the girl confused and puzzled for days, of a god made of crystal and frost, different from Oronyx.)

He didn’t know how long he had been battling the flames in his own mind, but Hyacine was still with him when he blinked and returned to the present, chest tight and painful, lungs aching with echoes of ash and iron. Her hands were still on his shoulders, only now they glowed a soft green and white. It smelled of ozone, he noted absent-mindedly.

“Welcome back,” she said, rueful and a bit pained, but making a valiant effort to stay as composed as she could. “I’m sorry. There was no softer way of saying it. I haven’t had the need to say it much – most people seem to ignore it or make up their own excuses – but I’ve found that saying it all at once is… easier. Like… ripping off a band-aid.”

“I– thank you,” he said, mouth dry and voice raspy, as if he had been screaming for– He shook his head and immediately regretted it when the world tilted on its axis. “For telling me the truth. I–”

“It’s a lot to take in,” cut Hyacine, not rudely, but soft. “You should return to your lodgings. I meant what I said: if you ever need help, you can come to me.”

She had omitted the part that included her companions, but that was something that only future-Hieronymus would notice, later, when he was safely in their shared room at the inn and Audata was once again by his side, trying to come to terms with this new truth.

For now, he just nodded and tried not to stumble as he stood up and took a couple of shaky steps back to the streets that now felt terribly noisy.

“Truly, thank you,” he nodded gratefully to Hyacine, because even in this state of shock, it was only polite.

Hyacine only grabbed the scrolls again and smiled at him, a glint in her eye that Hieronymus still didn’t know how to interpret.

And so, they parted ways.

—

(Thoughtful, pensive, curious – cautious. This man was terribly familiar in a way that she couldn’t quite place.

She stopped suddenly, opening her mouth slightly when the thought came to her.

“Ah… I didn’t ask for his name,” mumbled Hyacine.)

—

They decided to stay in their room all day. The gruff but kind innkeeper even visited them when they missed lunch and offered them some calming tea, but they refused.

It was probably for the best, seeing as their minds were a chaotic mess. There were too many thoughts running through their minds, cruel and heavy thoughts, the kind that left the both of them dispirited and quiet.

And why wouldn’t they be? They had died. And now, they had been revived.

It put things in perspective.

That was why they hadn’t aged a day – of course they hadn’t, they hadn’t been alive to turn older, to have birthdays, to–

And no one in Aedes Elysiae had changed, so did that mean–? Of course, then it would make sense for Phainon and Cyrene to have already left the village; there had been nothing left for them, no one, no–

They had been – were? – the survivors. The only survivors. Was that because of their golden blood? How did they–?

It was already nighttime by the time they both felt strong and composed enough to step outside of their little temporary sanctuary and it was only then that they could bring themselves to eat something without puking it all out immediately.

One look at their red eyes and shaky hands and the innkeeper gave them warm broth and a few sweet pastries with an empathetic smile and words of comfort. She probably thought that they had just learned of some bad news, maybe a lost relative – and Hieronymus almost burst out laughing, because it was actually the opposite.

(They had been the ones to die.)

They found shelter on the roof and they ate their broth silently, looking up at the new stars they were still getting accustomed to. As much as Hieronymus tried, he could find none of the constellations history books had talked about.

“What are we going to do now, dear?” came Audata’s hoarse whisper.

Hieronymus took a deep breath.

“What do you want to do?” he asked back.

Audata’s grip tightened around the spoon.

“This might be very selfish but…” Her jaw trembled, but no tears fell and no sobs climbed up her chest. Not anymore. “I want to see our son, Hieronymus. I want to see Khaslana. I want to see Elysiae.”

Hieronymus let out a long breath.

“Then… so be it.”

Chapter End Notes

Poor parents, getting bombs thrown at them every day. Even I feel bad for them.

Also, fun fact: This fic was initially planned to be more comedic and funny. And then everyone (me included) started taking their issues very seriously and now... well, here we are. I can't even tag this as 'humor' anymore, even though there's some funny stuff down the line (I swear!).

chapters.title: Chapter 5: Audata
chapters.html:
Things were both harder and easier, after that.

It was hard to reconcile their present with the reality that the world and Hyacine had presented to them. It was hard to finally accept and embrace the fact that, yes, they had died, they had left people behind – their son – and they had come back with no memories of that fact, thrust into a new world in which they were still strangers. The feeling was similar to having misplaced the farming tools they used daily, to having missed a step, but so, so much more painful.

And yet, it was easier, because now they had all the answers they needed and they had chosen their path moving forward, ready to face whatever consequences may come their way.

So, now they just needed to find a way to get in contact with Phainon. Easier said than done, because apparently, the Chrysos Heirs were all over the place and even finding kind Hyacine, who had been so willing to help, was as difficult as finding the kids before dinner. And it was understandable, thought Audata, thinking back to what they had learned about the Era Nova, the confusion that spread all over Amphoreus. Managing all this chaos had to be a nightmare, and she thought back to Lady Aglaea's tired eyes and tense shoulders. She hoped the Chrysos Heirs were faring okay, but she acknowledged that they were probably drowning in work.

They had seen more of them, actually. It came as a surprise, but apparently, the red-haired triplets that they had seen various times running around Okhema were actually Chrysos Heirs too. Thousand-year-old Chrysos Heirs.
