During one of their walks to gather more information and find any way they could get in contact with their son, Audata had tried to catch up to one of the Tribios sisters, only to be left in the dust as the little girl rushed off before Audata could even open her mouth.

For now, the only leads they had were poking and prodding at the citizens of Okhema, in the hopes that one of them might have any advice on how to get in touch with the Crysos Heirs and ask for… maybe a meeting, maybe just a conversation with them.

Not that they had much to show for it, anyway. After nearly a week of running around the Holy City like headless chickens, the only thing they had managed to find was a mix of confusing and contradicting rumors about the title of Deliverer.

“How can there be two Deliverers, but also just one?” asked Hieronymus, running his hands through his messy hair for the hundredth time that morning, head on the restaurant table. 

In front of him, their worn notebook sat innocently, quiet in the face of their endless questions.

“I don’t know, either,” sighed Audata, leaning back on her seat and rubbing her eyes.

A few tables away, a group of people continued their heated discussion about that very same topic – they pointed at each other and called everyone a liar or crazy, voices rising until they turned into yells and curses. It was giving Audata a mighty headache, which didn’t really help with the worry now permanently nested in her chest. Every word out of their mouths felt like knives stabbing her chest, each a spark of pain and panic that were quickly becoming old friends.

“I’m telling you, that guy– the one you swear was actually the first Deliverer– is dead! Or maybe he didn’t even exist! He–”

“Oh, then you should go to the Twilight Courtyard, because your head is definitely cracked–”

“No, no. Listen. I have an acquaintance that works at Marmoreal Palace, and she said that the guy was in such a bad condition that it wouldn’t really surprise her if he had, y’know, passed–”

“But he doesn’t exist, anyway! I swear, you people are all nuts–!”

“That’s enough!” came an unexpected voice, finally cutting through the endless debate like a knife. Suddenly, there was a red-haired kid standing on the group’s table, hands on her hips and eyes grave and too intimidating to belong to a child as she glared up at the men that had fallen quiet at her yell.

“A-ah, Lady Tribbie–” stuttered out one of them, the one with the loud voice that had been nailing invisible nails into Audata’s head for the past half a quint.

“No. We’ve tolerated these aimless rumors long enough.” And with that, she sent a pointed glance at the group, before she crossed her arms, like a disappointed teacher. “So listen closely, and stop spreading lies. There are indeed two Deliverers – one from Amphoreus, and one from beyond the stars. Amphoreus’ Deliverer is, of course, Phainon of Aedes Elysiae, the original Worldbearer. The Deliverer from beyond the stars is the Trailblazer, one of the Nameless that helped our world.” Lady Tribbie’s eyes rove around the people that continued to gather around the now-crowded restaurant, firm and sharp. “Hear that? There are two Deliverers. Both of them are alive and recovering from a long journey. Debate over.”

And with that, her entire expression changed – though her eyes remained too sharp to be called gentle – and she smiled, waved and then hurried away from the restaurant, leaving behind a quiet crowd.

The silence only lingered for a few minutes, and then– it all exploded in whispers behind hands, wide eyes and wide gestures, surprise and shock and–

Audata took a deep breath, grabbed Hieronymus’ hand tightly and tried to remain grounded, even as a wave of relief washed over her – if nothing else, at least they knew that Phainon was alive and resting. That didn’t brush off the other worries that still stuck to their minds like cold ice, but– it helped.

“Where to, next?” asked Hieronymus, that spark back in his eyes as he closed their notebook with a quick twist of his wrist, finished his drink with a long gulp and stood up from his seat.

Audata followed suit, letting herself be led by that same spark.

“Shall we try to catch up with one of the Tribios sisters again?” she asked, thinking back to sharp eyes and eye-catching red hair and cutting words in defense of their son.

Hieronymus’ eyes sparked with amusement.

“We can very well try again.”

—

They tried. Oh, they tried.

The Tribios sisters were only three by now – and Audata tried not to dig too much on what that ‘by now’ could mean – and yet, they bounced all over the city, bearing messages, checking on all areas of the city – most of them overflowing with visitors from far away – and helping with any pressing matters that called for their attention.

They were constantly on the move, so catching sight of them was not hard. What was hard was actually managing to talk with them, stop them in their tracks and have an actual conversation with them. They saw one of the Tribios talking with a treasure appraiser – and Audata couldn’t help but think of how Phainon would have spent days and weeks holed up in that store, surrounded by relics of the past – before she darted off before Aduata could so much as take a step in that direction. They saw one of them helping the kind couple that always gave out warm food for the little community of visitors Hieronymus and Audata belonged to, but when Hieronymus hurried to their table, the Tribios sister opened up a glowing gate in the air and disappeared through the light with most of the empty boxes.

“Maybe we should start a debate about the Deliverers again, just to lure one of them out,” joked Hieronymus, but his voice was tired and his shoulders were dropping lower and lower the longer they walked up and down Marmoreal Market, now boiling with people from all over – the merchants were clearly ecstatic about this new development, thought Audata.

“If we’re going for a more daring approach, why not simply break into the Palace?” she replied, nodding to the hulking building in the distance. 

She took note of the winding paths that led to the side-entrances to the Palace, the colorful gardens that usually remained quiet and alone. Audata wondered how far they could get if they just started running straight for one of the gates – probably not far enough. After all, there were guards in every corner, as far as she could see.

Hieronymus laughed, tired and quiet but not defeated, and Audata let her eyes move from one stall to the next, too tired to keep searching for that flash of red, for wings and quick feet. Today wasn’t the day. That was okay – it hadn’t been ‘the day’ for more than a week, now. It was… disappointing, but unsurprising.

So, she eyed the stalls, took note of the fresh fruits and vegetables, the beautiful amulets and necklaces – far too elegant and expensive for them – and the mountains of scrolls and tablets. And, not for the first time, she couldn’t help but feel that now-familiar longing, that name itching on her tongue, waiting to be called – a simple “Khaslana, come see this”. Her son would love this, she knew. It was like another world, too big for them, but maybe not big enough for a child full of dreams.

Then again– he wasn’t that child anymore, was he?

She bit her lip and tried to push those thoughts out of her mind, before she spiraled down a bumpy road she wasn’t particularly fond of.

In those moments, it usually helped to distract herself with something else – maybe an interesting scroll, a tasty-looking dish from somewhere in Amphoreus they had never been to, a tapestry with vibrant colors.

Vibrant colors…

Her eyes left the fabrics of a stall when she caught a flash of pink, too familiar, too similar to that particular shade of pink that had been stuck to her son's side most days when she wasn’t napping at her swing or–

And then, Audata saw a ghost.

Little Cyrene had… grown up. That was the first thing she noticed, and it broke her heart in a very familiar way.

She was wearing a billowing dress that glittered in numerous pastel hues under the new sun, her hair was now long and flowing, its tips a vibrant teal. She was smiling at one of the merchants, sipping at a cup of tea as the man explained its origins with lively gestures.

(And yet, a distant part of Audata wondered why Cyrene felt so… detached from everything around her. It was as if she was simply interacting with the reflection on a mirror, present but not really there.)

Audata– stared at her, frozen.

Hieronymus asked her something, maybe worried, maybe just confused, but Audata couldn’t look away from Cyrene, little Cyrene, little Elysiae, now so grown up, so changed, with a different aura around her– 

And then Cyrene’s gaze wandered away from the merchant and her tea and she found Audata in the ever-changing flow of people in the market and– Cyrene froze, too.

Oh, thought Audata, distant and weirdly untethered from her own body, Cyrene’s eyes had changed color.

Yet another change.

Cyrene’s differently-colored eyes widened – and Audata couldn’t figure out if it was out of simple surprise or if there was panic hidden in there, too – and she spit out her tea back inside the cup, coughing lightly and muttering something that could have been a soft “oh shit” under her breath.

“Audata, seriously, what’s–?” was asking Hieronymus, grabbing Audata’s arm.

Audata simply nodded to Cyrene, who was now returning the cup of tea with an apologetic smile to the vendor.

(Her smile was tight and her hands shook when she tried to leave the cup on the table without spilling the tea all over it.

She was cold.)

Hieronymus muttered something under his breath, too, shaken and thrown off-guard, because as much as they had wanted to reunite with both Phainon and Cyrene, actually coming face to face with one of them and having the most definitive and dooming confirmation of just how much time had passed for the children and not for the parents was–

It was hard.

And yet, as they both hurried to Cyrene’s side, Audata couldn’t help but wonder if they weren’t putting little Cyrene – always gentle, always smiling – a bit on the spot.

But Cyrene simply waited for them, falling back into a small crevice between stalls, hands folded on her chest and her smile small and delicate. Her hands were trembling slightly, noticed Audata when they were finally face to face, and so, she didn’t hesitate to drag the girl – still slightly shorter than Audata, even after all these years – into a warm hug.

It took her a moment, but finally, finally, Cyrene’s shoulders dropped and she returned the hug with a soft and wobbly exhale.

“I… didn’t expect you…” muttered Cyrene, and her voice had changed a bit too, or maybe it was just that she was still shaky and now pretty much clinging to Audata’s shoulders. Her hands were cold. Very cold. Then she laughed, breathy and maybe a bit teary, but when she stepped back from Audata’s hug, her eyes were dry and her smile was small. “Then again, I suppose it makes sense.”

“It's so good to see you, Cyrene,” said Audata, eyes teary. She looked Cyrene over again, eyes lingering in her long hair, her eyes. “You've… grown.”

“I… suppose I have, yes.” And there was a strange glint in Cyrene’s eyes, then. Her smile was weird. 

Audata tried not to let it bother her – it was probably the disconnect expected from seeing someone she remembered as a child now grown up into an adult.

“We were so worried when we didn't see you or Khaslana anywhere in the village,” admitted Hieronymus with his usual rueful smile. “We looked everywhere for you, before we found a trail leading… here, to Okhema.”

"Ah– I suppose we should have thought about the possibility that…” and Cyrene trailed off, eyes moving away to the distant horizon hidden by the mountains. She tapped her fingers on her arms, maybe nervous, maybe restless, and Audata felt another stab of pain when she couldn't figure out which one it was anymore. “I'm sorry.”

“Don't beat yourself up over it,” came Hieronymus' assurance, coupled with a hand on Cyrene’s shoulder and she– flinched, slightly, so discreetly that Audata almost didn't even notice, but she did, and Hieronymus hurriedly retracted his hand, a frown pulling on his eyebrows as Cyrene tried to laugh it off and took a step back.

“Ah- this does bring up quite a few concerns that we should check up on,” said Cyrene, and her smile was so strange, so pinched, and it reminded Audata of how she had used to cover for Phainon when they got into trouble, back in the day, but at the same time, it was different, why? “I'm sorry, again, but I should– I'll tell one of the Heirs to get in touch with you and– I'm really sorry–”

And before they could even begin to understand what was going on, Cyrene turned and– she was gone.

In her place, the misplaced air floated lazily in front of them, cold and mirror-like.

“What just happened?” asked Hieronymus, voice a mere whisper.

There was a restless feeling climbing up Audata's spine, a weight on her stomach, cold and warm at the same time with the suspicion of–

“Did we… mess up, somehow?” she muttered, aghast.

Hieronymus turned to her, jaw clenched tight, and grabbed her hands, squeezing them and glancing at the place where Cyrene had stood just moments before, before she had simply disappeared like a ghost.

“Maybe we were too... abrupt?” he asked, but he didn't sound particularly sure about it.

Audata bit her lip and lowered her gaze to the ground. There was something nagging at the back of her mind, something bitter and cold, a glaring sign that told her that things weren't so simple. Cyrene had seemed tense and distant, running away as soon as she saw the chance, and maybe it was simply a flight response to seeing people that she had thought dead, but–

“Let's go back to the inn,” she said, heaviness making her sigh and close her eyes. “Let's… let's give her space. We need to do this right.”

For themselves… but also for Cyrene and Phainon.

—

(The air in a random room in Marmoreal Palace turned cold and sharp, a kaleidoscope of colors, before a silhouette dressed in white and purple and pink stumbled her way in, gasping and clutching her hands to her chest.

She wasn't one to panic, or at least she had thought so, but she was learning an awful lot about herself these past few weeks and being faced with the parents of her best friend, the parents that could very well have been her own, the parents that should have been dead, but who were now alive was– hard. Surprising. Shocking.

She should probably try to breathe.

And then she needed to get her shit together, because this was a variable they had forgotten to account for and which could very well make a pretty big mess.

She was fine. She was completely fine. 

She wasn't worried about Audata's sharp eyes and how she had definitely seen the changes and differences between the Cyrene she had known back in the wheat fields and the one standing in front of her. Would she be able to figure out that they weren't the same? But they were the same, weren't they? Or were they–?

Time travel and the power of Remembrance was confusing in the best of days, but in Amphoreus it was a sure way to drive someone mad.

Breathe. She needed to breathe.

So she did, she clutched the wall like a mosquito for a few minutes, froze part of it in the process, and then finally unstuck herself from it and tried to gather herself – enough to be able to explain everything without making a fool of herself.

“It's fine. Everything's fine. No one's going to panic, least of all me. I'm too pretty for that.”

Oh, they would all freak the fuck out.)

Chapter End Notes

Heh.
The next few chapters are literally the reason why this fic is longer than I expected and why the reunion between Phainon and his parents is still a bit far. That's right, we get Chrysos Heirs POV! Exposition ... that I had planned to fit into one single chapter, but that ended up being three! Also, I will explain the Cyrene situation in this fic, don't worry.

chapters.title: Chapter 6: Mydei
chapters.html:
Irontomb was dead.

Amphoreus had been dead, too, once upon a time– but it had sprouted from its seed and turned into a real, living and breathing world.

They were all safe, free, and stepping into tomorrow.

The sky was blue and they could see a real sun over their heads. And the sky turned a myriad of other colors, now, too, until they could see the real stars that had been forbidden to them before.

And yet, that was only the beginning.

Amphoreus was a mess, a newly-born world that had somehow survived a universe-ending catastrophe. People were restored, cities were (in most cases) standing again, there was no more Black Tide, but how can an entire world stand back up again?

The answer was pretty simple: with hard work.

—

The first few hours after the battle with Irontomb were spent in Hyacine’s Twilight Courtyard in the newly reformed Okhema.

Mydei patiently waited for his turn, sitting on one of the klinai with his arms crossed over his chest, eyes heavy with exhaustion and the slowly creeping realization that this was it, they had done it, they had managed to defeat Irontomb– and they were all alive.

Tribbie, who had been the one to drag everyone to get checked out, fretted around Hyacine’s first and current patient – Phainon.

“Are you in any pain? The Coreflames–” asked Tribbie, voice trembling with worry, as Hyacine took Phainon’s pulse and frowned at the thermometer.

“Most of them have been extinguished by now,” was Phainon’s answer, and something in Mydei’s chest twisted at just how terribly exhausted he sounded. Still, when he looked over at him, Phainon was smiling – small, tired, half-asleep, but alive. Fond. “You don’t need to worry so much.”

“Oh, we will worry, anyway,” came both Tribbie and Hyacine’s reply.

Phainon’s smile twitched, then, before he lowered his head in resigned and fond surrender.

Cerydra, Aglaea and Professor Anaxa were talking amongst themselves by the door, expressions grave, but not panicked, which meant that whatever they were talking about couldn’t be as pressing as another crisis or a war.

… That reminded Mydei that, if everyone was indeed restored, then he would need to check up on his people. The Kremnoans were pretty independent by now, but seeing their former leader would do the weathered warriors some good, probably, and he probably needed to talk with Krateros and apologize for cycles’ worth of stress and–

His eyelids were so heavy, though.

A good nap would do him good. He would need the strength for whatever laid ahead.

And before he knew it, he fell asleep.

—

He hadn’t been the only one, he learned hours later.

Most of the Chrysos Heirs had left the Courtyard by then, but all of them had caved to Hyacine’s suggestion of taking a nap – at least for a moment. Hyacine seemed satisfied enough by that, for now, even though she had already written enough notes to put any scholar writing their thesis to shame.

“Aglaea wants to see you,” she told him, when he finally gathered enough strength of will to sit up on the kline. The blanket that had been covering him fell to his lap. He rubbed his eyes, feeling his mind ache under the new strain of too many memories in a too-normal body.

“Are things going that badly?” he asked, nodding to the open window. The new sun – warm, so warm against his skin – shone on them, as if it was welcoming them to their new tomorrow.

“Amphoreus is pretty chaotic right now, from what we’ve seen,” was Hyacine’s rueful answer, coupled with a small smile. Little Ica nodded by her side. “Trust me, you’re better off sleeping.”

“If only I could,” he lamented, a light joke that made Hyacine huff out a tired laugh. “Have you taken your own advice?”

“Of course,” came Hyacine’s quick response. “I’m not a hypocrite.”

Mydei’s lips twitched at that, a half-smile that soon crumbled to the floor when he realized that they weren’t alone in the room. Not in the physical sense, at least.

His heart skipped a beat when he saw a nest of mismatched feathers on one of the klinai, hiding a certain someone behind their embrace. For a moment, all he could see was Phainon, surrounded by red, bleeding gold, letting them tear him apart, not even fighting back– Phainon had died, then, and with him, a part of Mydei as well. And when everything was said and done, they had both survived, anyway.

“Is he…?” he asked, a heavy weight on his chest, making it difficult to breathe, thin blades stabbing his heart.

His feet made him walk to Phainon’s immobile figure hidden under his feathery cocoon, but he didn’t dare touch him. Not if it would make this gentle dream shatter, like so many times in the past.

“He’s alright. He’s just exhausted.” And Hyacine, as always, broke through the clouds and brought light. Her hand, careful and delicate, brushed some of the feathers away, just enough for Mydei to see the peaceful expression hiding underneath. “He’s fought hard. He deserves a good rest.”

“That he does,” he mumbled, and he hoped Phainon would hear it.

Then, his eyes sought the other guest at the Courtyard, squinting against the light reflecting off the crystalline shards of ice protruding from the ground around her, the corners of her blanket covered in a thin layer of frost.

“She’s also…?” he asked, gravitating towards Cyrene’s form and having to stop by the wall of shards around her. He frowned at them, vaguely reminded of his own blood-crystals, but– not. These were much different.

“We don’t know what she’s done.” Hyacine’s voice was now cautious and worried. “The Nameless are looking into it, but– she’s alive. And technically healthy. She’s just– also asleep.”

She didn’t seem tense, at least, from what he could see. She looked– peaceful. As if she was simply dreaming. He hoped it was a gentle dream.

Mydei turned and looked back at Phainon, and then he turned and looked at Cyrene. These two– they had sacrificed everything, even their own identities, their entire beings, for this tomorrow. Maybe this Cyrene wasn’t exactly the one he had met all those cycles ago, but it was her legacy. The seed and flower she had nurtured.

(And later, when he finally learned of what she had done, he realized that the flower had simply watered its own seed all along.)

So, he took a deep breath.

“Let them rest,” he mumbled to himself. “They have stepped onto the tomorrow they’ve fought so hard for.”

And with that, he nodded to Hyacine and left.

There was much to be done.

—

And indeed there was, he soon came to learn.

Amphoreus was a mess.

And yet, it was their responsibility to fix and deal with it, as they soon pointed out to the Astral Express when the Nameless tried to stay to help – and so, threatened to abandon their Trailblaze, if only momentarily.

“This will be a years-long quest, I'm afraid,” Aglaea told them, when their discussion started to stagnate in the same arguments over and over again. “You have your own quest to attend to. Go, help other worlds as you've helped us. We can handle this ourselves – Amphoreus has weathered worse storms.”

The Nameless seemed reticent, but not offended or resistant to the idea, so they heeded Aglaea's firm words and after making sure that they couldn't do more from their side, their train streaked through the skies, leaving behind a promise to visit when Phainon and Cyrene finally woke up.

And so, the Chrysos Heirs took a deep breath and prepared to deal with the mess of a newly reformed world.

First, it seemed like everything had returned to how it was before the Black Tide came and destroyed everything. That meant that previously destroyed and abandoned cities and towns and villages were restored, though not always in the best condition – and with the citizens being none-the-wiser about what exactly had happened.

“Oh, the census is going to be a nightmare,” groaned one of the newly-appointed Council members.

To combat this wave of confusion and panic, Tribbie rallied her other selves and they acted as messengers, delivering the news of the Era Nova to all corners of Amphoreus and bringing light and hope with them. Once again, Tribios decided to offer her own self to aid Amphoreus and usher their world to the new tomorrow, even if that meant shattering herself – though, now only temporary – into fragments that could spread the good news as quickly as the stars.

“This will only give us more time, but it won’t be the solution to the problem,” reminded Cerydra, now in charge of the new Council. “People will flock to Okhema seeking answers. We must be ready for that moment.”

And just as the Imperator had expected, weeks later, Okhema’s gates were overflowing with visitors from all over Amphoreus, all of them with dozens of questions ready to shoot and petitions of aid for their little communities and neighbours.

The new Council struggled to stay on top of things – it was to be expected, after all, as Amphoreus was bombarded with change after change, revelation after revelation. Aglaea and Tribbie had chosen most of its members, making it clear that it was only temporary until a true assembly could be planned in the future, when Amphoreus was back to normalcy. Aglaea had even asked for Anaxa’s advice when choosing the professionals who would be in charge of the rebuilding and re-planning process. Something about seeing those two actually work together – though, not without their usual spats – felt terribly surreal.

“Are you seeing this too?” whispered Castorice, hands folded in front of her, scroll full of notes from the meeting abandoned on the table.

On the other side of the table, Aglaea and Anaxa poured over a map and snipped at each other.

“No, I see it,” he mumbled back, just as wrong-footed as his companion.

Finally, Aglaea sighed loudly, gathered the map in her arms and stomped away, leaving a grinning Anaxa in the dust.

“Six wins to five, Goldweaver,” he muttered to himself, terribly satisfied.

—

As the Holy City filled to the brim with each passing day, the new Council had to come forward and give aid to those who had only ventured into Okhema seeking answers or help – especially since most of those visitors were just humble families acting as representatives of their own communities.

That put things in perspective and, for a moment, Mydei wondered if that meant that he would have to worry about Castrum Kremnos suddenly filling with people overnight – but no, even though the Black Tide had been involved, he doubted that a conflict of this kind would merit a revival. Especially since, as far as they could tell, this new world was mostly based on the 33,550,336th loop, which– made sense, as that was the one the last Worlbearer had remembered the most.

Mydei decided not to think too hard about that, lest he ended up with a terrible headache. And he already had enough of those, what with him having to round up all the Kremnoan people to ask for their opinion on relocating to Castrum Kremnos, once the chaos died down.

He was met with plenty of different and contradicting answers – again, not really surprising. While the sentiment had always been that Castrum Kremnos was home for them, they couldn’t deny that Okhema was very close to that title as well. Many Kremnoans had found their matches with non-Kremnoans and most of them weren’t particularly interested in leaving their life in the city.

(He ignored the fact that he wasn’t their prince or king anymore. No one mentioned it, either.)

After days of running around like a headless chicken, talking with so many people that their faces blurred in Mydei’s mind, he finally sat down, wrote what Tribbie later called a referendum, and told Krateros to test the waters.

“Tell that weaver to keep her hands away from our heads, too,” said Krateros, before walking out of the chaotic meeting room where the Chrysos Heirs and Council members spent most of their time these days.

Mydei stared at the closed door for all of ten minutes, before he gave up on trying to figure out what his oldest advisor meant.

That matter came to the surface days later, when Hyacine entered the meeting with a frown on her face and a handful of scrolls full of similar notes.

“People’s memories are… a bit messy,” she said, careful and a bit lost. “A lot of people say that they don’t remember things that happened not long ago. Some of them remember conflicting things, like… a sister or a friend that left the village, but in reality they didn’t, but they swear they did.”

Cerydra sighed and noted it down on the long, long scroll where most priorities had been written.

—

After a week where Phainon and Cyrene didn’t wake, it was decided that they would be relocated to their rooms so they could rest without the Twilight Courtyard’s numerous patients disturbing them.

Cyrene froze part of the floor immediately, which made it difficult for anyone to get close to her without risking slipping on the ice. Still, Hyacine checked on her every night, when the new moon peeked out from behind a mountain.

Phainon only curled his wings around himself sometimes, which probably meant that he was aware in some capacity, which was… good. It took a heavy weight off Mydei’s chest. Just in case, and knowing what he had gone through, Hyacine checked on him every morning, when the sun peeked out over the horizon. 

Sometimes, Mydei spent the night in Phainon’s room, too tired to leave– or too paranoid and on-edge about anything going wrong to leave. After all, Phainon was too vulnerable like this, bundled up in blankets, capable of sleeping through the racket of a bronze jar falling and bouncing on the floor five times before Mydei could grab it. Knowing that they were safe and free was one thing, but it was different to believing it.

Safety was terribly fragile, after all.

So, Mydei soon tied himself to a new routine, one where he would visit Phainon’s room at least once a day. He would then either sit with Phainon, telling him about his day, about any new trouble they had to deal with, or he would tidy and clean the room until it was spotless and organized.

He always had work to do – after all, all the Chrysos Heirs visited Phainon from time to time, bearing get-well-soon gifts. Soon, all the tables around the room were filled to the brim with new clothes – courtesy of Aglaea, who had now made new clothes for everyone, unwilling to let the past linger for too long – and hand-made decorations – courtesy of Castorice – and numerous scrolls – courtesy of a hurried Anaxa – and curious trinkets – courtesy of the Tribios sisters and an ever-elusive Cipher. Mydei was also woken up with soft music more often than not, when he stayed at Phainon’s room to pass the night.

“You know, maybe this is good,” commented Mydei, once, reviewing another manifest where the city estates of the south of Amphoreus had banded together to ask for financial aid and materials to rebuild the only bridge that connected them to the mainland. “If you’re sleeping, you’re not running yourself to the ground trying to help all these people.”

Phainon, predictably, didn’t answer, curled on the kline with one of his wings brushing the floor.

And somehow, Mydei could still imagine the affronted look in his eyes, the sharp ‘get lost’ that Phainon would throw at his head.

He huffed a laugh.

—

Cyrene woke up after a month of sleep, but at first, no one other than Hyacine could see her. Mydei wondered why until he saw Hyacine’s frown and slightly-blue fingers one time and… he could guess. After all, no one that had gone through all of that would be feeling great.

It was a few days later when their little group of Chrysos Heirs was cleared by Hyacine to talk to Cyrene, with the promise not to overwhelm her.

“I’m fine, really,” she assured them, laughing softly. She waved her hands, placating and gentle. “I think I just– overdid it, a little.”

“What exactly have you done?” asked Aglaea, cautious and worried. “The Nameless mentioned that an ally of theirs had talked to you… and then we found you, unconscious. What…?”

Cyrene smiled, a bit wry, a lot tired. She fidgeted with the blanket covering her legs, flicking off specks of frost that still lingered. Now, after the battle, when everything was said and done, she looked– small. Lost. Like a writer that had reached the end of the story she had written and had finally realized that it was also her story.

“I made sure that Amphoreus’ future was safe,” she said, in the end, as cryptic as always.

“And that means…?” pressed Anaxa, frowning deeply.

Cyrene’s smile trembled.

“Say… where’s Phainon?” she said, instead, and there was something terribly vulnerable about her voice that made the group of Chrysos Heirs that had gathered in her room pause, cross glances and then grimace.

“He’s… still asleep,” answered Hyacine, soft and cautious, like someone approaching a scared cat.

“... Oh.” A moment of disappointment, of hurt, before Cyrene smiled again, shaky and so obviously forced it hurt. “It’s– it’s fine. I just– wanted to talk to him about something.”

They still took her to Phainon’s room, anyway, even though she couldn’t quite have a conversation with him yet.

After that, Mydei found her in Phainon’s room more often than not most nights. He tried to include her in his self-imposed tasks of cleaning and tidying, but Cyrene usually refused, wandering aimlessly around the room and looking at the trinkets spread all around with curious but distant eyes.

It was days later when Mydei decided to break their mutual silence.

“Are you afraid of something?” he asked, sitting on the bed and trying – and failing – to brush Phainon’s hair before it turned into an unsalvageable bird’s nest.

Cyrene paused.

“Maybe,” she admitted, hesitant. As if she was still insecure. “I’m not sure of what, though.”

Mydei hummed, not really surprised – though he couldn’t say why.

“Are you afraid of hurting him?” he asked, nodding to Phainon’s head on his lap.

Cyrene turned and looked at Phainon, something heavy in her gaze, both recognition and not, both fondness and not– Until the former of the two was finally chosen, definitive and unmoving.

Cyrene bit her lip and gulped down her hesitation.

“Maybe,” she said, again, and this time it sounded more breathy, softer.

“He’s stronger than we think,” reminded her Mydei, pointed. “He would hate for us to treat him like glass.”

That finally made Cyrene smile again, but instead of the forced cheer she hid behind like a veil, it was smaller, wobbly.

“That is true,” she said, and she even managed a lilting laugh.

She wanted to get closer, that was obvious. Her hands fidgeted with her dress, the ribbons around her wrists. And yet, she didn’t move. She didn't approach them.

A silent observer.

Mydei offered her a hand. An invitation.

Cyrene, of course, hesitated.

But after a steadying breath, she took his hand and let Mydei guide her to sit on the kline, side by side with them, close enough to feel Phainon’s encompassing warmth. Mydei offered her the brush, but she refused with a small smile and simply– stayed. Sometimes she hummed under her breath, sometimes she readjusted the blankets, sometimes she stared out the window, distant and quiet.

And that was enough.

Chapter End Notes

Sorry I kicked the Astral Express out of Amphoreus this quickly, but I feel like they would be a bit overkill for this plot. Everyone is already dealing with too much rn.

Next up, Cyrene POV hehe.

chapters.title: Chapter 7: Cyrene
chapters.html:
Her mind was a nest of memories.

A cradle, almost, though she couldn’t quite figure out what was supposed to come out of it when the time was right.

At the moment, her choice had been clear – save Amphoreus, make sure it couldn’t be toyed with again, make sure that ‘tomorrow’ remained available for this scarred new world.

In practice, though, things… took a turn she hadn’t expected.

Peach – Philia093 – had accompanied her through the path to the past, encouraging her to leave behind traces, little seeds that would sprout when they were needed. And when they finally reached Aedes Elysiae, that place that had always felt like home, even though it shouldn’t have, Peach – little Peach, so brave, so unrelenting – had smiled and then she had pushed her and then–

A crack in time, a crack in her mind, a crack, a crack–

Causality shattered like a broken mirror and she had gasped, because this wasn’t supposed to happen.

(But Amphoreus had sprouted, beautiful like a flower of glass, and so, the loops shattered with the yesterday that became the past.)

One became two, and two became one, and suddenly Peach was her and she was Peach and they were Philia093, but also Demiurge.

Her head hurt.

She remembered things she shouldn’t have – it wasn't her the one to give Phainon the Deliverer card, she had never ran through the golden wheat fields barefoot and laughing, a white dog chasing after her cheerfully, she had never eaten home-baked pies and she had never– but she had– but–

“We were always... one and the same–” she gasped, even though her brain seemed to want to become liquid, the sea, a river, and flow out of her ears. 

She was cold. She was so cold. And yet, she felt happy, so happy she could laugh and laugh and laugh–

She must be crazy.

She had always been playing a losing game, replaying it all, a loop, a never-ending loop with no end. She was the very flower she had watered, had nurtured, with her very own stories, over and over and–

Amphoreus had already bloomed, leaving this loop behind, stepping onto tomorrow.

“We should take a step forward too, right?” she heard her own voice, bright and hopeful.

“We should,” she breathed, and the air froze around her.

She took a step forward and there was another crack, loud in the nowhere she was plunged into every time.

One became two, and two became one, and–

The loop shattered and crumbled like an avalanche.

She couldn’t breathe, she couldn’t talk anymore, but she knew that the freezing chains she had tried to tie around herself were now melting off her skin, and so she took another step, another, another.

“Run,” whispered a voice, encouraging, full of hope and dreams and light. “Run, run, run, and don’t look back anymore. Run towards tomorrow.”

And she did, gasping through the icy crystals on her skin.

Crack, crack, crack.

One became two, and two became one, and–

Cyrene became Philia093, and Mem, and the demigod of Time, and Demiurge, and Peach, and Elysiae, and her.

And her freezing arms finally embraced all the memories that made her her, as it was her wish, her right.

Because at the end of time, she was simply Cyrene.

And she would always have her charm.

—

She woke up feeling cold and with a terrible headache that made her squint against the bright light coming from the window.

For a moment, she didn’t know where she was. Her memories were scrambled, so her sight wavered between a wheat field, a cold and towering archive, and then a colorful nebula, before she blinked hard and suddenly, there was a cozy room, with sun rays streaming down an open balcony and beyond that–

Okhema. Just as she remembered it. Bright, colorful, majestic.

“You’re awake!” came a relieved voice, and suddenly, Hyacine was next to her, looking into her eyes with clear happiness and yet the sharp attention of a healer. “How do you feel? Probably sore, but any lingering pains? Confusion? Hypothermia?”

Cyrene blinked a few times, trying to catch up to her words, and then she smiled, just like always, and sat up on the kline. Her arms trembled for a second, but she ignored it.

“I’m fine,” she said, and when Hyacine waited patiently, her smile wavered. “Really. I feel fine.” An arched eyebrow and Cyrene folded. “I just– have a bit of a headache. Too many memories, probably– I’ll sort it out.”

“Lay down again,” said Hyacine, or more like ordered. And yet, her hands were gentle when she pushed her back down. “I’ll get some water and food for you. You’ve been asleep for practically a month.”

And Cyrene– froze. Not in the literal sense like before – even now, she caught sight of half-melted ice around her – but just…

A month.

Asleep.

Had she been really asleep, or…?

She felt tired, as if she had been running for a very long time. When she tried to remember what she had been doing – because she was sure that she had been doing something – she could only remember running, leaving behind a trail of cracks and whispers in her ears that sounded like her voice, but also not.

And then came the torrent of memories – millions of them, of herself, but also not. Not her as the Demiurge, but as Peach, as Philia093, as–

Her.

She huffed out a laugh and then she couldn’t quite stop, until she was pretty much laughing hysterically, lying on a nest of soft blankets and with tons of scrolls and books she was quite sure she hadn’t bought herself littering the tables in the room like a forest of offerings.

By the time Hyacine came back, with a light breakfast in hand, Cyrene was sitting up again, hugging her legs to her chest and laughing and crying and trembling like a leaf caught in a merciless storm.

Hyacine left the tray on a random table and hurried to her side, hovering by her side with worried eyes and hesitant hands.

“Cirey? Are you… okay?” she asked, careful, so careful, like a mother checking on a child, like a bird singing a lullaby, like– Hyacine huffed. “Of course you’re not. It’s okay. I’m with you.”

Somehow, that helped, but Cyrene couldn’t quite figure out why.

She couldn’t quite describe what was going through her mind and that was… also strange. Because what was a writer, if not someone that could put feelings into words? And yet, all she could do was cry and laugh through her tears and shake like a newborn fawn as Hyacine wrapped her arms around her and tried to guide her through what was... probably a breakdown. Maybe. Could she even have those?

Was she even human, now? From Demiurge to Peach, to a demigod, to a memosprite– What was she, now?

When Hyacine left a long while later, Cyrene pinched herself and frowned at her cold and soft skin. It felt no different from how the Trailblazer had felt – real. But then again, so had the Chrysos Heirs and they hadn’t been real either, right? But they were human. But also– not.

Cyrene – because she would always be Cyrene, the pen name she had taken up in that golden wheat field, the one that encompassed everything that she was and wasn’t – took a deep breath and forced herself to smile. She was fine. She had– broken out of the loop. Yes, indeed. She was– free.

She flinged the blankets off her legs and stumbled her way to the balcony, breathing in deep and squinting at the bright sun peeking from behind Okhema’s tall mountains and spires.

Amphoreus was saved. They were all real, whatever that made them. And she– she didn’t need to remain trapped in the loops, anymore. She could simply– exist.

The next time she smiled, her lips held in place, even though tears streaked down her cheeks again.

—

Truth eventually came to light, and even though she tried her hardest to brush over whatever she had done to end up sleeping for a month, the Chrysos Heirs were too sharp and used to avoidant strategies and turns of phrase to let her be – not without getting to the bottom of it first.

She was doing so well, leaving her words vague and her explanations too broad, until… the extra page she had hidden in As I’ve Written was placed in front of her. Her own written prose stared at her and talked of a hard choice that would safeguard Amphoreus, though at the cost of her tomorrow.

And after that… well, weaving stories was her specialty. 

If this one turned out to be a bit too messy and too short as words failed her for the first time… the Chrysos Heirs were too busy processing the fact that she was, for all intents and purposes, still the same Cyrene they had walked along with on their first Flame-Chase Journey. Technically.

When all was said and done, they welcomed her back, warm and inviting and–

And Cyrene didn’t know what to do with that.

So, for the first few days after waking up in the ‘tomorrow’ they had fought so hard for, Cyrene holed herself up in her room, alone and isolated.

But as tempting as it was to read all the scrolls and books she had been gifted by the Chrysos Heirs and the Nameless, and as nice as the quiet in her room was, and as helpful as riffling through her own memories was to try to get a firm understanding of who she was – or could be – now, she soon came to learn of a few strange consequences that had come about after Amphoreus sprouted from its seed.

The most pressing one was the fact that some people had conflicting memories about the same events. It probably had to do with the Eternal Recurrences, she soon decided, and while having a cause was helpful, it didn’t really solve the issue.

So, she shadowed Hyacine as she went about her duties as a healer, hoping to come face to face with people that had the same problem.

“I think you’d have more luck going to the city, Cirey,” said Hyacine the third day, smile rueful. Cyrene, who had been absorbed by a scroll detailing historical facts that seemed to be the official truth for this newly-born world, looked up and tilted her head to the side. “I’m just saying… people with that problem don’t usually come here anymore.”

Cyrene’s smile froze on her face for a moment.

“Ah, but going to the city would be– I can’t very well just shout it out and hope that someone will answer,” she said, voice light and airy. Cheerful. She could do that, easy. She was fine.

“Mm, that is true,” nodded Hyacine, a troubled look passing through her face.

Now, that wouldn’t do.

“Don’t worry! I’ll think of something,” she said, waving a hand in the air. She almost sent the rolled up part of the scroll to the ground, where it would certainly keep rolling and rolling until it reached a wall. That simple act made Hyacine huff a small laugh – that was better. Cyrene winked. “After all, memories are my thing.”

Even as she said that, her hope of finding a sure-way of fixing the problem started dwindling as the days passed and she found– nothing. She did find where the problem stemmed from, of course – indeed, it was simply a big knot of memories from the Eternal Recurrences – but figuring out a way to fix it, now that Amphoreus was real and tangible, now that these people were amassing more new memories, was– difficult. Almost impossible.

She could reweave the memories of the galaxy to recreate it anew, but she couldn’t unmake the knot of memories that confused so many people – not without cutting some ‘threads’, that is, and somehow, sacrificing memories that probably meant something to those people– it didn’t feel right.

“Don’t overdo it,” advised Trinnon, voice as soft as always. “You don’t have to overwork yourself, not for this.”

Cyrene flicked away frost from her nails, trying to be as discreet as she could, but even then, Trinnon caught her movement. Cyrene smiled, trying for something cheerful like always, but it fell a bit remorseful.

“I’m sorry,” she said, just because she felt like she had to.

Trinnon squeezed her cold hands, silent, but understanding.

—

Her mind, her sense of self was... a bit of a mess, if she was being honest, which she tried to be, at least with herself, at least when she was back in her own room – hers, her room, full of her things, her books, her scrolls, a new feather and glittery ink she hadn’t managed to bring herself to touch yet – alone and… vulnerable.

She was Cyrene. She would always be Cyrene. But she was also Demiurge, someone that learnt love from Peach, someone that had been the Trailblazer’s companion, their memosprite, Amphoreus’ heart. But she was also someone that had turned into the first ever Philia, the lament left behind as a seed, and she was the someone that Philia had grown into, the someone that had taught love to Demiurge, which was also… her.

It was confusing. She didn’t know where she started and where she ended. She was like Amphoreus: a loop.

And when the loop shattered and crumbled– what was left? What did that make her? What–?

She wondered if Phainon would understand. After all, he had gone through something– not exactly similar, but similar enough that maybe, just maybe–

But Phainon was still asleep, still resting, and Cyrene understood perfectly why Mydei especially gravitated to him, like a moon to a planet, a planet to a sun.

(Cyrene’s memories were clear now, after riffling through them countless times, as if she was reading a book. An observer to her own life.

And she would never forget Phainon, tired and exhausted and as willing as always to sacrifice himself for a tomorrow, even if that sacrifice entailed letting them kill him, shatter his body–)

She had done the same, unconsciously. She wanted to talk to him, ask him questions–

(“Am I still Cyrene to you?”)

Or maybe just– spend time together. Like… old times? She remembered long afternoons in the fields, running through the gold and then climbing trees and then trying to sneak into Pythias’ office to check the questions in their next test and–

But other than spending a couple of hours wandering and snooping around Phainon’s new room as he slept, she– mostly kept to herself. She read more scrolls, more books, stared at the ink and the feather left on her desk and reached out with a hand, before she remembered something or other she had to do and hurried out of her room.

Some days, she holed herself in her room until Parting Hour, reading and shuffling through her memories, trying to slot the pieces of her very own puzzle into their correct place. Some days, the silence in her room was too heavy, too reminiscent of the Demiurge Matrix, of the Path Space, echoing and yet so bleak and blurry it made her hands shake, as if the book she was holding up was simply too heavy for her. Those days, she wandered around the Palace, taking note of the overworked Council members, the guards, the other Chrysos Heirs that floated from one place to the other.

She was still a ghost, she realized then. Silent, smiling, a benign spirit that watched over them, recorded their stories–

One day, though, Tribbie’s hand found hers and Cyrene startled, blinking down with wide eyes. Tribbie simply squeezed her hand, just like Trinnon had done, and looked up at her with sharp eyes.

“Don’t isolate yourself anymore, Reney,” she said, firm and terribly heavy. Cyrene, as always, twitched her lips up, a smile, optimistic and– Tribbie tugged on her hand. “C’mon, there are too many scrolls to sort through! You’re good with scrolls and books, right? You can help us archive them!”

Cyrene, caught off-guard, let herself be dragged off by the first demigod.

And, hours later, as she helped the triplets sort through mountains of scrolls in the Palace library, she paused and realized– ah, she felt more present than ever.

And so, she existed.

—

Phainon woke up more than half a month later than her, just as quiet, just as unassuming.

Cyrene found out about it hours after the fact, but when she did, she crossed a glance with Tribbie over yet another mountain of scrolls and Tribbie nodded at her with a gentle smile and Cyrene– disappeared in a flurry of crystals.

She appeared outside of Phainon’s room, silent and soft, but even then, she managed to startle him when she opened the door. She grimaced, smiling guiltily when Phainon placed a hand on his chest, trying to calm his poor heart. It had indeed suffered enough.

“Sorry, sorry, I just–” and for once, Cyrene found herself lost for words.

Phainon, blue eyes tired and smile crooked, stood from the triclinium he had been sitting on, surrounded by the various gifts the Chrysos Heirs had left him over the weeks, and gestured for her to follow him out to the balcony, where the sun still watched over them, a bright embrace.

She sat down on one of the benches, fidgeting with her dress, her hair. Once again, she was awfully conscious of the frost clinging to her nails.

Phainon plopped down on the same bench as her with a soft sigh, eyes a bit unfocused, hands tightly fisted on the blanket around him – maybe he felt cold, now that he didn’t have all those Coreflames consuming him from the inside. Cyrene, just in case, shifted away, taking the cloak of freezing air with her.

They remained quiet for a long moment – Cyrene running through countless ways to start the conversation she had wanted to have for weeks, but coming up short, Phainon looking to the sky with a distant gaze, detached and tired.

Finally, it was Phainon the one to speak up.

“It feels unreal, doesn’t it?” he mumbled, soft and painfully emotionless. “When I woke up, I– panicked. I found myself back in Okhema, back in my room, and I thought–”

“That you were back,” finished Cyrene for him. She took a deep breath, let it out slowly. She lowered her gaze – the sun felt too heavy. “I know the feeling. I–” And she bit her lip, clenching her hands tight around her dress. “Do you… see me as Cyrene?”

Phainon blinked for a moment, slowly coming back to reality, like a bird landing softly on a patch of dewy grass. He stared at her, she could tell. His gaze was old and heavy, now, like the sun over their heads. But– also gentle. Warm.

“What do you mean?” he asked, tilting his head to the side.

Cyrene opened her mouth, closed it, and then her lips twitched into a half-hearted smile – not her best, she was sure. She stood up, one of her feet wobbling on her high heels, and turned to leave.

“Nothing, it’s– I shouldn’t–” she stuttered out, and where had her eloquence gone? Teacher Pythias would have been so disappointed that one of her best orators and storytellers had fumbled this so badly.

She took a step, but a hand closed around her wrist, gentle and cautious.

When she turned back, Phainon’s distant gaze was more present, more real. It bore into her with a sharp glint, a spark of realization, of– recognition.

“Would you tell me a story?” asked Khaslana, soft and patient, tilting his head to the side just like he had done when he was a young boy.

And something twisted in Cyrene’s chest, then. Proof that she existed, maybe. Evidence that she was just like that girl with ink-stained hands, waiting for a shooting star, with a deck of cards hidden in her bag. Memories, like the waves against the rickety dock of the village, gentle and parsimonious, rocking her, him, them.

“Of course,” she answered, voice wobbly, smile trembling on her lips.

And so, she did what she did best: tell stories.

Only, this time, she told her own.

She talked of a cage, of a girl that described a journey of loss and hope, of happiness and love and flowers.

She spoke of a change, a shooting star and a final penstroke.

She tried to narrate what happened after the story’s ‘big bad’ fell and it was then that her words faltered, trailing into a backwards tale, a gardener spreading seeds, rain watering small buds, a girl with pink hair looking at a flower and realizing that the flower was simply– her.

It all ended, as it were, with a golden wheat field… and a crack in the glass, from where she managed to escape.

After the last written period, they both fell quiet.

The Palace was calm, with no bathers and no visitors, no ruckus, no festivities. Only the wind rustled the vines creeping around the balcony, and only the sun moved through the sky.

And then– a laugh, tired and stilted, but genuine.

“We’re both a mess, aren’t we?” said Khaslana through his huffs of laughter.

“We really are, huh?” said Cyrene – or was it Elysiae, now? – smile falling more into ruefulness.

They both laughed softly, weak huffs of laughter that reminded her of the past, when they were young children that always managed to get into trouble.

The following silence was easier, like a gentle blanket over their shoulders, warm soup after a cold day of hard work at the fields.

“How are you holding up?” asked Khaslana, eyes now tracking the sun as it moved through the blue sky.

“How are you holding up?” shot back Elysiae, sending a pointed glance at him and his slumped posture. It reminded her– it reminded her of how he had been after a full week of sickness, back… back home.

(She was reminded of an awful lot, now.)

“I asked you first,” shot back Khaslana, arching a knowing eyebrow at her, and even though his lips didn’t twitch, she still knew that he was amused.

“I asked you second–” she tried, too hopeful.

And then hit a wall when Khaslana sent her a pointed look, eyes tired and– something she couldn’t quite place.

Elysiae smiled, but somehow, it was harder to bring it up in front of him. Maybe it had something to do with him knowing her better than others at this point. Maybe it was simply in her head.

“I'm alright.” She looked down, at her cold hands, so clean, no ink-stains in sight. She hadn't touched a pen or feather in– a long time. “Really, I am. I’m okay. I’m…” A deep breath that rattled on her chest. It caught, like a fish biting the bait and ending pierced by the hook. Her smile trembled, but she didn’t really notice. “I’m perfectly fine. The sun is really warm here, everyone is– so nice, there are so many great books to read, so many people to meet…”

Her hands were shaking, she realized, but they seemed awfully blurry too. Why?

There was something cold running down her cheeks, down her chin, but it was only when it finally fell on her hands that she realized that it was–

An arm wrapped around her shoulders, warm and gentle like the sun, but firm and real, like the wheat that once ran through her fingers. She was trembling hard, she noticed a bit distantly. She couldn’t quite unclench her folded hands on her lap. She couldn’t–

She couldn’t quite keep her smile in place.

“I’m perfectly fine, I swear,” she said, but her voice sounded twangy and thick even to her own ears. She sniffed, finally raised a hand to rub at her teary eyes. The arm around her tightened, then, and it only managed to make a sob escape through her lips – she couldn’t keep her smile up. Not anymore. “I… I’m–”

“We’re alright,” mumbled Khaslana, and it felt distant, like an echo, just as unreal, like a dream. He didn’t sound like he believed it either, but–

But maybe, saying it out loud could make the both of them see the new tomorrow they had survived to witness and be a part of.

Chapter End Notes

The 'Cyrene is a paradox' thing is pretty tight in canon, so I had to improvise. I just want Cyrene to feel whole and have (technically) her childhood memories back. It's confusing, so just in case: Amphoreus became real, the causality loop was completed, and because the past remained in the past, Cyrene could slip through the cracks.

Next chapter: Mydei time again! And so, we come back to the 'present', finally.

chapters.title: Chapter 8: Mydei
chapters.html:
Having Phainon awake was… freeing. But also, a new worry, because as relieving as it was to see him open his eyes and smile at Hyacine as the poor healer fretted around him like so many times in the past, it was still clear that Phainon was struggling under the weight of... well, everything.

And why wouldn’t he? No one could imagine what he had gone through, all the suffering and pain he had carried for millions of cycles – but they could guess, based on their own experience, and those guesses were enough to make them feel cold as ice.

It wasn’t as bad as it could have been. Their words of encouragement and support in the Ruins of Time had helped a lot. Tremendously, really. At the very least, their assurances had seemed to get it through Phainon’s thick head that the Chrysos Heirs didn’t hate him or wish him any ill will or nothing of the sort. Which was good, because the last thing they wanted was for Phainon to have to doubt even something as fundamental as that when dealing with… everything else.

That said, Phainon was still having a hard time.

“It’s like… I’m here, but also not?” tried to explain Phainon one night, eyes locked on the stars visible outside his balcony. He still kept his wings out some days, curling them around his own shoulders like a makeshift giant feathery blanket – he felt cold and distempered every time he remembered that he didn't have the Coreflames consuming him anymore, he explained when Mydei nagged at him enough. “I feel like… I will wake up one day, and I’ll be back in the cycles and I’ll have to do everything all over again and that– that terrifies me, Mydei.”

Mydei could only hold him in his arms, pressing him tight against his own body, trying to ground him into this new tomorrow he had sacrificed so much to reach.

He couldn’t punch his problems away, that was the problem. They lived in a new era of peace – hopefully – and that brought along the realization that now… they had a tomorrow to look forward to. In the past, everyone had preached about the Era Nova and the prophesied future it would bring, but most of them had known and accepted the fact that it was very possible that they would never get to see it with their own eyes. And now–

Mydei held onto Phainon and Phainon held onto him and, together, they tried to step into tomorrow and not crumble under its weight.

(It was during one of those nights, when their new moon was high up in the sky, when Mydei tried to keep them from falling apart when reality felt too real, that they finally said aloud what in many cycles had been impossible.

Eternal partnership, called it Mydei.

Phainon huffed a tired laugh and joked that it sounded like a business deal.

Mydei bit him.)

Striving forward and leaving the past where it belonged was easier said than done, though. The road to recovery was a long and arduous path, but one that all of the Chrysos Heirs were willing to walk together, as a team, like always. All of them struggled in some capacity, after all. The past was a heavy weight for all of them, countless memories of millions of cycles looming behind them like shadows. Mydei still had to remind himself that he didn’t need to wear his full armor for daily matters – not anymore. There were no more Black Tide outbreaks, no more surprise attacks, no pressing conflicts. He still trained, of course, as routines were helpful, per Hyacine’s words, but he didn’t see the need to push himself as hard as before.

(It was strange to train mostly alone, with no Phainon riling him up into nonsensical challenges or a long chain of spars.)

He was also aware of how much the other Chrysos Heirs struggled, too – particularly Cyrene herself, whose isolation during the cycles haunted her even now. It didn’t really surprise him; after all, no one would get out of such a hell unscathed, no matter how powerful.

So, when Phainon started wandering Marmoreal Palace’s halls, they all kept a close eye on him. He was still tired and drowsy most of the time, taking hours-long naps and becoming adept at finding the best patches of sunlight to lay on. Mydei usually found him by the gardens on both sides of the Palace, now off-limits for the people of Okhema.

“You’re going to get a sunburn,” grumbled Mydei once, frowning at Phainon’s pale skin and poking him on his side and getting a sharp slap for his trouble.

“But the sun is so warm,” mumbled Phainon, eyes closed and looking the most at peace Mydei had seen him, surrounded by colorful flowers and comfy cushions and his backlog of unread scrolls from countless lifetimes.

Mydei looked up and squinted at the blue sky.

“That it is,” he said, and then plopped down next to Phainon to spend the next half an hour basking in the sun as well.

And yet, Phainon still had what Hyacine called ‘bad days’. On those days, it wasn’t unusual to see Phainon wandering the halls with a distant and unfocused gaze, like a ghost, looking disoriented and confused when someone inevitably found him and tried to redirect him to a safer place. The first time it happened, Mydei panicked hard enough for Aglaea’s now more relaxed threads to notice and his panic soon dragged everyone into the same frenzy, until they finally found Phainon staring blankly at the place where Kephale had once stood.

“Dissociation,” explained Hyacine, once again surrounded by countless medicinal scrolls and with her hands stained with ink.

Which basically meant that, sometimes, Phainon would just– leave his body. Move on autopilot. It wasn’t dangerous, per se, only a bit… uncanny. Worrying. But also understandable, after everything that Phainon had gone through.

Giving Phainon something to do usually helped, though.

“A speech?” asked Phainon, frowning down at the messy notes that had been written during their latest meeting with the new Council. He quickly read them and then his eyes lit up with understanding. “Ah. I’ve heard about it. Are there really that many people in the city?”

“I’ve heard that the inns are bursting with people from all over,” nodded Mydei, coupled with a sigh. He arched an eyebrow at Phainon – it had been a couple of days from his last dissociative episode, which meant that he was getting better. Hopefully. “So, it’s your time to shine, Ten Times Debate Champion. Make it so that the people at the speech don’t try to murder Aglaea.”

Phainon’s mouth twitched into a grimace, clearly remembering something unpleasant, but then he shook his head and hummed, considering and interested.

“When is it?” he asked, voice a bit distant and distracted, but not so distant that Mydei should worry – it just meant that Phainon’s mind was already boiling with ideas.

“Tomorrow,” said Mydei, and immediately, Phainon turned to him with pinched eyebrows. Mydei sighed again and leaned back on the bench they were sitting on. “I know. It really snuck on us.”

They had almost forgotten about it, in fact. Word had reached them about a possible revolt in one of the city states to the West of Amphoreus and Cerydra had almost jumped to arms, before Aglaea reminded her that they were in a time of peace and raising weapons now would end badly for everyone involved. The last thing they needed was a civil war.

“I’ll… try to finish it today,” said Phainon, and with that, he started scribbling in a spare scroll, ignoring everything around him. Good. It would keep his mind off… other things.

—

Phainon had always worked best under pressure, so it surprised no one when Cyrene delivered the finished draft of the speech that very night.

“He’s sleeping now,” she said cheerfully, her smile softer than other times, which meant that she had spent most of the afternoon with Phainon, probably helping him finish the speech. “I’ve already looked over it – a few times, in fact. It should do the trick.”

As Aglaea reviewed it with tired eyes and tense hands, Mydei hung back with Cyrene, relaxed.

“You’re both closer, now,” he noted, shooting a pointed look at Cyrene.

She paused, hands behind her back, her satisfied smile falling into a considering frown.

“I… guess we are,” she said, hesitant and careful. Her next smile was a bit crooked, a bit rueful, a bit longing. “We’ve been… talking. Hanging out. Reconnecting, I guess you could say.”

“Is it easier now?” he asked, pushing softly.

After all, it made his heart ache. These two were childhood friends, best friends, and they even had to sacrifice that for a chance at tomorrow. The riff between them could be mended with time and care. They deserved better. They deserved a happy ending. They deserved their bond back.

“I… think so,” said Cyrene, and her smile was genuine, now, if only a bit small and wobbly.

That was enough.

The very next day, Phainon dragged Mydei to one of the gardens to make sure that the speech went without a hitch. Mydei rolled his eyes when Phainon started reciting the speech under his breath along with Aglaea and then Castorice, down to the pauses they did between words and their intonation.

“How many times did you revise the final draft?” he asked, knowing.

Phainon sent a crooked smile his way, rueful and resigned.

“Enough for it to not make sense anymore,” he admitted. “Cyrene had to read the final, final, final draft because I didn’t know what I had written anymore.”

Mydei cackled and hoped that the people at the entrance to the Palace wouldn’t hear his echoing laugh, lest they thought they were being laughed at or that the Palace was haunted.

—

“You’ve been lost in thought for a while,” commented Mydei, arching an eyebrow at Castorice. “Something wrong?”

Castorice startled slightly, almost poking herself with the knitting needle. Mydei grimaced, but Castorice sent him a smile and shook her head with a small huff of laughter. The half-done scarf on her lap had remained untouched for all of five minutes, in which Castorice had been staring listlessly at the ground, lips twisted into a thoughtful and confused frown. It reminded Mydei too much of Phainon’s now-too-common vacant gaze, so he didn’t hesitate to try to snap her out of it before it was too late.

“It’s okay. I was just thinking,” said Castorice, as soft as always. Her hands moved once again, counting the stitches she had left halfway, moving the small lantern closer to her work.

“Are the petitioners giving you a hard time?” he asked, thinking back to the yelling crowd Castorice and Aglaea had left after their speech. He understood the frustration and helplessness the citizens probably felt, but he also knew what was going on behind the scenes and how hard finally stepping into tomorrow was, so he only hoped and wished that their people could be more empathetic and patient.

“Mm, could be worse,” said Castorice, as diplomatic as always. Her hands finally resumed knitting, practiced and careful.

“Then… what’s bothering you?” he asked, a bit confused.

Castorice’s hands faltered for a moment, and Mydei almost took back his question.

“Have you ever… seen someone that you felt you had seen before, but that… you couldn’t remember ever meeting?” she asked, stilted and hesitant, as if she was trying to put a strange feeling into words and getting lost on the way.

Mydei frowned.

“I can’t say I have,” he admitted, feeling a bit regretful at not being able to help her find the answer she clearly needed.

Castorice hummed, before shaking her head again.

“It’s okay. It’s… probably nothing,” she said, with a small insecure smile. 

Mydei’s own answering smile was dry – famous last words, those.

—

It all started when Cyrene, who usually stayed with Phainon during their bureaucratic and boring meetings to keep him occupied and not doing something stupid, opened the door and promptly froze half of its surface in less than a second.

The room fell silent.

Everyone looked at her, eyes wide.

Cyrene looked at the door with equally wide eyes, surprised, and slowly retracted her hand from it. She closed it with her heel instead, but it didn’t close all the way and remained awkwardly ajar.

“Whoops,” mumbled Cyrene, before she turned to them with her usual smile and– there was something wrong.

“Cyrie, why don’t you sit down?” Hyacine pretty much ordered, moving one of the klismos towards Cyrene.

Cyrene turned to her and her smile widened, and it was then that Mydei took note of how pale she was – more than usual – and how frost covered her nails and how she was fidgeting with her bracelets with shaky fingers.

“I’m alri–” she tried to say, but Hyacine rushed to her side with a saccharine-sweet smile, grabbed her arm and dragged her to the klismos, ignoring how her own fingers turned slightly blue from Cyrene’s cold skin.

“I insist,” she said, and then, sat Cyrene down at the table.

Cyrene didn’t really complain, which said enough on its own.

Cerydra, as quick-witted as always, slammed a hand on the table and the Council members and advisors that had been staring and wrangling mountains of paperwork all jumped to attention.

“Everyone not a Chrysos Heir, out!” she ordered, firm and sharp.

Immediately, they all rushed out of the room, dragging some of the paperwork with them or just leaving it abandoned on the floor or table. It took less than a minute for the room to empty out, leaving their little group of Chrysos Heirs alone with a maybe-panicking Child of Anasrava. 

“Is Phainon okay?” asked Mydei first, because last he knew, Cyrene had been hanging out with him at the empty gardens. 

“Oh, Phainon is perfectly okay. I actually went to the market to find the tea he mentioned, a very strange blend that I’m quite sure he’s made up to annoy me and–” And Cyrene paled again, her smile trembling for a moment.

“Cyrene?” called Aglaea, careful and soft. “Did something happen at the market?”

There was an edge that Mydei was very familiar with in Aglaea’s voice, words cutting like her threads, tense and ready to give the order to apprehend whoever had the guts to bother one of them and leave them this shaken.

Cyrene laughed softly and rubbed her eyes, folding forward, and it sounded normal at first, before they all noticed how shaky it really was and– 

She was actually half-crying and half-laughing, and when she looked up at them with a trembling smile that never seemed to falter, her gaze seemed overwhelmed and lost.

“I’m probably overreacting, but…” She took a deep breath that rattled in her chest. “I saw Phainon’s parents. Here. At the market. We talked. I– pretty much ran away as soon as I could.”

The room fell silent once again.

Mydei’s mind stumbled on itself and fell into a chilling silence. All thoughts and worries he might have had dwindled into nothing until all that was left was a void.

The first one to recover from the shock was, of course, once again, Cerydra, who cleared her throat and looked around for a moment, before she frowned at Cyrene, who was trying to clean her frosty tears from around her eyes and cheeks.

“Weren’t they dead?” she asked point-blank, as direct as always.

Some of the Chrysos Heirs flinched, Castorice most of all, while others retreated into their own thoughts – Hyacine was one of them, which was curious, but Mydei didn’t get to wonder too much about that.

“They were,” nodded Cyrene, letting her hands fall to her lap and lowering her head. “Not… anymore.”

“The Black Tide,” breathed Professor Anaxagoras, lips twisting into an interested smirk. “They were remade, restored to their last moments. We’ve seen other cases like this.”

“Yes, we have,” mumbled Hyacine, still lost in thought and gradually returning to the present, eyes lighting up with realization, and why would she–? “I… think I’ve met Phainon’s father.”

For the third time, the room fell quiet.

“You… have?” asked Cyrene, and for once, her smile crumbled, surprised. She shifted on her seat, gesturing with her hands. “Blue eyes, same face-shape as Phainon, tan? A bit awkward when first talking with him?”

“Yes, exactly!” nodded Hyacine, hands grasping at the table.

“I… think I saw them once, too,” mumbled Castorice, eyes locked on the table but unfocused, lost in her own memories.

Mydei was reminded of what she had commented that one time, about feeling that someone was familiar but not knowing why. It… made an awful amount of sense, in hindsight.

There was another beat of silence between them as they all processed what had been said and finally understood the giant mass of trouble that careened towards their precarious peace.

“Are we… going to tell Snowy?” asked Tribbie, hands fidgeting with a stray scroll. Her lips twisted into a grimace and her eyes shined with concern. “Somehow, it doesn’t seem like a great idea right now.”

Mydei… didn’t know if he should agree to that. Phainon was still recovering from an extremely traumatic event that no human would have survived, he was struggling with his shattered mind and trying to make peace with everything that had happened. It seemed cruel to keep his parents away from him, but… would it only hurt him? Would he want to see them? Would he–?

“Cyrene? What do you think?” asked Aglaea, tapping a finger on the table, no doubt drafting countless plans in her mind for whatever agreement was reached during the next few minutes.

“Huh?” Cyrene jumped, straightening out from her slump, eyes wide and surprised again. She pointed her finger at herself, confused. “Me?”

“Yes. Also, Mydei. Both of you are the ones who spend the most time with Phainon currently,” nodded Aglaea, sending sharp glances at the two of them. “Do you think he would be… willing to see his parents?”

Mydei struggled to find a definitive answer.

“I’m… not sure,” he admitted.

He crossed a glance with Cyrene, full of worry and doubts, and once again, he found a kinship with her that he hadn’t expected.

“I think… we should give him more time,” she said in the end, once again fidgeting with her bracelets.

Give Phainon more time to process everything, more time to find himself in this new tomorrow, more time to regain his strength, more time to–

They could do that. Probably.

Trianne jumped on the table, then, grabbing one of the scrolls with a wide grin that usually meant trouble for everyone involved.

“So… Operation Distract Snowy’s Parents is a go!” she announced with a loud cackle, writing said name on the scroll and presenting it to their group with a flourish.

A beat of silence in which Tribbie sighed, Aglaea closed her eyes, Hyacine and Castorice exchanged dry smiles, and–

“No thanks,” said Cipher, before promptly leaving the room with a flash.

Mydei stared at Trianne’s scroll, a foreboding feeling in his chest.

—

Cyrene had apparently told Phainon's parents that one of the Chrysos Heirs would get in touch with them later, so by the time Mydei managed to run away from the meeting room, the group that had stayed – Aglaea, the Tribios, Hysilens and Castorice – was trying to think of a plan that wouldn't blow up in their faces.

Mydei felt like a wraith walking down the hallways – weightless, light-headed, thoughts too loud but also too soft, like whispers but also screams.

How could he go back to Phainon, look him in the eye and not tell him that his parents were in the city, looking for him? The same parents that Phainon had mentioned only sparingly, with that deeply sad glint in his eyes, that painful smile that had always made Mydei want to punch a wall or hug him for an hour, resigned and yet longing for a past that would stay gone.

He would have to lie to Phainon, or at least not tell him the truth – was this truly their best option?

But he remembered Cyrene, sitting quietly at the meeting, gaze distant and lost, hands still half-covered in frost. She was shaken, she had run away from the pair of humble farmers, panicking and freezing everything in her path – Cyrene, who had stood against a universe-ending threat with a smile on her face and who re-created the cosmos when they failed.

Mydei felt something just as cold as her ice spreading through his heart – how would Phainon react, then? Phainon, who sealed a demon with his own regret and shattered memories. Phainon, who still faltered, even now, free, who still struggled to make peace with everything that had happened and how it had changed him and what it had made him do.

Phainon, who now remembered his parents’ millions of deaths.

Maybe they had made the right choice. Maybe they hadn't. But Mydei felt that it was something that was better left to those involved – and in this, Cyrene was the one who should have the loudest voice.

(He wondered how he would react to seeing his family, his friends. His memories of past cycles were chaotic, but he could still make sense of most of them, and the differences between cycles were sometimes so stark that it was difficult to reconcile them and tie them to the same people, the same names.

Would he avoid them, too? Would he awkwardly let them get close again? Would he run to them, hug them?)
