His feet led him to the gardens, and for a moment he wondered why, mind still stuck in that meeting room, but then he saw a flash of white and blue sitting on one of the benches, with his usual mountain of scrolls by his side.

And like a fool, Mydei walked over to him.

Phainon greeted him with a smile that looked a bit pinched and worried eyes that glanced behind Mydei, searching for something– or someone.

“Have you seen Cyrene?” asked Phainon, a bit hesitant, stumbling on the name. “She ran off to the markets to find a type of tea – that definitely exists, by the way – and I haven't seen her again. Is she–?”

Mydei’s brain short-circuited for a moment.

“I think Tribbie needed her help with something,” he said, and then almost hit himself over the head – that was so obviously a lie it hurt.

And yet, Phainon blinked, tilted his head to the side and then smiled.

“Ah, I suppose that makes sense,” he mussed to himself. Mydei blinked, like an idiot. “After all, they do work together in the library. Which reminds me– I should go there to take a few more scrolls. I’ve already read through this batch–”

Oh, that wouldn’t do. After all, Cyrene was probably trying to get a hold of herself alone in her room and freezing her surroundings in the process. And Tribbie was actually still in the meeting room, trying to think of a plan that wouldn’t bite them all in the ass.

A clump of words choked Mydei, and for a moment, he was terrified of opening his big mouth and telling Phainon the thing he mustn’t hear. Instead, his mind scrambled for something, anything that might take Phainon’s ever-active attention away from the library.

“Do you… want to go to the baths?” he asked, stilted and terribly awkward.

Phainon turned to him with an arched eyebrow and an amused glint in his eye.

“Oh? Have you been spending too much time with Aglaea?” he asked, teasing and light, but his eyes were a bit too heavy for Mydei to be thrown back to the past when everything seemed more straight-forward. “What brought this on?”

There’s no one at the library right now, but you can’t know that, screamed Mydei’s mind.

Instead, he forced himself to groan and roll his eyes and turn around to walk back into the Palace’s peaceful hallways.

“Maybe I’m just trying to learn how to relax,” he said, and it could have been a self-burn in any other moment, but now, it made Phainon pause where he was stuffing the collection of scrolls he had already read through into his bag.

“Yeah, I suppose we all should, huh?” he mussed to himself, and his eyes got that dangerous glassy look that Mydei now hated with a vengeance, so he opened the door with probably too much force.

“Are you coming or not?” he called back.

“I’m coming, I’m coming,” came Phainon’s more present answer, and soon, Mydei could hear his long steps rushing to his side.

A flash of red caught his gaze, so he offered to carry Phainon’s bag. Predictably, the stubborn man only huffed and sped up to walk ahead of Mydei.

Mydei gave Trianne a thumbs-up behind his back.

—

“You know, I’ve been thinking…”

Mydei probably slammed the door to Phainon’s room too hard, startling at Cipher’s unexpected voice next to him. He sent a slightly disappointed glare at her and almost admonished her – for making him slam the door when Phainon was now resting, and for probably intending to talk about The Topic near the one person who shouldn’t learn of it. But she only grinned and followed him as he walked down the hallway, hands behind her back and eyes glinting with amusement.

“I thought you weren’t interested in this… task,” he grumbled, thinking back to how fast she had escaped from the meeting room.

“Oh, I’ve been… talked into it,” she admitted easily enough, which was probably Aglaea’s doing. It was just as well – having the Trickery demigod would do wonders for their plans. “But this is something else. Say, little prince, are you and the deliverer boy a Thing again?”

Mydei stumbled on air and turned to her, a frown pulling at his eyebrows that only made Cipher’s grin widen.

“A ‘Thing’?” he asked, trepidation clear in his voice.

And oh, he had made a mistake.

“Yes, well, I don’t know what you Kremnoans call it, but in Dolos it was something like… a couple, or boyfriends, or even– married? I seem to remember something about a ring, but y’know, these things change a lot depending on the city state you’re in,” rambled Cipher, grin turning sharper and sharper the longer she talked. “for example, the nerds at the Grove of Epiphany liked gifting poems and essays about–”

“If you’re here to get content for more rumors and gossip, I’m leaving,” cut Mydei, with a tired sigh, speeding his steps. But, of course, Cipher was nothing if not fast herself.

“Oh, don’t misunderstand. I’m just wondering, well– The deliverer boy’s parents would be your in-laws, then, right?” she asked, completely oblivious to the cosmic bomb she had just thrown to Mydei’s head. “Do you guys give– I dunno, gifts or something?”

Mydei stopped in the middle of the hallway.

Cipher, who didn’t notice immediately, walked a few steps forward alone, before she caught his still figure and blinked. And then, she laughed, loud and terribly amused.

“What? Don’t tell me you didn’t even think of that, little prince,” she said between cackles.

Mydei stared at the too-clean floor, his blurry reflection, eyes wide in cold realization and maybe horror.

He hadn’t thought of that, actually.

He really hadn’t.

It made sense, thought a distant part of his mind. Of course, a few of his own selves in the cycles had once dreamed of introducing Phainon to his mother, sometimes to his father, when he hadn’t been driven mad by prophecies. In some of the cycles, Phainon had even admitted that his parents would have loved him.

Now, all of that felt– terribly real.

Oh, no.

Oh, fuck.

Shit.

How did in-laws work? What did he need to do? Should he–? It wasn’t as if he could ask Phainon, or Cyrene – he would send the poor girl into another nervous breakdown, and she already had enough on her plate with her own identity crises.

The only answer he had to that was Cipher’s loud cackles and his own sense of doom.

Chapter End Notes

Some of that original humor! ... Hopefully. Someone help Mydei. Also, will this decision blow up in the Heirs' faces? We’ll see.

chapters.title: Chapter 9: Hieronymus
chapters.html:
They returned to their room at the inn feeling defeated and wrong-footed.

Both of them were lost in thought and quiet, cutting through the loud life of Okhema like ghosts. The receptionist, already used to their changes in mood after the various bad news they now collected like ancient artifacts, simply took a look at their faces, sighed and sent word to the kitchen for some comfort food.

Hieronymus felt more and more grateful as the days passed. Maybe people from the big cities weren’t as individualists and stuck up as they had feared, after all.

“It feels as if… ever since we arrived in Okhema, everything has–” Audata cut herself off, probably to avoid cursing. Instead, she sighed, loud and sharp, and let herself fall on the bed.

“Gone to shit?” finished Hieronymus, who had never had a problem with cursing – Audata had spent Phainon’s early years glaring at him to shut up before he could curse out loud and their son, who had been like a sponge at the time, could internalize it.

Audata opened her mouth, closed it, and then sighed.

“Yes,” she grumbled.

“Want to go up to the roof again?” he offered, because as loud and chaotic as Okhema was, the roofs were small pockets of calm where they could see everything in perspective – the sky opened up over them, just like it did back in Aedes Elysiae. If the new sun tilted just so, the other buildings would become tinted with gold, similar to the sprawling fields of wheat back home.

… He missed it. 

He missed the simplicity, the easy routine, the calm and security their little village provided. Aedes Elysiae was a safe haven, compared to Okhema’s lively streets, the parading merchants, the rich assholes that elbowed everyone in their path, the imposing mountains looming over them.

In any other moment, were they just simply visiting for the joy of adventure, Hieronymus was sure that he would have been able to at least– like Okhema. But now, after days of running around with desperation manifesting as a tight collar around their necks, after countless revelations and bad news that fell on them like rocks, after coming face to face with how much they had already lost... Hieronymus couldn’t wait to leave this Holy City for good.

They both escaped to the roof, the innkeeper’s comfort food in their hands.

The blue skies and warm sun shining on their faces finally let them take a deep breath. Here, it was easy to ignore the racket from the streets.

“What should we do now?” asked Audata, resigned, lost, sipping at the broth. Her eyes, glittering like honey under the sun, found the towering silhouette of the Palace, once again.

“I don’t know,” sighed Hieronymus, not for the first time, and certainly not the last.

“Cyrene… she said that she would send someone to talk to us?” continued Audata, a spark of hope in her voice.

“What are the chances that she was just bluffing to get away from us?” he asked, a bitter smile appearing on his face before he could push it down.

Audata turned to him with a slight frown, disappointed and a bit hurt. Hieronymus let his smile fall with another sigh, running a hand down his face.

“No matter what, I’ll trust in her,” said Audata, and it sounded like a bow. A promise.

Hieronymus rubbed his eyes with a soft groan. Her words made him feel like a terrible human being – of course, he knew Cyrene, and she would never do something like that, not without good reason.

Even now, they didn’t know enough. They were approaching the light, yes, but the entire situation seemed to be much more complex than they had thought, back when Aedes Elysiae’s fields still embraced them.

In those days, it had seemed simple: find the children, reunite, and go back home together.

Now, after learning of their past deaths, the fact that those two children were now heroes, demigods – maybe? – and that they were important enough to live in a Palace, finding out about the Era Nova… it was anything but.

Still, he knew better than to doubt Phainon and Cyrene. More than that, he knew better than to doubt their strength and will.

“I’ll… try to trust in her, too,” he acquiesced.

Audata hummed, mostly satisfied.

—

The sun was already climbing down the sky when a blur of red streaked through the streets in their direction. 

Audata, who had been nodding off against his shoulder, perked up with a stifled yawn, and Hieronymus frowned, intrigued and – maybe – hopeful.

“What did I tell you?” whispered Audata with a small smile as one of the Tribios sisters hurried to their roof, blue eyes finding them with no trouble.

“Yeah, yeah,” grumbled Hieronymus, rolling his eyes, but even then, he couldn’t really feel bad about being proven wrong – not on this.

They didn’t have to wait long for the red-headed Chrysos Heir to get to their roof. She flew up and up and only then did Hieronymus finally notice the pair of wings at her back. He blinked, caught off-guard, eyes wide, as the child – child? That wasn’t right – finally landed on the roof with a soft huff and then immediately turned to them with a wide and cheerful grin.

“You’re Snowy’s parents, right? I’d hate to bother the wrong people,” she greeted with, hands on her hips.

“Snowy… that was–” he mumbled, mind jumping back to the big and fluffy white dog they had when Phainon was younger. A ball of energy that could somehow keep up with Phainon’s own restlessness and hunger for adventure and stupid ideas.

“You mean– Phainon? Khaslana?” asked Audata, with a slightly pinched smile, sending a pointed glance at him.

Hieronymus closed his mouth. Right. This child was actually pretty important – she was a Chrysos Heir, even though she looked to be around ten years old. Talking out of his ass was probably not the best idea.

“Ah, right– yeah. I meant him. Sorry, old habits die hard,” explained the demigod, cheeks flushed and smile a bit dimmer.

“Don’t worry. That simple nickname has put my mind at ease, actually. You’re quite close to him, right?” said Audata, smile now much more calm and soft. 

Ah, Audata, always so eloquent. Her ability with words had already saved him countless times in the past, during tense arguments with merchants and sometimes even villagers that forgot that Aedes Elysiae was a small community that depended on each other for survival. Phainon had seemed to inherit that from her – Pythias liked to remind them that Phainon could have been a great debater and orator in the future… if only he’d applied himself and taken it seriously, instead of daydreaming about heroes and adventures.

“Yes! We are indeed!” nodded the red-head, grin wide again. “We are Tribbie, the demigod of Passage– or we were? Ah, it’s a bit confusing right now. But we looked after Sno– Phainon, back in the day.”

Hieronymus blinked, surprised once again, and then he couldn’t quite stop a smile from appearing on his face.

“You looked after him, huh? Then we should apologize – we know our kid is quite a handful,” he said, smile falling more into ruefulness.

“Oh, no, no. He was a sweet and gentle child, bright like the sun.” Tribbie shook her head, and got closer, accentuating just how short she was. “He was also very energetic, but… I wouldn’t call him a handful.”

“That’s good to hear.” And Hieronymus huffed out what could be called a laugh. “I’d like to think that we raised a well-mannered child.”

“You did, don’t worry,” said Tribbie, and even though her grin was wide and her eyes sparkled under the sun, there was also an old shine to them that finally solidified her age in Hieronymus’ mind.

“Um, Lady… Tribbie? Is Cyrene…?” Autodata cleared her throat, hands folded on her chest, her worry bleeding out into her voice. “I mean, she left in such a hurry– and we know that… their memories of us are–”

Tribbie’s gaze softened, then, and somehow, she looked even older. Centuries older. It made Hieronymus' chest ache, because she had seemed so young just moments before, but now– now her eyes gave away her longevity, the tragedies she’d seen, the losses in the way.

(Would Phainon have changed like that, too?)

“You gave her a bit of a scare, that’s true,” admitted Tribbie, voice soft as the breeze, and Audata flinched and Hieronymus reached out to put an arm around her shoulders. Tribbie got even closer, looking up at them with a slightly-crooked smile. “But don't blame yourselves. Please, believe me when I say… it wasn't your fault.”

“Is she… okay?” asked Audata, voice small and so, so worried.

“She’ll be okay,” nodded Tribbie, now more up-beat, smiling again. “She just needs a moment to process.”

Audata sighed, relieved, but when Hieronymus turned to her, a heavy question ready on his tongue, she met his gaze and didn’t look away. She wanted to ask, too. He wanted to ask. So–

“And… our son? Phainon? Can we…?” he asked, voice more and more falling into a soft murmur. A small hope.

Tribbie’s smile turned a bit rueful, and Hieronymus’ heart fell to his feet.

“That’s what we wanted to talk to you about… Phainon is currently at the Grove of Epiphany, resting,” she dropped the bomb, and yet, it was soft like a leaf falling off a tree, like the waves lapping at the dock. Audata lowered her head, Hieronymus dropped his shoulders with a sigh of defeat, and Tribbie jumped up with a half-grimace, half-soothing-smile. “But! He’ll come back soon! I’m sure you’ve already noticed, but Okhema is… a bit of a mess. Very loud! And Snow– ah, Phainon was so tired, we thought he would be more comfortable at the Grove, where he could even read everything he wanted from the Library of Philia…”

As Tribbie rambled about the Grove, Hieronymus found himself huffing out a half-laugh, not really surprised. Of course his son would love Amphoreus’ most notorious library. Of course he would take every chance to get lost in its books – especially if said library had numerous myths and legends he could get lost in.

“So, he’s still an avid reader,” he tried to joke, and he was rewarded for his trouble with Audata’s tiny smile.

Still, her gaze was heavy and tired.

“He is,” nodded Tribbie, and once again, she softened. Her eyes seemed to look right through them, deep and unfathomable, something that was the completely opposite of the childhood innocence one would expect from her appearance. “He really hasn’t changed that much from what you probably remember, you know?”

At that, they both fell quiet.

That was the one fear they hadn’t managed to quell, even after days and weeks of knowing and digging into rumors and news and the new reality that now enveloped them all and didn’t let them escape.

Tribbie’s words helped, of course, but Hieronymus knew that this fear of theirs would remain nested in their hearts, in their minds, until they could see their son with their own eyes.

Maybe Phainon hadn’t changed that much, like Tribbie had said, but– Hieronymus thought back to Cyrene, to how much taller she was now, to how her hair curled in a way they had never seen before, to her different-colored eyes, to the distance that now opened between them like a bottomless riff. They could still recognize her, they could still talk to her, but it was clear that whatever she had lived through had left its scars on her, to the point of changing her irreparably.

(Was that bad, though?)

Cyrene had changed. 

Why wouldn’t Phainon have changed, too?

(And yet, Cyrene was still Cyrene–)

“Can we… go to the Grove? To visit him?” came Audata’s soft request. Her hands, still folded on her chest, above her beating heart, tightened.

Tribbie looked at them for a moment, but yet again, her face fell with a soft sigh and a shake of her head.

And once again, Hieronymus had to close his eyes to ward off the disappointment that washed over him. A part of him roared in anger, unable to understand why this child-like demigod was keeping them away from their son, why she had gone out of her way to separate them, not even letting them speak again with Cyrene – did she think herself as powerful as the Titans, that she could simply order them, puny humans as they were, around? Did she–?

“I’m sorry, but the roads to the Grove are still dangerous and chaotic.” Tribbie sighed, rubbed her eyes, and in that moment, most of Hieronymus’ anger evaporated away. She looked– tired. Exhausted. “If we weren’t so busy trying to organize the rebuilding and sending aid to other city states, we might have been able to spare one of us to go with you and protect you, but–”

Aglaea’s speech, asking for patience. Castorice, nervous and worried, trying to organize the impatient and restless people into something resembling compliance and facilitating channels for requests and mutual cooperation. Tribios sisters rushing through the streets with numerous messages. People from all over, all with their own worries and petitions and–

Hieronymus let out a long sigh and all the anger and annoyance bled out from his heart, his shoulders.

He couldn’t blame the Chrysos Heirs, that was the thing. A part of him wanted to shout, point a finger at them and demand to see his son, curse their name when they didn’t – couldn’t – help them achieve their self-imposed mission of finding the two children who had left home.

He couldn’t stay mad at them, not when a simple slip up of a nickname left it abundantly clear that they were close to Phainon. Maybe even– maybe even family.

(How bad of a person must he be, to feel jealous of people he had never met? Of people that had probably helped fill the hole in Phainon’s heart after everyone in Aedes Elysiae had–)

He couldn’t stay mad at them, not when they had seen Cyrene reacting badly to their presence and immediately answered her plea to visit Audata and Hieronymus in her stead– and they asked for them to leave Cyrene her much-needed space as she came to terms with everything.

He couldn’t stay mad, which was why he sighed, loud and long, and nodded with a crooked smile and resigned eyes.

Tribbie’s lips twitched at that, maybe a grimace, maybe a teary tremble. She fidgeted with her gloved hands, her puffy dress, her hair. She was clearly debating with herself, conflicted about something, and for a moment, a foolish part of Hieronymus hoped that she would go back on her words and agree to lead them to the Grove.

“I know it probably won’t compare to seeing Phainon, but… Please, accept our invitation to Marmoreal Palace,” she said, in the end, smile a bit nervous. Audata and Hieronymus crossed surprised glances. “I could be your guide! And you can probably meet some of the others! Agy could probably tell you embarrassing stories about Phainon! And Naxy, too, he definitely has lots of them!”

Hieronymus– yes, this was too much for him. He looked over to his wife, expectant and lost. Audata almost rolled her eyes at him, but she cleared her throat.

“Won’t you… get in trouble? After all, we’re just… humble farmers from a small village in the corner of the world,” she said, a bit awkward.

Tribbie blinked at her, puzzled.

“Eh? But you’re Phainon’s parents! Of course you’re welcome!” She frowned at them, and Hieronymus was thrown back to the past, to how his teacher had looked at him when he’d answered something wrong. “The next time you go to the Palace, you can enter, no problem. Oh!” She reached up to her hair and took one of the flowers into her hand. She examined it with a critical eye, before she nodded, satisfied, and offered it to them. “Here! Show the guards this flower and they’ll definitely let you in and they’ll let me know.”

Audata accepted the flower and took it with careful hands. They both looked at the flower, shocked and a bit overwhelmed.

“Thank you, Lady Tribbie,” breathed Audata, as polite as ever, once again saving their image.

Tribbie simply grinned wide, eyes glowing under the sun.

“Don’t mention it! Just– come visit, okay? We’ll be waiting!”

And with that, she was gone in a flush of red and white and tilting laughter.

Hieronymus stared at thin air.

“What just happened?” he asked, voice terribly flat.

“You know… I’m not quite sure myself,” was Audata’s equally lost answer.

—

(Back at the Chrysos Heirs’ meeting room, a group of groans echoed off the walls and tables half-hidden under mountains of paperwork.

“Teacher…” sighed Aglaea, rubbing her eyes and slumping in the chair that had chained her to the table for hours.

“I’m sorry! I just felt so bad!” wailed Tribbie, eyes teary and lips trembling. Trinnon and Trianne sighed, but still they held Tribbie’s hands and stuck to her side. “They are so nice and– and yet I lied to them! To their faces!”

“But inviting them to the Palace?” frowned Cerydra, arms crossed on her chest. She sighed. “That’s just asking for trouble.”

“What if Sun Fish sees them? Or they see him?” pressed Hysilens.

“I know, I’m sorry!” Tribbie thunked her head against the table leg once, twice. “We’ll figure something out.”

“Oh, so now it’s a we problem,” complained Trianne, throwing her hands up.

Aglaea sighed again.

“I’ll… weave the threads all over Marmoreal Palace again,” she mumbled to herself. “Please, someone tell Mydei to keep Phainon away from the entrances.”)

Chapter End Notes

Once again, this will definitely not blow up in their faces, right?

chapters.title: Chapter 10: Audata
chapters.html:
After that confusing day, both Hieronymus and Audata felt terribly lost on how to proceed. They had clear indications of where their son was and where not-so-little Cyrene was, but they couldn’t see them.

It hurt, but Audata knew that it would hurt more if they let themselves get swept away by their frustration and force their way into meeting with them. She spent most of the night lost in thought, unable to sleep, thinking back to the panicked glint in Cyrene’s eyes and how quickly she had run away from them. It was nothing like how Audata had imagined their reunion happening. She had imagined far more hugs and tears and maybe a nice cup of tea and a pleasant conversation, but she was starting to realize that, once again, she had been too naive – she had to remember that the two children she remembered had grown up, had gone through something terrible.

Her mind was full of unpleasant thoughts, so when she managed to sleep for just a couple of hours, only to wake up cold and unsettled, she decided to get up and start her day early.

The inn’s kitchen was empty when she climbed down the stairs quietly moments later and for a moment she hesitated at the door. Back when they were still in Aedes Elysiae’s golden embrace, Audata had always turned to cooking and baking when she was stressed about something – usually a bad harvest or Phainon’s uncommon bouts of sickness or persisten nightmares. The simple process of following a well-known recipe let her mind focus on something other than her worries.

Now, she sneaked into the kitchen and took a look at the available ingredients with curious eyes. She had enough to make a simple chicken broth with carrots and peas and a decent fruit salad.

It would do. It was the perfect way to repay the innkeeper’s care, after all.

Said innkeeper appeared half an hour later, startling at her presence and then– sighing.

“You don’t have to do this,” she said in her gruff but kind voice, getting to work side by side with Audata.

“I know,” replied Audata, smiling slightly. She glanced at the older woman. “But… this helps."

The older woman hummed, but she didn’t object or kick her out of the kitchen. She only gathered a few more ingredients and shared the counter with Audata.

“In that case, we’ll need more carrots. And more apples,” mentioned the old innkeeper.

Audata jumped at the chance to get out and breathe some fresh air, hoping that it would also help calm her raging thoughts. Cooking was doing wonders, but she always found a way to tie everything her eyes laid upon back to the two children that weren’t children anymore.

Marmoreal Market was coming alive by the time she reached the area. Her eyes sought the Palace first, as always, a towering silhouette in the distance that called for her with soft whispers. She ignored it, but it was getting harder each time.

She soon found a nice stall with pretty fresh produce that reminded Audata of their neighboring village – their onions were always of the best quality. She frowned at some of them, wondering if she should add them to the broth.

“They’re the best in Amphoreus,” commented the man at the stall, eyes and smile sharp. It was clear that he was used to people from the city, exaggerating his words and talking with confidence – only, in this case, Audata could see that his wares were of the quality he spoke of.

“I don’t doubt it,” she said with a knowing smile.

The man’s wide grin changed into understanding then.

“Vegetables again?” complained the loud voice of a child, and for a moment, Audata startled, turning around, heart in her throat. It had sounded familiar, but the voice was all wrong, and when her gaze finally found red hair instead of the pure white she had been searching for, she huffed out a disappointed – but not surprised – sigh. “Cipher, please! Can we go back to that other stall and buy those sweet pastries–?”

“No, I’ve already told you. Celebrations are over for now. You need to eat something that won’t rot your teeth,” said the woman who was leading the child to their stall, steps sure and legs covered in gold. Cipher, the child had called her. Audata crossed a glance with the man, who had straightened out at attention. A pretty important client, then. “Plus, you’re only here to help me carry everything back.”

“Then give me something in return!” tried the kid, too smart for his own good.

The woman – Cipher – arched an eyebrow at him.

“Oh? Using my own tactics against me, huh?” She grinned wide, then, showing sharp teeth. “Smart. But it won’t work.”

“Oh, c’mon!” groaned the kid.

Cipher took a look at the stall’s produce, eyes careful and more cautious than Audata would have thought from her previous careless attitude.

“Huh, most of these are fresh,” commented Cipher under her breath, one of her clawed fingers tapping on her chin as she considered the vegetables.

The kid still hanging on her hand groaned again, even louder than before. Audata’s lips twitched, reminded of her village’s unruly children.

Her smile fell immediately when the kid threw himself on the ground, hitting his head on the stall’s corner when Cipher’s tight hold didn’t let him fall completely.

“Hey!” yelped Cipher, crouching next to him and slapping the kid’s hands away from the very obvious bump on his forehead. “Don’t do that, you’ll hurt yourself!”

The kid pouted.

Audata, after making sure that the child was mostly okay, huffed a laugh and crouched next to them, too, smile gentle and patient, but also secretly amused.

“You don’t know the legend of the hero who outran the sun?” she asked, making her voice sound more mysterious. The kid’s attention was picked with just that, and Audata found herself stifling a laugh. “It’s a very old legend that my grandparents told me. It speaks of a legendary hero who ate a lot of fruit and vegetables when he was young. He grew up big and strong, with long legs that let him run and run, faster than anyone in his village. He could run so fast that the sun challenged him. And… who do you think won the race?”

“The hero did?” The kid’s eyes were wide open, just as his mouth.

“Indeed. It was all thanks to his diet as a kid,” nodded Audata, feeling as satisfied as she had felt back in the day, when she managed to get her own son to eat his veggies with this very same fake hero. “So, listen to Cipher and–”

“And then I’ll be faster than her!” the kid cut her off, looking up at Cipher with shining eyes.

“Don’t test your luck,” was Cipher’s dry response, but then she ruffled the kid’s hair and stood back up. “But she’s right. You’ll be closer to beating me in a race if you eat your food without complaints.”

And even then, Cipher’s eyes glinted with clear amusement as the kid offered to carry the few bags of vegetables Cipher bought. Audata watched them, a small smile on her face. It reminded her of the good old days.

“Ah– I should probably thank you,” said Cipher, a rueful smile on her face. The kid struggled with the bags in his arms, but when Cipher offered her help, he sniffed and refused. “I don’t know how I would have changed his mind without your… vegetable hero.”

Audata laughed softly and shook her head.

“No thanks needed. I think all parents and caretakers go through this at least once,” she said, nodding to the kid who was now sniffing at the vegetables and making faces at them, not really a fan of them but forcing himself to act otherwise. “That little story is the one I used with my own son when he was too stubborn to eat his vegetables. I’m only glad it works with other kids, too.”

“With your own son, huh…?” Cipher’s gaze was sharp, then, like a dagger, maybe. Like a blade. Then that sharpness in her feline eyes turned into realization. And then, it was gone in just a second, replaced with bright amusement and laughter. “Well, thank you, anyway. I’ll use that little story when someone refuses to eat their vegetables.”

Somehow, her words seemed to have a double-meaning Audata was unaware of.

—

Her next stop was another stall, this one closer to the main street, where she could get a perfect view of Marmoreal Palace. From what she could see, the fruits it sold seemed to be of good quality, colorful and vibrant.

There was already someone else at the stall, someone tall and imposing, and Audata hesitated for a moment, wondering if she should just take a detour and wait for him to finish his business. After all, he seemed like someone important, dressed in expensive clothes and wearing plenty of shining jewels on his person, and people that important didn’t usually take well to someone else bothering them.

But then again, important rich people didn’t usually shop at the local markets, and they definitely didn’t chat with the vendors – and this man was doing exactly that.

So, Audata got closer, slowly, cautiously, and then she took a look at the fruits available, making sure to stay out of the way. Indeed, the apples had a healthy shine to them, their green and red shining under the new sun.

“Anything I can do for you, sweetheart?” asked the woman at the stall, smile soft and friendly.

“I’d like a few apples, please,” she said, and then her eyes moved to the small hill of grapes she could see, too. She missed their taste – grapes were one of the few things they raised, back in Aedes Elysiae, after all. She knew that Hieronymus would appreciate it if she bought a few.

“Of course,” nodded the woman, shuffling around the stall as she grabbed a bag. Her gaze turned to the man on the other side, then, amused and familiar. “And– Lord Mydeimos, you can come later. I’ll probably have more watermelons for you to take.” Her smile turned good-natured. “Just in time for dinner.”

The other man – Lord Mydeimos – huffed, but his lips twitched. Unconsciously, Audata found herself relaxing at that simple show of familiarity with the vendor and that lack of pompous pride the other rich nobles wandering around Okhema flaunted.

“If they complain, I’ll just point them to you, then,” came his dry response, voice gruff but amicable.

The other woman laughed and handed Audata the bag of apples with a small wink.

“You do that, I won’t say no to more clients,” she said, terribly amused. “Anything else?”

It was then that Lord Mydeimos finally turned to her, relaxed and calm, and Audata’s curious gaze found his. She met amber, then, and the other man met soft honey and–

Lord Mydeimos froze.

Audata took note of the red tunic he wore, the gold jewelry, the red-tipped hair that hung over his broad shoulders. She wondered if he was one of the Kremnoans she had heard so much about – honorable and battle-obsessed, but good people as far as the other visitors from beyond Okhema could tell.

And then, the moment was broken and Audata blinked and she turned back to the vendor with a polite smile.

“A few grapes, please,” she pointed to the purple grapes and then she laughed softly. “They kept calling me. I must miss home more than I realized.”

“Oh, you’re one of the visitors from outside?” came the vendor’s curious question.

“Yes, I’m here with my husband,” she said, and then she bit her tongue when more words tried to escape her mouth. “We come from a pretty small village, so all of this is…”

“Overwhelming, isn’t it? Oh, I felt the same way when I first came here,” sighed the other woman, understanding and empathetic. Audata nodded. “Everyone feels out of their depth when they first come here. Why– even Lord Mydeimos here probably felt the same, right?”

They both turned to Lord Mydeimos, then.

Lord Mydeimos stared at them like a deer about to be shot down by an arrow.

“You’re not from Okhema, Lord Mydeimos?” asked Audata, when the man only blinked at them for a few seconds, almost– shocked. Which was weird, because Audata was quite sure that she didn’t know this man.

Her question seemed to drag Lord Mydeimos out of his thoughts, because he cleared his throat and adjusted the bags in his arms.

“I’m from Castrum Kremnos, actually,” he said, voice tight and a bit strangled.

Again, weird, but maybe he was just awkward or shy. He kept avoiding Audata’s gaze, after all, staring at the fruit of the stall instead, as if it was the most interesting thing he’d ever seen.

“Ah, I’ve heard about your people,” commented Audata, hoping that talking about his people would make it easier for him to open up or, at least, not look as wrong-footed as he did.

“All good things?” he asked, finally glancing her way and voice finally taking on an almost joking tone.

“Don’t worry, all good things. I swear,” replied Audata with a soft chuckle.

Lord Mydeimos nodded, appeased.

“That’s good to hear,” he said, before he turned back to the vendor. “I’ll come by later.”

And with that, he struggled for a short moment to get a watermelon under one of his full arms, before he turned in a flurry of red and gold and walked off, steps long and– not quite hurried, but Audata had the impression that he still wanted to get away from the stall as soon as possible.

(It reminded her vaguely of how Cyrene had chosen to retreat as soon as she could.)

The other woman sighed, hands on her hips and a small smile on her face as they both stared after the curious Kremnoan.

“Chrysos Heirs, am I right?” she threw to the wind, and Audata froze, just like Lord Mydeimos had done moments before. “I hope they’re all okay. They’re all sweethearts.”

Audata quickly took her bags, thanked the kind woman and then rushed off in the direction Lord Mydeimos had taken.

She was too late, however; she couldn’t find any vestiges of that vibrant red and gold anywhere in the market.

—

(Mydei left the bags and the stupid watermelon on the counter and then slammed his head right next to them.

“Mydei?” called Phainon, appearing at the door like a timely reminder of just how stupid Mydei had acted mere moments before at the market. “Are you…?”

“Kill me,” he grumbled, voice stifled against the counter.

“No?” came Phainon’s immediate answer, a curious mix between offended and confused. “You’re not even immortal anymore, HKS.”

“You’re still pronouncing it wrong,” he shot back.

“No, I’m not, and you know it.”)

—

“Excuse me,” came a soft voice from the door to the kitchen.

Audata had returned to the inn a while before, bearing the needed ingredients and immediately resuming her task of chopping vegetables and fruit before setting about cooking the broth. She was now waiting for both the broth to be ready and for Hieronymus to wake up and come down for breakfast, talking calmly with the innkeeper, who was regaling her with amusing anecdotes from the city’s daily life. The weathered old woman reminded her of her own mother, then, with her firm and yet gentle demeanor.

The two women turned to the door, blinking in surprise. It wasn’t common for people to come into the kitchen – many of them took advantage of the fact that the inn served meals, content to not cook themselves. And yet, as soon as Audata laid eyes on the girl, she was sure that she wasn’t any of the inn’s guests. After all, the girl in front of them was, in fact, Lady Castorice.

“Do you need anything?” asked the innkeeper, more gentle than usual.

“Um, I was chasing down one of the youngest chimeras– I’m pretty sure it ran into this inn, but…” she trailed off with a sigh, before she straightened up and folded her hands in front of her. “I’m sorry for bothering you.”

“Oh, no, it’s no trouble,” soothed Audata, waving a hand. Immediately, Lady Castorice’s eyes turned to her and– widened in clear recognition, before the girl tried to reel it in. Audata checked the broth, nodded, and then turned to the innkeeper, who was already looking at her with a knowing glance. “Can you keep an eye on it? I’ll help Lady Castorice.”

“Ah, there’s no need–” tried to refuse Lady Castorice, waving a hand in the air.

“Really, it’s okay. Chimeras can be quite slippery, after all,” said Audata with the gentlest smile she could muster and a wink – she wasn’t trying to cajole Lady Castorice into anything, after all. She just wanted to help. And maybe… get to know someone that might know her son and Cyrene as they were now.

Lady Castorice hesitated for a moment, gaze skittering around the kitchen, unsure and jittery. Her hands fidgeted with the rings around her fingers, and it reminded Audata a lot of how, during Lady Castorice’s speech at the Palace, she had sought out any and all mannerisms that would have painted the demigod in a more human light. Now that she couldn’t stop finding little tidbits of humanity in her, Audata couldn’t see her any other way.

“I– alright, if you don’t mind, ma’am,” came Lady Castorice’s soft acceptance.

“I don’t mind at all,” hurried to reassure Audata. She left the kitchen and looked around the – just as cluttered – dining and reception areas. “Now, what kind of chimera are we looking for?”

“It’s– here, I have a photo in here somewhere.” Lady Castorice took out her teleslate, and Audata couldn’t help but observe it curiously – after all, no one in their little village had something like that. Why would they? Their lives were simple and based on simple routines. One of the villagers already had a photostone, and the children – usually – returned home as soon as they heard their parents call, so why would they need a teleslate? “Ah– here.”

Lady Castorice showed her a beautiful and candid photo of a pink-colored chimera playing with– a certain cat-eared woman that Audata was quite sure she had seen before… And then it hit her. She had just met that woman a couple of hours before. Cipher.

So, Cipher was probably another Chrysos Heir? The mural did have a silhouette that could be similar to her. Audata stared at the photo with probably too-wide eyes, feeling a knot in her throat. She tried to remember every word they had said to each other, but hit a blank when she couldn’t remember everything. She did recall Cipher being terribly amused by the time she left, and Audata wondered if it was because she had figured out who she was. Did she know Phainon? Did she–?

Audata blinked and dragged herself out of her spiraling thoughts. The chimera. Right, they needed to find the chimera, before it ran away again and poor Lady Castorice wasted her whole morning chasing after it.

“So, pink… it shouldn’t be too difficult to find,” she muttered to herself, tearing her gaze away from the photo before she could do something stupid like analyse every white detail in it, searching for even a vague echo of her son where there wasn’t any.

“I think the difficult thing will be to catch it,” came Lady Castorice’s wry answer, coupled with a small smile. She had a very sweet smile, noted Audata.

“Well, we can very well try,” nodded Audata, and so, she rolled up her sleeves and looked around. “I’ll take this side. You can take the other. I’ll put something in front of the door for now, just in case.”

Lady Castorice nodded, firm and focused.

They both moved through the room, looking under tables and furniture, squinting at the few cupboards. Audata had to admit: this little chimera was smarter than the ones they had in Aedes Elysiae. They had already looked through the tables and chairs, under the furniture and even inside a few cupboards that didn’t close all the way. Audata was ready to go up the stairs and look around the hallways as a last resort.

“Um, ma’am?” called Lady Castorice, and something in her voice made Audata pause and turn to her, humming to encourage her to continue. Lady Castorice lowered her gaze, nervous. “I just– maybe I’m mistaken, but could you be… Phainon’s mother? Mrs. Audata?”

Audata’s heart skipped a beat, then. Her breath hitched in her throat. Her eyes flew wide open, her mouth felt dry as a patch of dirt. For a moment, she couldn’t find her voice, but then she cleared her throat and tried to smile.

“I am, yes,” she said, and now that she had already managed to get that out of her mouth, the rest was easier. “And you… you’re Lady Castorice, right? One of the Chrysos Heirs?”

“I am,” nodded Lady Castorice. And then she blinked and flushed. “Ah– just ‘Castorice’ is fine. I, um… Well, you’re Phainon’s mother. He told us about you– about how you taught him how to make salads and–”

Audata couldn’t help but huff out a laugh, and then that soft laugh turned into a real one. Her shoulders shook and she had to cover her mouth to keep her laughter from getting any louder and waking up the entire inn. The innkeeper wouldn’t like that.

But the relief flowing through her was too bright, like the sun over their heads. A warm embrace. Fond memories sprouted in her mind like flowers – of a small kid wanting to help, of her teaching him how to wash the ingredients, how to chop them up, how to make the most of the leftovers from other meals to make original salads.

“Ah, it’s good to know that he still remembers that,” she managed to get out, even as her laughter turned too teary, too wet. She didn’t let her tears out – not now. And yet, she couldn’t quite help herself. “Phainon… how is he?”

(“Is he eating okay? Does he still have trouble sleeping? He always had nightmares as a kid. When can we see him again? Does he want to see us–?”)

A glint of something Audata couldn’t quite catch passed through Castorice’s eyes, before her timid smile turned softer, gentler, assured.

“He’s getting better by the day,” she said, and it didn’t sound like a lie, so Audata took a deep breath and let it out slowly. Castorice watched her, an understanding shine in her pink-ish eyes. “I’m sure that you’ll see him soon.”

It didn’t sound like a lie, either.

Audata took another breath, nodded in gratitude when words failed her once again and then– she jumped when a shout came from upstairs, from one of the rooms.

Castorice sent her a startled and worried glance, before Audata turned and took a few steps up the stairs. Not that she got to take many, because a blur of pink came barreling down, straight to her feet.

“Caught you!” she hissed, moving fast after years of dealing with sneaky chimeras and mischievous children. Her hands closed around a furry torso and so she lifted the little chimera to the air, meeting its surprised and disgruntled glare with a satisfied smile. “You’re too smart for your own good.”

A couple of seconds later, a messy-haired and still half-asleep Hieronymus appeared at the top of the stairs, clothes a mess. As soon as he found the little chimera in Audata’s hands, he sighed, loud and slightly aggravated.

“You caught it. Good. It gave me a good fright, standing menacingly over me when I woke up,” he grumbled, throwing a slight glare at said chimera as he climbed down the stairs. The chimera sniffed, raising its nose in a mix of pride and offense.

“Here, Castorice. We caught the little criminal,” said Audata, amused, still trying to shake off the vestiges of longing and worry from her shoulders.

Hieronymus’ gaze sharpened at that, looking at Castorice with a new shine to his eye. Castorice accepted the little chimera, smiling down at it with an amused huff. Her grip was firm and measured, so when the chimera tried to escape again, it found it impossible.

“Thank you for the help, Mrs. Audata,” nodded Castorice, terribly polite. Audata’s smile came up easier now, warmer. She didn’t feel quite as cold as before.

“Please, just call me Audata,” she said. After all, this was probably one of Phainon’s friends.

“Audata, then.” Castorice’s smile widened. It made her look younger, brighter. “I’ve heard from Lady Tribbie that she invited you to Marmoreal Palace. Please, don’t hesitate to take her up on the offer. We’d all be honored to have you.”

‘All’, she said, as if having the attention of all of the legendary Chrysos Heirs wasn’t as intimidating as the gaze of the Titans themselves. Audata swallowed down her nervousness – no, that didn’t sound right. The Chrysos Heirs were– just like them. Human. Maybe more powerful, with more responsibility upon their shoulders, but just as approachable as any person on the streets.

So, she crossed a glance with Hieronymus and, when she saw the clear interest in his gaze, she turned to Castorice again and smiled.

“We’ll be there,” she said, and it sounded like a promise.

Chapter End Notes

A bit more light-hearted! Also, Castorice digging their hole deeper! Yay! Next chapter we'll have more chaos too.

chapters.title: Chapter 11: Hieronymus
chapters.html:
It still took them a couple more days to bring themselves to once again take the passageway to Marmoreal Palace.

Even then, they loitered around the area for a moment, taking the time to admire the tall building from outside without the previous frustrated crowd. It was a truly beautiful place, after all, and once again, Hieronymus felt a bit bitter that this once-in-a-lifetime experience had been soured so much that he couldn't even enjoy the sense of adventure it would have brought him in different circumstances. But they couldn't stall forever, so they moved slowly to the entrance, feeling a much too familiar apprehension in their chests.

Only to be startled badly when a Dromas stomped on the ground, to the side of the Palace's tall shape. Audata clutched her shaking hands to her chest, but Hieronymus had handled enough Dromases to know that the guy was just… a bit annoyed about something.

Curious – and a bit worried in Audata’s case – they drifted to the side, following the loud huffs and a clear and light voice that was trying to calm down the Earth Titan’s creature.

Hieronymus frowned; he knew that voice. He had heard it not long ago, in fact.

He mulled over it as they walked, and then his mind screeched to a halt when they finally laid eyes on the Dromas that still huffed and puffed in annoyance and impatience and– 

“Lady Hyacine?” he mumbled, mostly to himself, but said girl still caught them hovering to the side and her eyes brightened in clear recognition and Hieronymus wondered if she had known, back then, when they first met, that he was–

“Ah, it's you!” she greeted, waving a hand at them. “It's nice to see you again… knowing who you are, this time. Nice to meet you properly, Mr. Hieronymus and… Mrs. Audata, right?”

“It’s good to see you too, Lady Hyacine,” greeted Hieronymus, a bit wrong-footed, smile a bit too awkward.

“Ah, please, there’s no need to be so formal,” she said with a slightly rueful smile. “After all, you’re Phainon’s parents. I got so confused when I first saw you, you’re pretty alike!”

People had always said that Phainon was a perfect mix of his two parents, so Hyacine’s words weren’t really news for them. And yet, somehow, they seemed heavier when she said them, with an unexpected weight that Hieronymus wouldn’t have expected.

The Dromas chose that moment to stomp on the ground again, startling them all out of the light lull in their conversation. Hyacine huffed out a slight chuckle at that, shaking her head.

“Do you… need any help?” asked Hieronymus, just in case, though Hyacine seemed to have it all handled anyway. Still, from what Audata had told him, talking with the Chrysos Heirs came with new revelations and maybe even reassurance.

“Oh, don’t worry! This mister is just feeling huffy because he’s had to travel a lot lately,” she said, hands on her hips. Still, her eyes shone with regret and guilt as she patted the Dromas’ side. “I’m sorry. As soon as I check you over, you can go and eat as much red soil as you want.”

“Wouldn’t it be better to get them to the stables?” came a different voice from behind the same Dromas, clearly male. They all turned to the newcomer – a man with green-ish hair and an eyepatch whose presence was as heavy and intense as the mountains surrounding them. “If those idiot nobles return with their yelling, they’ll no doubt bother every poor soul that find themselves here.”

“That is true,” mussed Hyacine, tapping a finger to her lip. And then she seemed to remember that she wasn’t quite alone and she jumped, smiling at them and gesturing for the mysterious man to get closer – not that he did, not at first. “Ah, allow me to introduce you to Professor Anaxa, from the Grove of Epiphany. He’s also a Chrysos Heir–”

“Much to my annoyance,” cut in the man, Anaxa, crossing his arms over his chest and standing right next to Hyacine. His heavy gaze rove over them and, not for the first tsime, Hieronymus felt terribly underdressed, with his humble and worn clothing and calloused hands. “Also, it’s Anaxagoras. And you two– you’re Phainon’s parents, right?”

“A-ah, yes,” nodded Audata, just as lost as Hieronymus, which was a first, because she always seemed to know just what to say to just about anyone.

“One of my most promising students, that one,” commented Anaxagoras, which was– huh. Hieronymus blinked, caught off-guard, because this man couldn’t really be that old. He was definitely younger than them – and Pythias, as well – and yet, he was already a professor at the Grove of Epiphany and had even taught Phainon. “His sense of style is still atrocious even now, though.”

“Professor,” hissed Hyacine, elbowing her possible teacher on the side with a too-wide smile. “You can’t just say that.” And then she paused and grinned at him, a glint of something that looked a great deal like amusement in her eyes. “But… you could tell them about Phainon’s studies. After all, they’re his parents.”

The professor’s eyes were unimpressed when he looked back at her, lips slightly twisted in resigned annoyance. Hieronymus found himself torn between opening his big mouth to ask for any crumbs these people might have about his son, and remaining silent to avoid any trouble – as friendly as Hyacine seemed, she was still a Chrysos Heir, and even though these two seemed close, the matters related to the Titans were often described as… fickle. Explosive, sometimes.

“I think Phainon is a bit too old now for me to go behind his back and talk to his parents about his studies,” pointed out Anaxagoras, which only made Hieronymus and Autodata flinch slightly from the direct reminder about their lost time. “Especially the studies he’s already graduated from.”

“So, Phainon has graduated from the Grove of Epiphany?” asked Audata, a bit breathless. And why wouldn’t she be? After all, the Grove was said to be the cradle of knowledge and the brightest minds of Amphoreus.

“Yes,” was Anaxagoras’ short answer, to the point. Hyacine rolled her eyes slightly and smiled wider.

“He graduated with the title of Ten Times Debate Champion under his belt,” she added, a glint of amusement in her eye.

Audata and Hieronymus crossed a glance with twin trembling smiles – of course he would go into debate. Of course. Hieronymus had already seen the vestiges of a dangerous silver tongue before, words that had been woven carefully to pull people into his trail and that had tried to change Pythias’ mind over their exams countless times, to various ends.

“If that’s all, I shall mingle no longer,” came Anaxagoras’ voice, final and firm. Hyacine sent him a knowing glance, too heavy to unpack. “I will remain at the stables for a while longer.”

“I’ll send this little one to you as soon as I’m done, then,” said Hyacine, terribly knowing, even as the professor huffed and walked off with his head held high. They all stared after him, and only then did Hieronymus notice that the cloak of sharpness that had been covering them had left with the professor. Hyacine sighed, but she was still smiling as she turned to them. “I’m sorry about him. He can be a bit… eccentric.”

“Ah, don’t worry. He was pleasant,” came Audata’s, as always, diplomatic response. And it was mostly the truth, thought Hieronymus – Anaxagoras had been cordial enough, if not a bit blunt and dry.

“That’s good to know,” nodded Hyacine, seemingly a bit more at ease. “In any case, how are you holding up? I told you about the– Black Tide and all and I didn’t see you again… Are you okay? Do you need anything?”

Ah, just another bitter reminder. Hieronymus tried to go for a comforting smile, but he was quite sure that it fell a bit flat – and maybe a bit too similar to a grimace. Hyacine did catch it, if he had to guess from the slight downturn of her eyebrows, but she was gracious enough to not comment on it.

“We’re… adapting,” he said in the end, a bit pinched. He had to bite his tongue once again to avoid mentioning that they would feel much better if they had their son and his childhood friend back with them, but he couldn’t quite bring himself to throw bad-tempered words at Hyacine of all people. “We’ll be fine.”

Hyacine stared at them for a moment, eyes almost searching, sharp. For a moment, her eyes looked too old – just like Tribbie’s – but then she sighed and smiled again.

“You really are similar to him, huh…” she muttered, mostly to herself, but they still heard it, anyway. Hieronymus opened his mouth, not really knowing what would come out, but Hyacine shook her head. “Just– tell me if you ever need anything, okay?”

“We will,” nodded Audata, soft and yet firm like a promise.

Hyacine held her gaze for a moment, before she looked up at the Palace with a wistful smile.

“You’re here to visit Marmoreal Palace, right?” she said, then. There was something in her voice he couldn’t quite name but that sounded a bit too soft compared to the cheerfulness she wore around her shoulders like a cloak earlier. “I won’t keep you, then. Tribbie’s flower should be enough to get you through the guards at the entrance. You can just wait for her at the hall. Have fun!”

“We’ll… try to,” he said with a small nervous smile that finally got Hyacine to huff out a laugh. Audata elbowed him on the side with a sharp glance. “What? Have you seen this place? It’s probably bigger than ten Aedes Elysiaes put together.”

Audata opened her mouth to apologize for him and his rude comment, but Hyacine shook her head with a soft laugh and waved at them to hurry to the entrance, all potential rudeness forgotten.

And yet, even as they bid farewell to Hyacine and the small flying pegasus that now floated by her side, Hieronymus couldn’t help but look up to the Palace, to its verdant gardens they could only see from the distance, the falling waterfalls.

For a moment, he could swear he saw a flash of pink.

—

They showed Lady Tribbie’s flower to the guards and, just as both Tribbie herself and Hyacine had said, they were ushered in with no trouble, if only with a good deal of confusion from the guards themselves, who stared unabashedly at their clothes and hair and calloused hands.

Tribbie herself hurried to them only a few minutes later, while Hieronymus had been admiring the decorations on every corner, every golden statue, every inscription. It was like walking into a museum – only, Hieronymus had never been to one, anyway, so he could only guess.

“You came!” cheered Tribbie and– another Tribbie. And another. There were three Tribbies.

Hieronymus blinked, a bit lost. They had known about the Tribios sisters, of course – they were usually running around Okhema all day, delivering messages and helping anyone that was quick enough to catch them near – but they had never expected to see them all in person and– they really were mirrors of each other, if only slightly different in personality.

Should they… call them simply Tribios? But Tribbie was– well, Tribbie. Did they have different names? Hieronymus was quite mortified to realize that he had never paid enough attention before to catch them.

“Um, what should we… call you?” asked Audata with a small smile, a bit lost.

Fortunately, Tribbie herself – at least, Hieronymus was more or less sure that it was Tribbie – didn’t seem to mind.

“Oh! These are Trianne and Trinnon,” she said, gesturing to each of her… sisters? Hieronymus was starting to doubt that they were simply triplets, the similarities were uncanny. The only way to distinguish them was their hair and accessories. “So! What do you want to see first? Should I just guide you around?”

“Please, if you don’t mind,” nodded Audata, a bit frazzled. After all, there was no way that they would know where to start in such an enormous place. Before leaving Aedes Elysiae, the biggest building they had ever seen was the Sacrament Courtyard.

“Then, follow us!” chirped Tribbie, before she and the other redheads skipped away, through another curtain of water and into–

Hieronymus whistled under his breath. Now he understood why the people of Okhema had mentioned the baths so often – they were magnificent, elegant and open, but– empty. Tribbie followed his gaze when she noticed them lingering by the entrance to the baths, looking around with wide eyes.

“Ever since the Era Nova, we closed Marmoreal Palace to everyone not a part of the new Council or the Chrysos Heirs. With how crowded it became daily, working on everything that needs to be done would be… well, it would have been a nightmare,” she explained with a slightly rueful smile, gesturing to the empty pools and abandoned hallways.

“Here! There are even more baths around– here,” pointed Trianne, eyes sparkling with mirth and energy.

For a moment, Hieronymus was reminded of how Phainon used to grab his hand to lead him into the fields numerous times, dragging him to his newest discovery in the trees or behind a particular bush or around the river. One time, Phainon had led him to Hieronymus’ old hiding spot – a small crevice between a gnarly tree and a tall rock, where he had stashed his favorite stories about heroes and any sweets his parents had bought him from the few merchants that found their small village – and Hieronymus had thought that that would be the most surprising place Phainon would lead him to, and yet– Here they were, in the Holy City, walking through the elegant halls of Marmoreal Palace.

The Tribios sisters showed them around the baths, showed them the beautiful sights from the tall windows, guided them through confusing hallways until they reached the gardens they had only been able to see from a distance.

(When Hieronymus and Audata weren’t looking, Tribbie, Trinnon and Trianne passed around their teleslate, checking in with the others and making sure that there was no one in the places they were going to.)

“How are you liking it so far?” asked Trianne, as their little group walked leisurely to the library. Behind her, Tribbie discreetly typed into her teleslate, tongue peeking out from her lips.

“It’s certainly… big,” was Hieronymus’ eloquent response, coupled with a small dazed smile. In any other moment, he would have been able to come up with something at least a bit more befitting of the place, but as it was, his head was spinning with all the turns they were taking to go anywhere in the Palace and all the decorations that shone like lanterns in every corner.

Trianne laughed, loud but not disrespectful.

“Don’t worry, we know it’s a bit overwhelming,” she said with a grin. “Why, Snowy got lost so many times when he first came here. He always ended up on the opposite side of where he wanted to go.”

Ah, that stabbing feeling in his heart was becoming more and more familiar as time went on.

He cleared his throat.

“And you?” he asked, a bit curious about the demigod leading them.

“Oh, I was present when it was being built,” she said, terribly unbothered.

Hieronymus stumbled on air and Audata turned her head to them so quickly her neck cracked.

“Ah… is that… so?” he managed to get out, blinking quite a few times and wondering if he had heard correctly. When he met Audata’s gaze, he saw the same confusion he felt.

Tribbie froze behind Trianne, fingers hovering over the teleslate. If Hieronymus hadn’t been as busy as he was trying to come to terms with the fact that the three – seemingly – children that reached up to his waist were in reality thousand-year-old demigods, he might have noticed how Tribbie paled at whatever she had read and immediately reached out to tug at Trianne’s scarf.

As Audata and Hieronymus had their little crisis, the three sisters had a quiet conversation via mind-link and expressions and badly-hidden gestures.

“Actually!” ended up half-yelling Trianne with a nervous laugh. Tribbie hid her face behind a gloved hand. “Are you hungry? You must be, after all the walking we’ve done. We can leave the library for later and… we’ll go to the Garden of Life. Yes! I’m sure there’s lots to eat there–”

“And maybe Agy will be there too,” added Tribbie, hurriedly making her teleslate disappear into thin air, a pinched smile on her face.

Not that Audata and Hieronymus noticed, anyway.

“Oh… Okay?” mumbled Hieronymus, as the three children turned on their heels and power-walked down the hallway again, spines tense and hands tugging at each other’s scarves.

And then, there was a loud noise coming from the direction they had been heading in – the library.

The three Tribios stopped. 

Tribbie sighed and mumbled something under her breath.

“What was that?” asked Audata, a bit distant, probably dragging herself out of a well full of questions.

“Nothing!” Trianne’s answer was a bit too high-pitched, her smile a bit too crooked. “It was probably– De likes to train with very weird stuff sometimes, he must–”

“C’mon, let’s not keep Agy waiting!” interrupted Tribbie, waving at them to hurry up. “I’m sure it’s nothing serious. Someone probably dropped something, that’s all. There are plenty of thick scrolls at the library.”

That made… sense.

Though, Hieronymus wondered how thick that scroll would have to be, to sound like a shelf full of tools falling to the ground.

… Maybe three shelves. At the same time.

—

(Phainon had wanted to take a walk around the Palace, was the thing.

And Castorice’d had a pretty hard time telling him “no”, lately. It just felt– wrong, after everything he had done for this world. So, the most logical course of action had been to sound the alarm to the other Chrysos Heirs and update the Tribios sisters on their route as Phainon led them on an aimless walk around the Palace’s grounds.

Of course, they ended up at the library. And of course, Castorice hid between the shelves to let the others know, as Phainon roamed around, muttering a long string of “already read”s under his breath, checking scrolls and books off his mental list.

And then, Castorice had heard Trianne’s loud voice– talking to someone.

That someone was Phainon’s father.

Castorice was old, composed, calm – she was the Maiden of Death, Aidonia’s Executioner, the demigod and Titan of Death, she was–

She was panicking.

“Shit,” she muttered under her breath. She sent a random sticker to the groupchat, looked around– 

She closed the doors to the library with a slam.

Phainon immediately snapped his gaze in her direction, eyes sharp and shoulders tense after millenia of fighting. He looked a second away from summoning Dawnmaker, in fact, and Castorice felt a bit bad about spooking him, but–

Trianne was still too loud.

With a grimace, she stumbled her way to the shelves and– pushed one of them. Her strength was as reliable as ever, so the shelves crumbled like a house of cards, like a domino, and soon, at least three of them had tilted over onto each other and to the floor.

“Castorice?” called Phainon, hurrying to her side and checking her over with his gaze. “Are you okay?”

“Yes, yes, sorry,” she said, a bit breathless. But, at least, she couldn’t hear Trianne’s voice anymore. “Sorry, it was just– a spider.”

“A spider?” Phainon frowned at her, confused. “Since when are you afraid of spiders?"

Castorice screamed in her mind.)

—

The fresh air that hit their faces helped to alleviate the overwhelming feeling of the Palace and the confusion and slight shock of the Tribios sisters'... everything. As the three ‘children’ hurried off to run through the verdant grass, both Audata and Hieronymus lingered at the gate, breathing in the sweet aroma of flowers and sunlight.

“Ready?” asked Audata, grabbing his hand. Hieronymus turned to her with a slight frown.

“For what?” he asked back, still reeling a bit. Every bomb that the Chrysos Heirs threw at them felt stronger than the last – at the very least, Cyrene and his son’s ages would remain known to them, no surprises.

“Meeting Lady Goldweaver,” said Audata, nodding to the other side of the Garden of Life. Hieronymus followed her gaze– indeed, Lady Aglaea was talking with the three Tribios, relaxed and as elegant and intimidating as she had been during her speech.

Hieronymus swallowed.

“I don’t think I’ll ever be ready to meet more Chrysos Heirs, but let’s go anyway,” he muttered back. Audata’s answering smile was small, but amused.

The grass was healthy and soft, and the flowers and plants around the Garden were colorful and vibrant, and maybe it was simply the fact that they were once again surrounded by nature that made Hieronymus relax a bit. Even then, Lady Aglaea’s eyes were heavy and old, and yet, with a brightness that he hadn’t expected. It reminded him of the glint of satisfaction they – humble farmers that they were – got when they finished a day of good work.

“It’s a pleasure to meet you,” nodded Lady Aglaea, nodding at them with grace. “I hope my Teacher hasn’t tired you out with their endless energy.”

‘Teacher’, she said. Okay. Hieronymus wouldn’t comment – not that there was much to comment, anyway.

“Oh, no, of course not,” said Audata, her smile the most nervous he had seen of her. “The Palace is– magnificent. Very different to what we’re used to, honestly.”

And Lady Aglaea’s smile softened, then, a glint of understanding, a glint of… maybe nostalgia. It made her age shine, then, old and weathered, but pushing forward into the future.

“Please, come with me,” she said, gesturing to the table full of food and drinks with a hand adorned in elegant silk. “Let’s sit. I will try to answer all the questions you might have.”

They did, because no one could bring themselves to refuse such a polite request. They sat, a bit tense, and the other four demigods sat, too, and they all lapsed into a somewhat awkward silence.

Audata, always Audata, polite and proper and more brave than Hieronymus often was, cleared her throat and accepted the cup of juice Trianne offered her with a wide grin.

“Um, we wanted to ask… first, um…” She stumbled on her words, but even then, that was more than Hieronymus was able to do, which was just nibble on a few grapes and try not to explode.

“You want to ask about Phainon,” said Lady Aglaea, soft and patient and knowing. Her eyes were sharp but cautious as she regarded them. Her words weren’t a question.

“Yes.” Audata swallowed her doubts and looked Lady Aglaea right in the eye. “How is he? We only know that he’s at the Grove, resting, but– We don’t know much more than that.”

Lady Algaea paused, hummed. She took a sip of her own chalice, its surface glittering under the new sun, and Hieronymus tried not to think too deeply about how much money all of this food and drink and cups and plates could cost.

“Physically, he’s quite alright,” she said in the end, cautious.

“But mentally…?” Hieronymus trailed off, feeling cold dread climbing up his spine.

Aglaea took another sip and then leaned back on her seat, sighing deeply with her eyes closed.

“What you need to understand is that… both Phainon and Cyrene have gone through a long and arduous journey. They have both sacrificed much to give this world the Era Nova we now stand upon,” she explained, and her words were as heavy as rocks, as mountains, as– as truths that had floated in the air but that had never been heard.

“The last thing we want is to hurt our children,” muttered Audata, hands clasped tightly on her lap.

“I know,” was Aglaea’s response, softer than they expected, coupled with a slightly sad smile. “Sometimes, a little pain is necessary to get to true happiness. They know that better than anyone else.”

That didn’t sound particularly uplifting, but–

“We don’t want to hurt them,” he said, thinking back to Cyrene’s different-colored eyes, the panic in them, her trembling hands, the way she had turned away and– disappeared. 

“You won’t,” answered Aglaea, staring into his eyes. “They deserve a happy ending, too.”

“They deserve everything,” choked out Audata. When Hieronymus looked at her, he saw her eyes finally overflow with tears, even as she stared at Aglaea with a steely gaze. Tribbie immediately went to her side, taking her hands in clear support.

“One more thing we’re in agreement of,” nodded Aglaea, hands gentle and elegant as she twirled her drink. She tilted her head to the side, then, as if she was listening for something, and then she closed her eyes and took a sip of her drink, humming. “This is just a suggestion, but… the gardens to the west of the Palace are especially beautiful during dusk.”

And her eyes glinted with something that Hieronymus couldn’t quite understand.

—

(Hiding in a dark room, a certain pink-haired girl paced around, fidgeting with the ribbons around her wrists, her hair, her dress.

“C’mon, you can do this. You faced the Lord Ravager Irontomb head-on, you went through millions of cycles, you re-created part of the universe– You can do this. It’s just– Phainon’s parents. Khaslana’s parents. They’re nice and gentle. They will understand,” she muttered to herself.

With every step she took, her heels left behind frost on the marble floor.

“You will go up to them, explain everything, apologize, and then you will hug them like you’ve wanted to do for days and then you’ll go find Phainon and everything will be fine–” she continued, eyes distant but determined but also still wavering.

She stopped in front of the door, clenching and unclenching her hands, taking deep breaths.

“C’mon. You can do this.” And with that, she nodded, firm and resolute, and reached out with a hand, closing her cold fingers around the elegant doorknob and–

It immediately froze in a thick layer of ice that reflected her wide eyes.

It froze the doors shut.

She gave it a cautious tug, but her only answer was a concerning crack of ice and wood. She tugged harder, but it remained stubbornly shut. Frozen.

Cyrene groaned, took the frozen and now-deformed doorknob in both of her hands and tugged harder–

“Oh, c’mon, don’t do this to me! Not now!” she cursed, tugging on the door and then immediately letting go when the poor wood threatened to splint.

She groaned louder and slumped against the frozen door, head lowered and eyes teary. Did fate really hate her that much? Was it retribution for something? Was it karma–?

Cyrene punched the door weakly, and then flinched when the door cracked again in response. She eyed it warily – the last thing she wanted was to have to explain to the other Chrysos Heirs that she had destroyed a door when she was trying to pump herself up to meet Phainon’s parents.

So, with a loud and long sigh, she leaned on the door and rubbed her eyes, defeated.

… Forgetting completely that she had the ability to teleport.)

—

Even after a pleasant chat with Lady Aglaea and the Tribios sisters, the Goldweaver’s words still echoed around their minds as they were escorted back to the Palace’s entrance.

The sky was already tinted with orange and warm tones to the west by the time they made it out of Marmoreal Palace. They could still hear Marmoreal Market bustling with people, the guards at all corners of the Palace relayed their posts to their replacements, the birds flew off to their nests.

“Should we…?” asked Audata, looking to the side of the Palace, where the sun was climbing down slowly, swallowed by the mountains.

Hieronymus only nodded.

Lady Aglaea’s words had been meaningful, heavy with something that reminded Hieronymus of the prophecies the Titans had loved so much. Was it related? He didn’t know, but in a world where Titans no longer existed, the very next thing to divinity was– this.

So, they followed Lady Aglaea’s ‘suggestion’, they walked calmly down the path that surrounded the Palace, and tried not to hope for something that they knew they wouldn’t get.

And yet–

A laugh, lilting and familiar, but also not, because it was too deep, too tinted with exhaustion, too old. It echoed and bounced off the walls, reaching them in their path, and so they followed it like lost adventurers without a map, hurried and with a knot in their throat making it difficult to breathe.

Hieronymus was gasping by the time they laid eyes on the high gardens, hands shaking and legs aching. Audata was clutching his chlamys, but he didn’t really notice.

A flash of white between green and red and blue and pink, pure and bright, and that very same laugh, and a tall silhouette standing up from one of the benches, draped in more white and gold and blue.

“Phainon?” And only when the name had escaped his lips did he realize that it wasn’t a simple murmur – no, it was a call, a yell, and it bounced off this little refuge’s walls all the same, until it reached–

Phainon startled, blinked, and turned towards them and–

It really was Phainon.

Too far away for Hieronymus to see him clearly, too far away to do anything other than stare like idiots, but close enough for him – for them – to recognize their son.

And for their son to recognize them in turn.

Before Hieronymus could so much as open his big mouth to call for him again, Phainon’s eyes widened, his lips parted, his shoulders climbed up to his ears and–

Phainon turned on his heels and ran away.

Hieronymus could do nothing but stare, rooted to his spot, feeling like a stranger in his own body, watching as Phainon opened the door to the Palace and ran inside in a blur of white, as quick on his feet as always, a blur of red and gold rushing behind him, calling his name–

And Hieronymus felt cold, because this wasn’t how he had imagined this reunion with his son to go.

(He had expected hugs, he had expected tears, he had expected warmth and laughter and teary smiles and–)

But they remained there, cold and numb and–

Alone.

Chapter End Notes

There goes Aglaea with the steel chair!
