chapters.title: Chapter 12: Phainon
chapters.html:
Later, Phainon would feel like an idiot and decide that he could have dealt with this in a more elegant and calm manner.

In the moment, though, he could only rush through Marmoreal Palace’s hallways like a headless chicken, bumping into corners and stumbling on decorations and slipping on the expensive rugs littering the rooms. He could hear Mydei following him, calling his name, but it all twisted in his mind, and – maybe aided by his wings, he couldn’t be sure – he managed to lose him on the way at some point.

He didn’t know how, but he found an empty storeroom and then proceeded to have a full-blown panic attack inside of it.

He didn’t know how long he spent slumped against an old bench full of dusty scrolls and ancient artifacts that could have been preserved better, but by the time the world settled around him and his head stopped doing somersaults and his heart remembered that he wasn’t in the middle of a do-or-die fight, he felt… tired. Exhausted, really. Also cold, so he pulled his wings out and tried to feel less like an ice cube – even though he knew that it was mostly in his head, unused to… not being burned alive. He had been doing so well, before–

Well. Before he saw his parents, alive and well, standing in front of the gardens, just as surprised to see him as he was to see… them. Because he had seen them, right? It wasn’t a trick of his mind, right? It wasn’t an illusion, right? He half-remembered Lygus doing something, back when he was still trying to push back Irontomb, using his parents against him. But that made no sense, right? Lygus was dead, now.

But if it really had been them…

He shouldn’t think about it too hard. He could feel another wave of panic looming over his head and like an idiot, he would end up jumping head-first into it.

So, he stayed hidden in this random room for a moment. And then two. And then three. He blocked the door shut with a chair and then curled up between old crates and a very delicate-looking amphora that depicted Aquilla and Seliose during their clash, hiding in his feathery cocoon.

And he tried to breathe. Only breathe. Breathing was good. He was alive and corporeal now, so he needed to breathe.

Just like Hyacine had told him, he let his eyes wander around the room, taking note of all the artifacts surrounding him. He dug into his most dusty memories, trying to dredge up anything related to relic appraisal he might remember from countless cycles, that short time where he could be – had been – almost normal. A young boy from the countryside with too much on his shoulders and a box closed tight with withered memories of a village that didn’t exist anymore.

Or did it?

The Chrysos Heirs had been reluctant to give him too much work after just waking up, but they were overwhelmed, and his help could be invaluable, so Phainon had heard something or other about missing memories, chaotic memories, and also…

Cities, towns, villages that had fallen to the Black Tide in the past were now reviving, maybe not-quite intact, but their people, the citizens, some buildings–

Huh.

Aedes Elysiae had also fallen to the Black Tide. Sure, sometimes Phainon himself had to hurry it along so it would swallow it and its fall would push that cycle’s Phainon forward and to Okhema to fulfill his destiny. And sure, Phainon had killed Cyrene himself every time to get the power to rewind time and–

It made sense, when he thought about it. Aedes Elysiae met the criteria to be– revived. Reformed. Huh.

It all felt a bit too distant to Phainon, though. He should have felt… more. He should be more affected by it – these were his parents, his neighbors, his childhood friends. He should– 

It felt as if he was looking at it from behind a window, or through fog, or–

Ah. Hyacine had called it dissociation, when he asked her about this new distance between him and the world. At first, he had wondered if it had anything to do with the fact that he wasn’t technically a demigod or a new Titan anymore, that this Era Nova had started without him and thus, it wouldn’t accept him – not after what he had done to stop Irontomb, during the cycles and after. But the Coreflames in his chest still sung, and when he used his powers they still answered his call. And then Hyacine had explained her suspicions and–

Phainon blinked. And then he blinked again.

And his movements felt sluggish and distant, as if his body wasn’t really his own. Had it ever been? After all, he was simply a–

He shifted and accidentally kicked one of the crates that surrounded him. Its contents clinked – probably silver – and then something fell on top of his head, hard but not too heavy. He moved a hand to instinctually catch it; a disc, made from old ceramic, an ancient prayer written on it with elegant letters. It reminded him of the old hymns the people of Aedes Elysiae would sing during the Month of Harvest – he remembered Cyrene standing next to the priests, their heavy gazes and expectations always weighing on her small, small shoulders.

Right. His parents were alive.

Phainon hid in that room for most of the night, alone.

—

(After running around the hallways in search of a runaway Phainon for a few minutes, Tribbie and Aglaea finally found him in turn.

“Where’s Phainon?” he asked Aglaea, eyes probably a bit too wild and worried – after all, Phainon had panicked quite hard after seeing his parents, and knowing how messy his mind was, Mydei didn’t really want to leave him alone.

“He’s hiding,” said Aglaea with a soft sigh. Mydei opened his mouth to ask where, but Aglaea raised a hand. “He’s… mostly fine. Panicking, but he probably needs a moment to himself.”

“I should–” he said, only to be cut off by Tribbie this time.

“Snowy will be fine. Let him come to us when he’s ready,” said Tribbie, and there was a glint of something in her eye when she looked up at Aglaea, so Mydei frowned and looked at their previous leader with confusion clear in his gaze.

“I gave them some clues. I didn’t expect them to– call out to him, just like that,” admitted Aglaea, and for once, she seemed a bit contrite. A bit wrong-footed. A bit guilty. Her smile was rueful and bitter. “I should have guessed. After all, they’re his parents.” And she looked out of the window, eyes distant. “I… suppose it has been too long for me. That’s all.”

Too long since she herself had seen or maybe thought about her parents, about what they were like, what they would do for her, if it came to it.

Mydei thought about a mad king and about a ferocious mother and– 

He sighed.)

—

By the time the sun peeked through the open balcony of the room, Phainon had taken a couple of not-really-restful naps and organized his thoughts enough that any mention of his parents’ revival didn’t push him over the edge anymore. Hopefully.

He stepped out of the room with shaky steps, lingered at a window for a moment – staring at the place where his parents had stood the previous day, almost expecting them to still be present, like ghosts – and then continued on his path, head held high and eyes rimmed with red.

He opened the door to the new official meeting room, and he had hoped to at least seem like he had his shit together, but from the worried glances that everyone shot at him, he supposed that he hadn’t succeeded. Maybe he should have stopped by his room, changed his clothes, maybe even taken a bath, but he had feared that his resolve would crumble to dust at the slightest detour.

“We should probably… talk,” he said, and he cringed at his own rough voice.

“We should,” nodded Aglaea, and her eyes were tired, too, he noticed – then again, everyone looked tired, lately.

Immediately, Mydei was next to him, a firm hand grabbing his arm tightly – he always felt grateful that Mydei refused to treat him like glass. He didn’t think he could stand it if he did. Mydei’s firm grasp led him to one of the klismos around the table and he sat down next to him, like a silent and unyielding guardian.

Phainon remained silent for a moment, biting his lip. The other Chrysos Heirs followed his lead, silent, glancing at him and each other, worry and restlessness in their eyes. It was clear that they felt guilty in some capacity, and Phainon wanted to tell them that he wasn’t mad – how could he? Even if they had really done something like hiding the truth from him, he couldn’t really blame them. Not after the little show he had put up the previous afternoon.

“They’re… real, aren’t they?” he chose to ask, first.

It irked him, how small his voice sounded, how… young. Or maybe it was simply in his head after a long night of drowning in memories he had wanted to leave behind.

Predictably, Tribbie rushed to his side to grasp his hand. Mydei’s own came to rest on his shoulder, heavy and grounding.

“They’re real, Snowy,” came the damning answer.

Phainon forced himself to take a deep breath. He let it out slowly, even as it trembled in his chest.

“And you… knew?” he asked, but there was no real accusation in his voice.

“We did,” nodded Aglaea, as firm as always, but… softer. “Cyrene ran into them at the market. Seeing how she reacted… it was decided that we should wait some time.”

Oh, Cyrene. 

He should probably check on her. She probably reacted similar – if not worse – than him. She had, after all, been just as close to his parents as she had been with him. They were her second, or maybe even her first, home.

“We invited them to the Palace, and maybe it was a bit stupid– no, it was really stupid, but then Agy started talking to them and…” explained Tribbie, a flush of guilt climbing up to her cheeks, her grip tightening around his hand.

“Seeing them so desperate to see you, I left them some clues,” admitted Aglaea, and it was maybe the first time that Phainon had seen her actually lower her head in quiet guilt. “I didn’t expect them to catch on so quickly– or for them to call out to you from so far away, but… I suppose I can still be surprised.”

Everyone fell quiet after that.

Phainon lowered his head, his tired gaze roving over the countless scrolls and maps and half-done treaties and to-do lists and notes and crumbled papers abandoned on the table. Tribbie and Mydei’s hands served as an anchor, never letting him get swept away by his own thoughts – and there were too many of them, now, crashing like waves against his tired mind.

His parents. Alive. Even in his most delusional and most hopeful fantasies over the cycles, he had never– He never–

With a long sigh, he rubbed his eyes with a hand and then he just left it there, covering the upper half of his face. He was just so tired. He didn’t even know how to process any of it, when he was still trying to process everything else.

He was trying to look to the future, but the world made him look back to the past in the form of his parents.

“Are you… angry?” asked a small voice. Trinnon. Phainon sat up straight and looked at her with a slight frown. “We kept it from you, after all. Are you…?”

With a soft sigh and something that could have been called a smile, Phainon shook his head and ruffled Trinnon’s hair.

“I’m not angry,” he said. His voice was beat, rough and tight, and when Hyacine passed him a cool glass of water, he didn’t refuse it. “Really, I’m not. I… I can kind of see your reasoning.” He huffed out something that might have been a laugh, if one was feeling optimistic. “After all, I did panic and run away as soon as I saw them.”

“Which is a perfectly understandable reaction to seeing your deceased parents alive once more,” pointed out Hyacine, sending a small smile his way

“I suppose,” he said, smile just as small and shaky, and he almost said that he might have had some experience with that, but– he had never really stopped to watch his family from a distance during the cycles. He had never hated himself that much. He only approached Aedes Elysiae when he had to, when it was time.

(He did remember a particular cycle where he saved Aedes Elysiae, but even then, he always maintained his distance from everyone. His will would have crumbled, then. He couldn’t afford that.)

After that, the air was less tense. The Chrysos Heirs visibly relaxed, even though they sent worried glances his way, but they knew by then that leaving him space to process and think everything through was the best course of action.

And so, they remained silent.

“Do you… want to meet them?” asked Castorice, minutes later, a bit hesitant, soft enough to be ignored if Phainon so wished.

He paused and took another deep breath. 

“I don’t know,” he answered truthfully, because lying was a waste of time at this point.

“You don’t have to answer right now, Phainon,” reminded Mydei, pointed and knowing. “You should probably sleep. And take a bath. You stink.”

And that made Phainon let out a half-hearted laugh.

“I should do that,” he said, a mumble for himself, rubbing his face once again.

“Go rest, Snowy,” said Tribbie, tugging on his rumpled coat and pants. “We’ll deal with anything that comes our way.”

“Thank you, everyone,” he said, finally standing up on numb legs. He looked around, met all the worried glances with his own, and tried to muster up at least a small smile. “Really.”

“Go take a nap,” pressed Mydei, and when Phainon looked at him, he saw the frown he had expected, the wrinkle between his brows, the downturned tilt to his lips. He followed his instinct and kissed him, which only got him an eye-roll and a push to the door. “And don’t get lost on the way.”

Phainon sent an unimpressed stare at him, but that simple interaction had lifted his mood a bit. Enough to be functional for the duration of his trip back to his room – or, at least, to act like it.

“Phainon,” called Aglaea as soon as his fingers closed around the doorknob. When he turned and met her gaze, he found a softness he still wasn’t accustomed to in her eyes. “Remember that you don’t have to do anything you don’t want to. We’ll be in your corner.”

“As always,” he muttered, lips twitching up, and Aglaea nodded with a smile of her own.

—

Cyrene appeared a few minutes after Phainon had already taken a nap and a much-needed bath.

Phainon knew from the way the air in his room battled between cold and hot for a moment, until each side of the room picked a side.

“I’m sorry. It was my fault,” was the first thing she said, sitting on the bench, head lowered and– alone. Again. She kept doing that. Phainon left the towel he had been using to dry his hair on a chair and then– sat down by her side. Cyrene glanced at him for a second, but she grimaced and looked away. “I just–”

“Panicked?” he finished for her. She nodded, small and with a heavy weight on her shoulders. Phainon smiled, rueful and half-amused. “Yeah. Been there, done that.”

“I just– I ran into them at Marmoreal Market. Remember? When you told me about that tea and I went to the market to prove you wrong and…” Cyrene trailed off, biting her lip. Phainon waited for her to pick her words – she was always so careful with them. “I found the tea. And… I also found them. They talked to me, we hugged. I... ran away as soon as I could.”

Phainon felt something twist in his chest. He could guess how it had gone. His mother, always soft and knowing, seeing Cyrene in the distance and rushing to embrace her. His father, always with careful steps and good-natured humor, smiling at her to reassure her. Both of them, seeing the differences in Cyrene and taking note of them.

How much did they know? How long had they been…? What had they heard around Amphoreus? When did they…? What…?

He could understand why Cyrene had reacted the way she had. He had reacted much the same way, after all, even though he had been lucky enough – lucky enough? – to be too far away for them to approach him, to talk to him, to hug him. Even now, the very memory of that moment made him freeze, made his heart beat wildly, made his hands tremble.

And the terrible thing was... going back to them would have been so easy, had his long journey through the cycles never happened. He would have finished his duty, and then he would have taken the road back to Aedes Elysiae, back to their embrace.

But after all this time– At this moment, he had to really dig through his countless memories to even remember their eyes. Their voices. Their laughs. And even then–

“Are they… real?” he muttered, shoulders tense, hands clasped on his lap.

Cyrene’s glance was knowing and a bit sad. She probably saw – back when the Trailblazers and her trudged through the ruins he had built as a seal to keep Irontomb contained – how Lygus had used his own parents to sway him, to break his will. It had never worked, but that simple strategy had managed to sour their memory for some time.

“They’re very real,” was Cyrene’s answer. It was the same answer the other Chrysos Heirs had given him, but Phainon let out a breath he didn’t know he had been holding. “They are very worried about us, I think.”

“From their perspective, we probably disappeared out of nowhere,” he muttered, thinking back to the various similar stories he’d heard from other families – they woke up, no memories, no news, only empty air. It had probably scared them half to death, he thought absent-mindedly.

Cyrene hummed, fidgeting with the ribbons tied around her wrists.

“You know… it’s funny. I tried to get to them yesterday, when they came, but– I froze my door and then spent the next half an hour trying to open it, and then spent the next hour after that feeling sorry for myself because I forgot that I could teleport,” she admitted with a small smile and distant eyes. Phainon could only shake his head, a million thoughts running through his mind. “I… want to see them. I think. But I’m afraid that they won’t see me as Cyrene. I’ve… changed. And I don’t…”

She trailed off, after that, words too heavy to float in the air for long.

“... Yeah,” he mumbled, because that pretty much summed up what was going through his mind in that moment, too.

Because, the thing was– Even if the memories he had of his parents had been muddled by time and suffering, even if looking at them would probably bring him back to a bloody moment in the past he had wanted to forget in countless lifetimes, even if facing them meant showing them how much he had changed from the smiling boy they knew, even if talking with them meant cracking himself open and bleeding all over their kind, kind hands…

Titans above, he wanted to see them so badly it hurt.

He wanted to cook side by side with his mother again, he wanted to help his father work the field, he wanted to learn how to make a scarf or gloves or even socks from his mother, he wanted to joke with his father about nonsensical things, he wanted to... he wanted...

“Do you want to see them?” asked Cyrene, small and careful, delicate like frost over a flower.

Phainon opened his mouth, felt his lips tremble, felt his eyes water – but no tears fell, not anymore. And yet…

“I think I do,” he managed to choke out, voice raw in a way it only ever was during the night, when the darkness encroached too close to his heart, when reality seemed far too distant, when his body ached and he could hear the cracked kindling inside his chest. “But–”

“They’re your parents,” cut him off Cyrene, and her smile was still small and ever-present, and her eyes were just as dry as his, but the emotions in them were bright. “They’ll love you, no matter what.”

“Will they?” asked his traitorous mind, but then he remembered the promise he had made with his mother, back in the day: to return to the golden fields of home, and let himself be embraced by them again.

He was just– scared. But he had been scared for a long time, right? Scared and furious, yes, but scared nonetheless. In this, he couldn’t let himself falter, either.

After all, even as the mere thought of seeing them again, face to face, terrified him and made him toe the line of panic, another part of him– longed for it, longed for that moment of reunion, where he could simply fall into his mother’s arms and he could feel his father’s calloused hands ruffling his hair and…

His heart ached.

And maybe that was enough to follow its guiding trail back home.

His memories were tainted after much suffering, after too many sacrifices, after countless never-changing ends and massacres – but he wouldn’t let the world take this away from him. 

He wouldn’t let anyone take his home from him, not again.

Cyrene saw something in his eyes, then, because her smile widened slightly and she huffed out a soft laugh, lowering her head. And yet… there was something that didn’t quite sit well with Phainon, because–

“They’ll love you too,” he reminded her, because even as someone that dealt with memories all the time, she still needed little reminders from time to time.

Even if she sometimes didn’t really believe them. Not yet. Phainon supposed that they were quite similar in that regard, after all.

“I’ll fix this,” she said, firm and yet delicate. A promise, a bow that wasn’t really needed.

“There’s nothing to fix,” he said, pointed, placing a hand on her arm and feeling her jump slightly – always apart, always alone, always an observer. His memories of his parents were far away, but he would always remember the moment his father had hung Cyrene’s swing at the tree. “Just… talk to them.”

“You say that like it’s easy,” she said, dry and maybe nervous. Still, she took a deep breath and stood up, determined and focused. “Okay. I can do this. I’ll talk to them. And everything will be fine.”

Phainon’s lips twitched up at that.

Everything would be fine.

—

(Cyrene spent the rest of the day and the entire night planning what she would say to Audata and Hieronymus. She wrote one draft, two drafts… many drafts, so many that she lost count at some point.

By the time she was done, her hands were stained with ink – just like old times. She stared at her hands, feeling terribly distant from her own body. For a moment, she blinked and her hands were smaller, her sleeves longer. And then, she was back, surrounded by too many abandoned drafts and scrolls.

She had never – even in her most hopeful and idealistic dreams – expected to meet Phainon’s parents again. Alive. Well. Healthy. Not corroded.

But then again, she had never expected to have a future.

She could still be surprised.

She looked over her messy handwriting, frowning at the long-winded words and explanations. Even now, she saw countless faults and points that could be worded better, and her hand itched to grab her pen once again and change it, but…

She already knew that no word written in this piece of paper would leave her lips. As soon as she saw Audata and Hieronymus, her mind would go blank and she would–

Did she really want to see them again? When looking at them meant looking at the past she had lived through too many times to count, when the golden fields behind them meant going back to the beginning of yesterday again?

But that was a stupid question. 

After all, she truly wanted to see them again.

Because even though it meant seeing yesterday, it also brought forth memories she would never forget, memories she would always treasure: Audata helping her bind her newest story into a handmade book, Hieronymus making her swing, both of them inviting her over for breakfast, lunch, dinner… Both of them listening to her ramblings when her dreams became confusing and foreboding, looking at her with understanding and love instead of the seeking and judgmental glances from the priests.

She wanted that comfort back, she realized. She wanted that yesterday, but in the new tomorrow.

And she would have it, she promised herself, standing up from the desk when the first rays of sunlight peeked out from the horizon. She looked over the final draft one last time and finally– tore it into tiny little pieces.

When she stepped out of her room, her mind was clear, her smile was genuine and her heart… her heart felt light.)

Chapter End Notes

chapters.title: Chapter 13: Audata
chapters.html:
Finally seeing Phainon, even if it was from a distance, had been… a surprise. A welcomed surprise, even if it opened a variety of options about why he was there to start with and whether the other Chrysos Heirs had lied. But it had settled something in her chest anyway, a worry she had never said out loud to anyone, not even Hieronymus – the possibility of having only heard lies about her son’s well-being, about his state, about him still being Phainon. But that laugh was him.

And then, Phainon had seen them in turn and he had clearly panicked and he had run away – just like Cyrene had done, days before. And it had been just another stab of longing and worry poking their hearts, just another knife, just another wound.

Audata had wanted to go after him, follow him through the maze that was the Palace, catch up to him and finally hug him like she’d wanted to do for months now. But she still remembered the glint of panic and hurt in Cyrene’s eyes when they had seen her last - surprise turned into panic, fondness and relief turned into uneasiness - and Audata had found herself rooted to the spot, unable to move.

She could only stare as who she recognized as Lord Mydeimos hurried after her son, throat closed tight and hands– cold, freezing, burning like ice.

They had returned to the inn in quiet acceptance and worry, with a million thoughts boiling under the surface of their mind, hands clasped tightly around the other’s.

They didn’t say anything as they climbed up onto the roof, knowing that they wouldn’t sleep a wink after that. Instead, they made themselves comfortable and stared out at the horizon, at the Palace, where their dear son was probably trying to wrap his head around what had just happened, and beyond it, up to the stars that watched over them.

Audata didn’t even know how to name all the emotions that wound her chest tight – sadness, worry, longing, a love so deep it hurt. She tried, nonetheless. It took her all night, but maybe, when morning came over them like a warm blanket, she could at least breathe through the wall of emotions.

And maybe, just maybe, she could find it in herself not to lose hope. Not yet. Phainon had always been able to surprise them with his resilience – this wouldn’t be any different, surely.

Cyrene appeared in a flurry of mirror-like ice and pink hair.

Audata, who had been nodding off on Hieronymus’ shoulder as they admired the dawn from the inn’s rooftop, longing for the warmth that only this new sun could bring them now, startled so badly she almost toppled over like a ladder with no helping hands, yelping.

“Ah, I’m sorry!” Cyrene rushed to them, alarmed and worried, her smile crooked and nervous. Her hands hovered in the air, never touching them. “I didn’t expect– well, there’s usually no one here, so–”

“It’s okay, it’s okay,” laughed Audata, even as her hands trembled in Hieronymus’ hold. Cyrene was here, with them, voluntarily. She had been the one to seek them out. “You just startled me, that’s all.”

Cyrene sighed in relief, a hand on her chest, and Audata blinked, because– it felt a bit strange, seeing such a… Cyrene-like behavior in this grown-up version of her. Strange, but not unwelcome.

“Um, I just– I came here because…” And yet, she stumbled over her words, hands fidgety and restless as she adjusted her dress, her hair. Her smile, always poised in her lips, wobbled. “Do you… want to have breakfast with me? I know the perfect place to see the dawn.”

Audata crossed a glance with Hieronymus, but even before meeting his gaze, she already knew what he would say.

“Lead the way, Miss Storyteller,” he said, the familiar and old nickname rolling off his tongue as easily as always.

Cyrene’s answering smile was less nervous, this time. Instead, it was tinted with relief and a hint of nostalgia that made her different-colored eyes shine.

She led them through the streets of the Holy City with assured steps, hands behind her back – just like her younger self. Audata couldn’t keep her eyes off her. A part of her couldn’t help but worry that the girl would suddenly disappear again, leaving behind a trail of ice. But every time they turned a corner, every time Cyrene smiled back at Hieronymus’ comments about how overwhelming Okhema was, she was still there, real and alive and bright.

The restaurant she had mentioned was, indeed, a perfect place to see the dawn, out in the open and mostly vacant this early. Audata couldn’t help but stare at the sky over their heads, now a pale blue with light streaks of pastel pink and yellow. They all chose their respective breakfast, and Cyrene sent them a smile when she noticed the grapes and bread Hieronymus sneaked into their order.

“First, I wanted to apologize,” said Cyrene, hands around her tea and eyes downcast.

“Apologize? For what?” frowned Audata, but she still tried to soften her tone.

Cyrene looked up and her eyes shone with guilt and sadness. Immediately, Audata wanted to reach out and take her hand – but once again, she was too afraid that any touch would make her disappear again. Cyrene probably saw it in her eyes, because her smile dimmed, even more guilty and dispirited.

“For running away from you,” she admitted. She huffed out a small laugh. “I… could have handled that a lot better, I think.”

“I feel like that was mostly our fault,” replied Hieronymus with his usual rueful smile. “We shouldn’t have rushed to you like that.”

“You were just relieved to see me. I understand.” Cyrene took a sip of her tea; Audata noticed how her hands shook a bit, the thin sheen of ice around her fingers. “I… also told the Chrysos Heirs to– keep you away from Phainon? Or, well, to give Phainon some more time before we told him about you… I'm sorry, this sounds pretty bad.” 

Her smile shook, guilt clearly eating at her, and Audata could admit that she felt a spark of hurt at the revelation that Cyrene had been the one to lengthen this goose chase. And yet– with Cyrene, grown up and yet seemingly so small in front of them, feeling guilty and pained about how the situation had turned out… Audata couldn't bring herself to feel angry about it. 

“Cyrene…” said Hieronymus, voice low, but there was no anger in his voice either.

“I just– I panicked when I saw you and I thought, ‘well, if I panicked this bad, I can't even imagine how Phainon would react’– And then I started overthinking it and instead of telling him, I hid it from him and…” Cyrene sighed, long and hard, and rubbed her face, clearly frustrated with herself and beating herself up over every choice she had made these past few days.

“Cyrene,” called Audata, soft and gentle, and when Cyrene finally raised her gaze to meet Audata's, nervous and maybe even a bit fearful – why? No one in Aedes Elysiae could bring themselves to get genuinely mad with the children, no matter how stupid their latest idea had been – Audata smiled. “From what you've told us, you never actually planned on keeping this a secret forever, right?”

“Of course not! I–” Cyrene almost stood up, hands on the table, eyes wide, but Audata's smile widened and she waved a hand.

“Then you don't need to worry,” she said, and Cyrene paused, a bit caught off-guard. She blinked.

“You're not… mad?” she asked, and something about that simple question, so small and hesitant, threw Audata back to a peaceful past, where her own son managed to get himself and his dear friend in trouble every other day.

“We're really not,” assured her Audata, careful and gentle.

“I think we've spent all our energy being worried. We don't have leftover energy to get mad,” tried to joke Hieronymus, his usual crooked smile on his face.

Cyrene stared at them for a long moment, as if she was looking for proof of their expected anger and blame, but she found nothing. And so, slowly, she relaxed back on her seat, hands still tense, but eyes becoming more and more thoughtful, until she ended up twitching her lips up into her usual smile. Only this time, it looked softer, more tired, older.

“You really are too kind-hearted,” she mumbled, mostly to herself. She sighed softly, then, lowering her gaze to her still full cup of tea. “I… I really am glad to see you. You’re… alive, and well, and– I must admit that my memories are… a bit of a mess, because of reasons I won’t bore you with…” And her smile seemed a bit painful now, thought Audata, heart aching, hands restless, ready to reach out and provide some of the comfort this girl needed. “But I still remember how much you mean to me. Everyone back home... Are they all okay?”

“They’re all okay,” nodded Audata, soft and assuring, and finally, she let herself move a hand closer to Cyrene’s, cautious, hesitant – if the girl didn’t want to accept her touch, she wouldn’t have to. 

Cyrene noticed the shift, of course, and her smile wobbled for a moment, before she finally– took Audata’s hand. Cyrene’s hand was freezing, it was like clutching a shard of ice, but Audata held on and squeezed, and Cyrene squeezed back.

Audata’s heart sang, relieved and warm, even as her hand turned a bit too pale.

“They’re a bit confused– after all, news are hard to come by in Aedes Elysiae, as you know,” continued Hieronymus, eyes lingering a moment longer on Audata and Cyrene’s joined hands, satisfied and relieved.

“Mm, I guess that’s the case for a lot of little villages,” muttered Cyrene, shooting a quick look to Marmoreal Palace, where her companions were likely still working diligently to figure everything out.

They remained silent for a moment, each relishing in the moment, the sun finally climbing up the sky slowly, bathing the buildings and mountains in brilliant gold and warm tones.

Audata tried to catalogue all the little details that were different from the Cyrene she knew – which were a lot, she came to realize, but none of them made her any less ‘Cyrene’. She was still her, Cyrene, Elysiae, little Ely, the daughter of Aedes Elysiae, the girl that had loved to sit on her swing and nap, the girl with ink-stained hands and divination cards, the girl that always faced the skies with a smile.

She moved her hand slightly, and it was then that she noticed the few ink-stains in the hand she had been holding.

Audata’s smile widened and her chest felt warm with relief and fondness and a deep sense of peace.

At some point, they resumed their breakfast, easy and familiar in a way that reminded Audata of the old days – that had been merely a few months ago for her, but that, for Cyrene, were probably a lifetime ago. Hieronymus kept pushing more and more fruit onto Cyrene’s plate, just like he had done when she was young, and Cyrene shot him knowing looks, but she never refused it.

They roped her into a relaxed chat about Marmoreal Market and the Holy city itself, mentioning the bustling streets, the people from all over, and the beautiful landscape around them. At first, Cyrene’s answers were a bit stilted, a bit too soft and polite, but Hieronymus was nothing if not relentless, and soon his poking and prodding managed to get Cyrene to laugh and joke around with him.

Finally, Cyrene’s shoulders dropped into a more relaxed posture. Finally, the next time she grabbed her cup of half-finished tea, she didn’t leave behind a trail of thin frost.

It was during one of the lulls in conversation that Audata finally reached out with a hand and softly brushed pink locks of hair away from Cyrene’s face. Cyrene’s multicolored eyes widened, surprised and caught off-guard, and she almost flinched away, before– before she visibly stopped herself and stayed put.

“Dear, Ely, are you really okay?” she asked, voice so soft it could be called a murmur. A secret, if Cyrene wanted it to be. And yet, Audata hoped that this dear girl could see the very real and genuine worry in her eyes.

Cyrene opened her mouth, lips twitching up to form her usual smile – some things never changed. 

Audata still remembered how one time, she had found this girl, much younger, still just as soft-hearted and smiling, hiding behind the trees, crying. She had sat down next to her and offered her a hug, no questions asked. Cyrene never explained what had ailed her so, but Audata could guess – her golden blood, her mysterious birth, it had all fascinated the few priests of Oronyx in the village, and so, they had put too much pressure on her… until the entire village had banded together and decided to keep her under their wing.

Only, this time, Cyrene sighed and let her smile drop into something softer, more tired and weathered.

“I’m… adjusting,” she admitted, voice just as quiet as Audata’s had been. A secret, indeed. “It has been... hard, but– I’ll be okay.”

Just like that time, Audata opened her arms and offered little Ely a hug.

And just like that time, Elysiae didn’t explain what storm brewed in her heart, but she did accept Audata’s hug.

Elysiae’s body was just as cold as her hands, but she was firm and tangible under Audata’s hands. She was there, with them. And that was enough.

Audata didn’t know how long they stayed like that, but she didn’t particularly care – she would stay for as long as Elysiae needed her to, even if her hands were becoming a bit numb.

“Ah– sorry, I’m… a bit colder than most people now.” Cyrene leaned back, eyes wide and a flush climbing high in her cheeks, her smile a bit embarrassed and guilty. She moved her hands around, not really knowing how to help. “I’m sorry.”

Audata couldn’t help letting out a soft chuckle. She reached for Hieronymus, then, grasping his hands and laughing harder when he flinched and tried to get away from her freezing hands.

“This is what you want me for?” he muttered, not really annoyed but acting like it anyway.

That made Cyrene pause and then huff out a soft laugh that Audata was quite sure was genuine.

“I… actually had another reason to come here,” said Cyrene, slow and meaningful, and that– Audata’s heart skipped a beat. Suddenly, she wasn’t only clutching Hieronymus’ hands to warm her own. Cyrene’s eyes were fond, soft, warm. “Phainon told me that he’d like to see you, too.”

Audata’s grip around her husband’s hands must have been painful, but he only held on tighter. Just as they had done for months, for the duration of this long and arduous journey, they leaned on each other to face every revelation that had been thrust upon them.

“Phainon?” she breathed, and she tried to find some trace of deceit in Cyrene’s eyes, but there was no way that Cyrene would do that – she only found understanding, warmth, a bit of nervousness.

“Yes. He– well, that’s not my story to tell. But he does want to see you,” nodded Cyrene, earnest. “He’s just… being a bit of a worrywart, is all.”

“Worrywart?” Hieronymus and her crossed a glance, confused. “Why?”

And Cyrene’s smile turned a bit pained, a bit too– old. It made Audata’s heart ache, again. It reminded her that, as nice as this breakfast had been, it didn’t fix everything. They had still died, years before, leaving these two children behind – and these children had clearly been through even more suffering and hard times.

It had… changed them.

She could see it clearly in the Cyrene in front of her – in her eyes, in her gaze, in the way that she moved, in the way she froze everything when she wasn’t careful, in the way that she walked. She wasn’t the same Cyrene Audata remembered – but she was still her.

“Please, tell him that… he will always be Khaslana, our son,” she said, soft and firm.

Hieronymus sent a knowing glance to her, before he nodded to Cyrene as well.

Cyrene watched them, smile dimmed and yet soft and warm – as if she had been proven right, all along. As if she had already written their words in her latest draft.

“I will,” she promised, heavy with meaning. And with that, she took a deep breath, smiled wider at them, and stood up, smoothing down her beautiful dress with her hands. They didn’t leave any traces of frost anymore. “Having said that, I should probably leave and get started on that reunion.” She winked, just like always. “I’ll send you the details later.”

She disappeared in a twirl of crystals and pink.

And Audata–

Audata collapsed against Hieronymus and cried.

Only this time, the only thing flowing from her poor heart was simply– relief.

And love.

Deep and undying love.

—

(Phainon waited at the Garden of Life, alone with his thoughts, gaze locked in the distance, where he knew Cyrene was talking with his parents. He bit lightly at his nails, an old habit he had when he was a kid– and how funny, that it was now when it reappeared.

Cyrene appeared next to him in a flurry of Remembrance frost and glass and Phainon turned to her with a slight frown and tense shoulders.

“How...?” he started, but Cyrene’s shining eyes and shaking hands folded on her chest were answer enough. His answering smile was wobbly and nervous and conflicted. “Have you…?”

“I have,” nodded Cyrene, soft. She grabbed his arm, her hands as cold as always, but her smile was warm as the sun. “I’ll leave the planning to you.”

Phainon took a deep breath that rattled on his chest and nodded. There was a very familiar spark of restlessness inside his chest, a mix of excitement but also trepidation. He really wanted this reunion to go well – and he knew that its outcome would rest solely on his shoulders.

He took another breath, and this time it was more steady.

“I’ll write the note and give it to Tribbie, then.”)

—

They received the note from Tribbie the very next morning.

The day passed by in a daze, after that. Both of them got ready to head out when the sun was already starting its climb down the sky during the Parting Hour, quiet and almost vibrating with nerves.

The walk to Marmoreal Palace was just as quiet, and when Tribbie met them at the entrance with her sisters, she smiled encouragingly and patted their arms with shiny eyes.

“Don’t overthink it,” she muttered, a glint of excitement in her eyes. “Just– hug him.”

Oh, they didn’t need to tell Audata twice.

Tribbie left them in front of a door that would lead them to one of the gardens, to the west of the Palace – the very same place where they had seen Phainon a couple of days before. It made Audata smile; it felt like Phainon was giving this reunion a second chance.

“Ready?” whispered Hieronymus, taking a deep breath and looking down at her with a nervous smile and eyes that were full of unsaid emotions.

Audata copied him – took a long breath and let it out slowly, feeling her heart flutter in her chest – and smiled back, just as nervous.

“Ready,” she said, and so, they opened the door together and welcomed the warm embrace of dusk.

Phainon was already waiting for them, sitting on one of the benches, looking out to the mountains and the horizon. Audata almost didn’t recognize him for a moment – her mind had still been thinking of her son as the young teen he had been, not as a grown man. But when she did–

She didn’t call out to him. She didn’t hesitate. She didn’t even wait for Hieronymus to catch up.

Instead, she rushed to his side, eyes already overflowing with tears, sight blurry, legs shaky. 

Phainon turned then, eyes wide and surprised, clearly snapped out of his thoughts by the noise Audata was surely making running to him with her arms already half-way open.

“Mom–” he choked out, only to be cut off by Audata’s tackle.

“Khaslana,” she gasped, and now that she had her arms around her son, she couldn’t bring herself to let go. Not again. Not anymore.

She choked a breath and tightened her arms around his back, his neck. Her hand found his hair, as unruly as always, those two strands of white hair still sticking out, and she couldn’t help but laugh through her tears.

And oh, how Khaslana trembled in her arms.

He remained still for a moment, tense and stiff, and when Audata noticed, she prepared herself to take a step back, release him from her tight hug, no matter how hard it would be– But Khaslana finally let out a trembling breath and relaxed in her arms, letting her finally bear most of their weight, winding his arms around her and burying his face into the side of her neck, just like he had done when he was a kid, scared from relentless nightmares.

It was only then that Audata finally collapsed on the bench. She could see Hieronymus finding his place behind them both, wrapping his arms around them and leaning his forehead against their heads, closing his eyes and just– relishing in the moment.

All the while, Khaslana shook in their arms and clutched their clothes with trembling hands.

(There were no tears, though, noticed Audata.)

Sometimes, Khaslana’s hold turned a bit too tight, a bit too desperate, and it reminded Audata of their previous deaths, of the little details they had managed to gleam after weeks of searching about their son’s story, of what he must have gone through. He held onto them like someone too afraid to let go. So, Audata held him just as tightly in return, running a hand through his hair and back.

He was taller than her. Taller than Hieronymus. Much broader, too, with strong arms and a firm torso and callouses that weren’t born from handling simple farming tools.

As her hand ran up and down his spine, she wondered how many scars he hid under his clothes, how many times he had been hurt, how much he had suffered. She pushed those thoughts away just as quickly – Khaslana was back in her arms, alive and well. And that was enough.

“My little sun,” she muttered, and Khaslana reacted to one of his oldest nicknames, shifting his head on her shoulder. “Here, let me– Let me see you.”

Khaslana hesitated for a moment, but when Audata’s hands moved to his cheeks, to both sides of his head, he let her separate them enough for her – and Hieronymus, who was now discreetly wiping his tears away – to see his face properly.

Once again, it hit her just how much he had grown. How much he had grown… without them by his side.

He was now a proper young man. Audata could see traces of her own face in Khaslana’s – her nose, her lips, her cheekbones – as well as Hieronymus’ – his eyes, his chin, his face-shape – and also small details from his grandparents, too. He had changed, but all those tiny details made him him, they made up the face Audata had seen grow from a baby to an infant to a kid to a boy. And now– now, she could see that boy turned into a man.

It brought more tears to her eyes, and even though she was smiling, her lips trembled.

He had grown so much, and they hadn’t been there to see it, to guide him, to support him.

But they were here now, and they would stay – oh, they would stay, no matter what came their way. Not again.

Audata finally met his eyes and– Khaslana’s eyes were old, now. Older than he should have been. Ancient. Just what had he gone through? It sent another spike of pain through her heart, just another stab of sadness, but she pushed it away again – they were here, now. They were reunited. They would be– fine.

With a sigh, Audata let their foreheads touch softly, eyes closed. He felt Khaslana’s sigh as well, how his shoulders dropped.

And then–

“I’m sorry,” whispered Khaslana, voice rough, deeper than it had been back in the day, the last stroke of maturity lowering his voice even more.

Audata scrunched her nose at that.

“No, none of that,” she scolded softly, pinching one of his cheeks. He uttered a soft ‘ow’, but he didn’t really try to get out of her hold. “We understand why both you and Elysiae reacted like you did.”

“Still…” he tried again, as predictable as he had been when he was younger.

And Audata was tempted to laugh, then, but she bit it back, knowing that her laughter would turn manic or twist into more tears. And she’d already had enough tears for a lifetime – this was the moment for smiles, for joy, for relief. So, she smiled, so wide it hurt, and hugged her son again, just because she could.

Even now, taller than both Audata and Hieronymus, with countless scars criss-crossing on his skin, with ancient eyes that had seen everything in this world… Khaslana still slotted perfectly into her arms.

Chapter End Notes

*Throws confetti* They're together!
Having said that, this fic is probably taking another lil break for now. New Years is like a repeat Christmas here so... lots of stuff to do. See you next week!

chapters.title: Chapter 14: Hieronymus
chapters.html:
It still took Audata and Khaslana a long while to let go of each other. Hieronymus himself remained right next to them, like a firm guardian, covering them from any curious glances, an arm around his son’s – wider – shoulders.

By the time they both found it in themselves to separate, Audata’s eyes were red-rimmed and her face was splotchy and irritated from all the crying. Hieronymus tried to wipe her face with his sleeves, smiling at her like an idiot, high on the feeling of relief and fondness now running through his veins and encasing him in a cocoon of warmth.

“Ah– I didn’t… bring any tissues, I think,” muttered Khaslana, looking around at the few tables and pillows and colored rugs.

“It’s fine, it’s fine,” laughed Audata, and her next smile was the most beautiful thing Hieronymus had ever seen. “We’ll make do.”

Khaslana still huffed and reached down to a bag, half-hidden under the bench. Hieronymus could see a chaotic mess inside it – scrolls, notes, mismatched pens and snacks – and Khaslana rummaged inside for a moment, before he finally straightened out with a crumbled napkin in hand and a soft ‘aha’.

“Thank you,” said Audata, accepting said napkin with a smile. 

She kept looking at their son as if she couldn’t quite believe that he was in front of them – and to be honest, so did Khaslana. Hieronymus wondered if he himself also had that look in his eyes, that glint of dreaminess. He sure felt it, anyway. It was just– really nice to have Khaslana back with them, even if he would need some time to reconcile the two images he now had of his son, and even though he had to look away from some of the scars littering Khaslana’s visible skin to avoid getting swept up by uneasy thoughts.

As Audata rubbed at her face and eyes, Hieronymus took note of all the little differences that made it abundantly clear that this Khaslana looked... not how he remembered. Not to say that that was bad, but it was certainly… different.

Because Khaslana looked the very image of a hero of legend, now, thought Hieronymus, feeling a manic laugh trying to escape his mouth. He didn’t let it slip out, though. Instead, he took note of the high-quality clothes that Khaslana wore – the dark pants, the thick boots, the golden-embroidered shirt, the white and blue and gold coat left on the bench. He couldn’t help but be reminded of that mural that had marked the start of all their subsequent crises. For a moment, he wondered if the wings and halo depicted in that painting had been simply artistic freedom on the artist’s part. But, in a world of wonders and Titans and legendary figures and heroes that were – apparently – real, Hieronymus doubted it.

All in all, Khaslana – Phainon – looked like a legendary hero out of the stories of old. Once upon a time, this fact alone would have filled Hieronymus with pride and excitement. He would have jumped at the chance to ask about the adventures his son would have lived through, the sights he had laid eyes on, the people he would have met. It would be like Phainon had stepped into one of Cyrene’s stories, only to give it his own spin and come out later, bearing anecdotes and triumphant tales of his deeds.

But now, he knew better. He had seen the tired gazes of Amphoreus’ heroes, he had seen how the Chrysos Heirs tried to finish their duties, get Amphoreus its happy ending after a long and arduous fight. He had seen Cyrene – little Ely – struggle under this new reality that she hadn’t expected to survive long enough to witness and live in – because no matter how good Cyrene was with words and avoiding telling them the full truth, Hieronymus could see it in her eyes.

He saw that same struggle in Phainon’s eyes, too. That exhaustion. Those invisible scars hiding behind his usual smile, dimmed like the sun climbing down the sky at his back.

Because the stories only ever told the adventures of those legendary heroes, their contests, their fights, their happy endings full of hope – but when all was said and done, those stories never ventured further. They never touched upon what that ‘happy ending’ truly entailed, especially for the heroes, those saviors and deliverers that had given everything they had, everything they were, and who would need to take a step towards the future after their tale was over.

It was… 'sad' wasn’t the word Hieronymus was looking for, but it was the closest he could get to the feeling twisting in his chest as he looked at Phainon’s small and tired smile.

Hieronymus tried to ignore just how old and ancient his son’s gaze was now.

“You really made us come all the way over here to find you,” he said instead of the millions of questions bubbling in his chest. He placed a hand on Phainon’s shoulder, felt a bit bad when his son jumped slightly, and then smiled amusedly when Phainon’s cheeks flushed.

“Yes, well–” Phainon cleared his throat, and Hieronymus almost let out a sigh of relief. No matter what changed, he could still poke at his son and watch him struggle to bring out his silver tongue. “We didn’t think you would… you know, come back.”

Hieronymus felt some of his amusement dim at the slight crack in his voice. He tightened his hold on Phainon’s shoulder.

“It’s fine. After all, it was the perfect excuse to actually leave the village and see the world beyond,” he tried to joke, and that finally made Phainon’s crooked smile turn more genuine, lighter.

“That’s right, you wanted to travel around too,” muttered Phainon, a bit distant, as if he was shuffling through decades-old – or maybe even older? That didn’t seem right – memories, trying to find his footing again. “So, how did you like Amphoreus?”

“Ah, we probably didn’t get to see all the good stuff,” lamented Hieronymus, and if he dialed up the disappointment and exaggerated his regret– well, that was no one’s business. “Even here, in Okhema, we haven’t actually seen much.”

“Yes. We’ve only been around the southern district and Marmoreal Market…” chipped in Audata, finally done trying to tidy herself up. “Oh, well. We did get a guided tour of Marmoreal Palace, too…”

Hieronymus had expected– maybe some annoyance, maybe some anger, at the fact that his companions had definitely gone behind his back to keep them apart – and Hieronymus could admit that he felt a bit wrong-footed and resentful himself – but Phainon only nodded in understanding and recognition.

“The Tribios sisters, right?” he asked, even though he seemed to be perfectly aware of what had happened a couple of days before. His next smile was a bit rueful. “They are good guides… They helped me a lot when I first came to Okhema.”

“It must have been very overwhelming,” mumbled Audata. Her hand found Phainon’s and she held on tightly, as if the world would take him away again as soon as she looked away, as soon as their hands separated. Hieronymus couldn’t blame her.

“It… was,” admitted Phainon, with a tilt of his head. He was struggling to open up, saw Hieronymus, but he didn’t bring it up – it was only natural, he thought. The air around them turned a bit too dark, a bit too heavy, and Phainon clearly noticed, because he took a breath and tried to widen his smile. “But, now I can say pretty confidently that I know every nook and cranny in this city. I know all the best spots, so… I can give you a tour, when things calm down a bit.”

When Okhema wasn’t overflowing with people from all over, he probably meant.

“That sounds lovely, Phainon,” said Audata, squeezing his hand, her smile brilliant and eyes alight with relief and love.

Phainon’s answering smile was just as relieved, and it hit Hieronymus, then – if Phainon was anything like Cyrene, then he had probably agonized over this reunion for hours, trying to calm himself enough not to mess it up – ha! As if he could ever mess it up.

They fell into a comfortable silence. They all alternated between looking at the orange and red skies and staring at each other as if they were trying to brand every little detail into their minds. It still felt surreal – Hieronymus looked forward to the day when it didn’t anymore.

“It’s getting late,” he commented, when more than half of the sky was already dark. Audata’s wide eyes turned to him immediately, hand tense around Phainon’s. Phainon himself blinked, dragging himself out of his thoughts – and it happened a lot, now, Hieronymus had noticed. “We should return to the inn.”

Audata opened her mouth once, then closed it, then grimaced. She took a deep breath and finally let go of Phainon’s hand. It looked like a monumental task, and it would have been amusing, if Hieronymus didn’t have to talk himself into standing up from the bench and parting from his son’s encompassing warmth.

Only, Phainon hummed, tapped his fingers on the bench and looked up. Something moved in the air, then – a flash of gold, thin and delicate. It was mildly familiar, but before he could bring attention to it, Phainon rose slowly from the bench as well and smiled, a bit nervously.

“Or… you could stay at Marmoreal Palace,” he offered, a bit too cautious to be called light and easy. “We have enough rooms, after all. And– it’s such a long way back to the southern district.” Phainon paused and blinked and then his eyes widened. “But– You don’t have to accept, if you don’t want to.”

Hieronymus crossed a short glance with Audata. They couldn’t refuse it, even when their humble origins clashed greatly with the grandeur around them, even when the offer made them nervous, even when– Because it was their son asking. This was an olive branch, an outstretched hand, an open door. And they would never turn their backs on him.

“If you’re sure,” was Audata’s soft answer.

Phainon’s eyes lost their previous apprehension and nervousness. Instead, they shone with relief and contentment.

“And if you won’t get in trouble for it,” pointed out Hieronymus, just as he had done back in the day, when Phainon got one of his best-worst ideas.

At that, Phainon’s eyes shone with a strange mix of amusement and confidence.

“Don’t underestimate how much pull I have around here,” he said, cryptically, amusedly. He gathered his bag and put on his coat, and Hieronymus had to admit: he did look like someone who was pretty influential. “Let’s go. Aglaea already knows and is probably figuring out the logistics.”

Hieronymus and Audata crossed another glance, a bit surprised about the entire situation, but... They trusted Phainon. They trusted their son.

And so, they followed him back inside.

—

Phainon and Tribbie had guided them to their new room, which was… almost as big as their house back in Aedes Elysiae, with its private bath and a balcony with a breathtaking view of the mountains surrounding the Holy City. 

The other two Tribios had carried their luggage to their room soon after, and Hieronymus had wondered how they had managed to be this quick with something that wasn’t planned – probably – before he remembered that these people were the ones that had been avoiding the countless crises all around Amphoreus.

“I’ll see you… tomorrow,” had said Phainon, smiling softly, still looking at them with a strange glint in his eyes. His words also grated in Hieronymus’ ears, but he couldn’t say why.

When they had finally been left alone, Audata and Hieronymus had crashed into each other’s arms and wept again, feeling tall waves of relief sweeping them off their feet.

That night, Hieronymus’ dreams were peaceful and pleasant. For the first time in months, he woke up feeling refreshed and rested. Audata seemed to share his newfound peace, because she smiled widely and pretty much glowed under the morning sun as they changed and took care to make themselves presentable – there was something intimidating about the Palace, with its grand halls and ridiculously expensive furniture and rugs and decorations. One single lamp probably cost as much as a year of meals in Aedes Elysiae.

After that, they soon found themselves a bit… lost.

“Should we… wait for someone to fetch us or…?” asked Audata, approaching the door with hesitant hands.

“I don’t really remember much about that tour,” admitted Hieronymus with a crooked smile and a light shrug. Audata sighed, troubled. “We would get lost immediately if we wandered off.”

“Let’s just–” Audata cut herself off, opening the door and stepping out. The hallways were peaceful and empty, but there were voices coming from somewhere near. Audata looked from side to side, trying to figure out where they should go. “Maybe…”

“Ah, you’re awake!” came a familiar voice, warm and sweet, and Hieronymus blinked when Hyacine appeared from a random corner and approached them, smile wide and eyes much brighter than before. “That’s good. Don’t worry, you can come with me to have breakfast.”

Hieronymus, once again, felt terribly grateful for this girl. He sighed in relief, a hand on his chest.

“That would be great,” he said, pushing a bit of amusement into his voice. He felt light, now, after all, reunited with his son and little Ely. Suddenly, braving this new world that had continued on without them didn’t feel as intimidating.

Hyacine’s smile widened and gestured for them to follow her and her… flying horse. Pegasus? Unicorn? Hieronymus shuffled through legends in his mind, getting caught up in some stories about the Sky people, but ultimately, he gave up when all he found in his dusty memory was vague names and conflicts.

“Are Phainon and Cyrene up?” asked Audata as Hyacine led them through twists and turns, down stairs and around corners.

Hyacine hummed, taking a moment to think.

“Cirey probably stayed up late, reading,” she listed off, amusement clear in her voice. “And Phainon… Well, he tends to sleep until late, now.” Hyacine probably felt their tangible disappointment, because she turned to smile at them. “Don’t worry, they’ll show up soon.”

They finally arrived at what seemed to be a dining room, connected to a kitchen hidden behind a thin wall. Hyacine gestured for them to sit at the table, where Castorice was revising a tablet with sleepy eyes. The girl noticed them and waved at them, but soon returned to her revising, taking small bites of her fruity breakfast from time to time.

At that, Audata took a sudden breath, before she dashed away from Hieronymus’ side. He stared after her, already halfway sitting on the klismos, a question on the tip of his tongue. Soon enough, he heard her talking with Hyacine in the kitchen, so he stood up again and inched his way closer.

“...  and honey.” Audata was listing off ingredients, but she soon noticed Hieronymus. He leaned on the doorway, arms crossed and staring curiously as Audata talked to an attentive Hyacine and… a tall and strong blond man that continued his routine while keeping an ear out for whatever Audata’s idea was. “If it’s too much trouble–”

“Oh, no, no, don’t worry,” cut her off Hyacine, smile blinding from how bright it was. “I’m sure we have the ingredients. Right, De?”

The other man stilled for a second, before he hummed and checked a few cupboards. He took out said ingredients and placed them on the counter, seemingly ticking off each one in his mind.

“Thank you,” said Audata, all warmth and relief. Then, she paused again and tapped a finger on her chin. “Now that I think about it… we’ve seen each other before, right? You’re…”

“Mydei,” said the man, a bit pointed, a bit… maybe awkward. Or maybe nervous. Hieronymus couldn’t figure out which one it was, but it was weird, because why would someone this important-looking feel nervous or awkward when talking with two humble farmers? He was decked in gold and red, probably Kremnoan if Hieronymus remembered the rumors about them correctly, probably a Chrysos Heir.

Huh. Oh, well. He only hoped that Mydei would open up and relax around them – and he also hoped that they could do the same, because right now, his shoulders were a bit too tense. He had to make peace with it – this man was just another Chrysos Heir, just like Phainon, just like Cyrene.

“Are you already taking over the kitchen?” he asked, forcing his voice to sound as amused as it would back home, even if he was now surrounded by quite a few important people – heroes.

Audata turned to him with an unimpressed stare, and Hieronymus widened his smile into a grin.

“I’m just fulfilling my promise to our son,” she said with a soft sniff, pointed. 

(Next to her, Mydei startled slightly and almost knocked over the cup of grapefruit juice he was pouring for himself.

Hyacine sent a confused glance at him, but Mydei shook his head, letting his long hair hide his flustered expression.)

“Should I help?” he asked, arching an eyebrow, knowing perfectly well that Audata would sooner carry him over her shoulder to get him out of the kitchen than let him anywhere near a pan.

Audata huffed and shooed him away, already making preparations to make… pancakes, Hieronymus guessed.

Oh. Pancakes. With honey and venison. Wasn’t that…?

“I’ll help,” said Mydei, a bit too firm and serious for an offer of help. 

But Audata seemed to see something in his eye when their gazes met, because she smiled softly and nodded, passing him the flour.

“My pleasure,” she said, good-naturedly. “You seem to know this kitchen well.”

“I’m in charge of cooking meals sometimes, yes,” answered Mydei, following Audata’s lead – Hieronymus wondered if cooks could communicate with their minds, because Mydei never asked what they were making and Audata never announced it, either.

“Oh! Then you should definitely tell me some of your most popular recipes!” said Audata. Mydei looked at her, eyes wide and seemingly surprised with just how friendly she was from the get-go, before a nostalgic shine passed through his eyes and he nodded.

Ah, Audata. As reliable as always. In just a couple of minutes, she had managed to get Mydei to relax and open up a bit to her. Hieronymus wasn’t surprised.

That settled, he eyed the fruit basket and then immediately picked a bowl of grapes as soon as he saw them. The taste was familiar, after all, and he could do with something familiar in a place that was the complete opposite of home– but that could become a second one, he thought, if given enough time. After all, part of his family was already here. And his family’s new family, too. Because he was no fool, and the more he saw the Chrysos Heir interact with each other, the clearer their tight bond became.

(What had they gone through together, to forge such a deep and unbreakable bond between them?)

Hieronymus returned to the other room with his bowl and finally sat down to eat and wait. Castorice only glanced at him for a second, before she continued writing away, but she did offer her own plate of sliced fruit to him.

He didn’t know what he was waiting for, exactly – for Audata to finish her new self-impossed mission, or maybe for Cyrene and Phainon to appear – but he let himself relax and gaze around the room, the landscape on the other side of the window, the little nick-nacks strewn around the place that made something warm nest in his chest.

“... for that, I can ask Phainon. He has been revising the historical records of that time, so he might have some ideas,” came Lady Aglaea’s soft voice, focused and serious. Soon, she was walking through the door, with scrolls under her arm and pinched eyebrows, talking down–

“There is no rush. The first step will always be rebuilding, the ceremonies can be held later,” replied the other girl… woman? She was short, but the air around her was alight with intensity and royalty, and the crown on her head was terribly noteworthy, so much so that Hieronymus was thrown back to the history lessons from his childhood.

Imperator Cerydra’s eyes locked on him after a quick sweep of the room, sharp and blazing. 

Hieronymus tried not to choke on his food, lowering his head in clear deference, berating himself for not paying more attention during the old priests’ etiquette classes, back in the day– why would he need to learn? He had argued that when he was just a naive kid, but oh, now it would have been helpful to know how to salute an old Imperator of legend.

“Don’t,” said Imperator ordered, raising a hand. Hieronymus’ panicking mind stumbled on itself as he stared at Imperator Cerydra, eyes wide. “You’re Dux Solaris’ parent. There is no need for useless salutes and shows of respect between us.”

“A-ah…” Hieronymus cleared his throat, wrong-footed and lost. Behind Imperator Cerydra, Lady Aglaea smiled, amused, and nodded. “Thank you, great Imperator…”

Imperator Cerydra – the real deal, apparently, decided Hieronymus’ hysterical brain – nodded, satisfied, before she made her way to the kitchen with quick strides. More voices came from inside of it, the sound of a ceramic bowl almost falling to the floor, and Hieronymus smiled to himself, because he could almost feel Audata’s panic through the wall, so similar to the panic he had felt just moments before.

Lady Aglaea sat down next to Castorice, leaving her scrolls on the table as well. Castorice, once again, offered her the half-empty plate of fruit, and Aglaea hummed in thanks and accepted.

“I’m happy for you,” said Lady Aglaea, then, and only then did Hieronymus notice that the woman was looking at him with a small smile. “I have it on good authority that your reunion with Phainon went well.”

“Yes,” nodded Hieronymus, voice falling into something softer, relief once again bleeding into his voice. “We must thank you, for your clues.”

Lady Aglaea’s smile turned a bit painful, a bit regretful.

“I was… too heavy-handed with them, I’m afraid,” she said and– ah. Hieronymus shook his head, but he couldn’t quite get the image of Phainon, panicked and overwhelmed, speeding away from them, out of his mind. “I should have been more careful.”

Before Hieronymus could say anything, the door opened once again and a soft laugh like bell chimes warmed the room.

“All’s well that ends well,” said Cyrene, elegant like her handwriting, hands behind her back. She eyed the now-dwindling fruit on the plate, hummed, and then offered the plate to her companion with a glint in her eye.

“I don’t blame you for anything, Aglaea,” was Phainon’s answer, coupled with a small smile. 

Aglaea returned it with a slight shake of her head, fond, but she didn’t say anything else. Instead, she accepted Castorice’s finished tablet and added it to her small pile of scrolls that she needed to carry away once again. She took a last piece of apple from the plate now in Cyrene’s hold and stood up to leave, not before crossing a knowing smile with Phainon.

After that, Phainon's gaze immediately sought Hieronymus. And there it was again, that spark of surprise, of dreaminess, of relief. Hieronymus could relate to that, because even now, even knowing that their son was okay and in touching distance, seeing Phainon in front of him, tangible and different from what they remembered, felt… strange. But also really relieving.

Hieronymus smiled at him and Phainon smiled back, looking a bit dazed.

“Ah, the sleepy-heads are finally up,” came Hyacine’s amused voice. She came out of the kitchen, dragging her little pegasus with her, even as the poor thing tried to return to the kitchen.

“Weren’t you the one who threatened– ahem, advised us to get all the rest we needed?” pointed out Phainon, amusement clear in his voice. And that glint of teasing in his eyes was very familiar.

“Yes, I did. But that means that I also get the right to tease you about it,” came Hyacine’s quick response, just as amused. She huffed a laugh as she walked over to Phainon, reaching out and... catching a golden feather that had been stuck to Phainon’s coat. “You should also check your clothes for any feathers before going out.”

Phainon’s smile turned a bit crooked at that, a flush on his cheeks as he accepted the feather from Hyacine’s hold. Cyrene hid a chuckle behind her hair as her hand hovered over the few pieces of fruit left.

Hieronymus, for his part, only stared as the sunlight coming from the window bounced off the feather, a brilliant gold that reflected on the walls. So, the wings on the mural were… probably real. Huh.

“Good morning everyone!” came the cheerful voice of Tribbie from the door, and soon, the previously peaceful room turned into a hurricane of people coming and going, as awake as the farmers during harvest season, where they needed to wake up before the ‘day’ even started.

Hieronymus waved at Phainon, then, and his son came over to sit between him and Cyrene, who also offered the plate of fruit to him. As Phainon debated which fruit he would eat, Hieronymus smiled, feeling that warmth flourish in his chest once again. Oh, how he had missed this. Even now, changed and different from what he once remembered, they could still sit down and have breakfast together.

“Ah, Phainon, Cyrene. There you are.” Audata finally stepped out of the kitchen, smile warm and fond. In her hands she held a plate of very familiar pancakes. 

Hieronymus turned in his seat, just in time to see Phainon finally realize what his mother was holding. His eyes widened, then, his breath caught in his chest. Hieronymus’ smile widened.

“Those are…” breathed Phainon, standing up as Audata reached the table.

She offered the plate of pancakes to him, smile a bit more wobbly than before, eyes a bit teary. Phainon gaped at her, at the plate of pancakes, looking at them as if they were the best thing he had ever seen. He took the plate with hands that should have been shaky, but that were as firm and steady as any swordsman’s, and placed it on the table, out of the way, just so he could give his mother another tight hug.

Audata laughed, but it sounded a bit too teary this time, a bit too close to tears.

“Thank you,” whispered Phainon, voice thick.

“I promised, didn’t I?” whispered back Audata, clinging to Phainon as tightly as he did to her. “Plus, I had help.”

Phainon’s head moved to the kitchen’s door, then, seeking said ‘help’. Mydei, leaning against the doorframe with his arms crossed over his chest, tilted his head. Phainon huffed a laugh at that, soft and fond.

“C’mon, then,” pushed Cyrene, looking at the pancakes with a shine of nostalgia in her eyes. “Let’s dig in.”

“Of course.” Phainon stepped away from Audata’s embrace, and he sat down on his seat again, but his eyes still sought out Mydei. He gestured for the other man to join them, a glint of– something, in his eyes. “You too. You helped, right? You have to eat them too.”

Mydei huffed and shook his head, but he still sat down to eat with them, anyway.

It hit Hieronymus, then, how nostalgic yet so unfamiliar this image was.

Conversation flowed easily between them, so easily that soon, Castorice and the Tribios sisters had been dragged into it as well. They reminisced on the old days, they got to know the other three – six? – Chrysos Heirs better, and they remained at the table for probably longer than the other demigods should have been, considering that they still had a mountain of work to do.

(He did notice how quiet Phainon got sometimes, a distant shine to his eyes, smile a bit too small. Hieronymus was still trying to figure out how to read him now that he had changed so much, but if what he was getting was right, then… Phainon wasn’t as dissimilar from them, after all. He was still having a hard time processing and realizing that this moment was, in fact, real.

And he did notice how Cyrene remained mostly quiet, even as sometimes she joked and winked. She never touched anyone. She kept still, hands fidgeting, almost as if she wanted to reach out, but she still held herself back. Everytime.)

Hieronymus felt a bit bad when Castorice looked at the time and immediately rushed off with flushed cheeks, leaving a streak of violet in her wake.

“I’ve been thinking,” said Trianne, and immediately, all the present Chrysos Heirs exchanged worried looks. “Don’t look at me like that! It’s a nice idea!” She cleared her throat, falling back into a more serious expression that threatened to crumble under the sheer excitement she felt. “The idea is… to make a banquet tonight! To celebrate! Just between us!”

At that, the Chrysos Heirs paused, considering the idea, a bit surprised. Hieronymus wondered what kinds of ideas Trianne usually came up with, for them to act like this hadn’t blown up in their faces.

“That’s… actually a good idea,” said Cyrene, slowly, a bit shocked. Trianne sniffed.

“Did someone mention a banquet?” came a new voice, and Hieronymus startled. The new woman, dark-haired and blue-eyed, clothes adorned with pearls and... straight-up water looked expectantly at them.

“Yes, yes, we can celebrate a feast,” said Tribbie, and even though she tried to be serious about it, she was almost bouncing on her seat. “We still need to ask Agy and Cery, but I’m sure they’ll say yes.”

The woman smiled wide, and suddenly, she looked younger than she probably was, eyes glowing like the sea under the sun.

“I’ll talk to the green dolphin.” And with that cryptid sentence, she rushed off again, with a skip to her step.

“Green dolphin?” asked Hieronymus at the group at large.

“That would be Professor Anaxa,” answered Phainon, as if it was the most normal thing in the world. It wasn’t.

Hieronymus crossed a glance with Audata. She only shrugged. That was fair. They were learning quite a lot about the eccentricities that all Chrysos Heirs – revered heroes – seemed to have. It was… nice. Humane.

“I’ll figure out the menu, then,” sighed Mydei, standing up from the table, gaze a bit distant, lost in thought as he most likely made a list of all possible dishes and available ingredients.

“Do you need any help?” asked Phainon, looking up at him with a knowing glance.

“I think you already have a task waiting for you,” said Mydei, arching an eyebrow at Phainon. When Phainon tilted his head to the side, confused, Mydei shook his head. “Talk to Aglaea. They need your input on something.”

“I can help,” came Audata’s predictable offer, once again.

“No, no! You’re our guest!” Trianne glared at her, hands on her hips, but Audata chuckled.

“It would be my pleasure, though,” she said, anyway, and soon the table was immersed into yet another discussion, throwing ideas to the wind and trying to organize a relaxed event between workaholics.

Hieronymus leaned back with a smile and relished in the moment.

Indeed, this could become their second home, no problem.

Chapter End Notes

I'm back! Man, Christmas season is always chaos. But now, back to the promised fluff!
This chapter ran away from me btw. It was supposed to include the dinner, but… *looks at word count* yeah, no.

chapters.title: Chapter 15: Audata
chapters.html:
Audata got her way, and so, she spent most of the day holed up in the kitchen as her husband ran errands for them at the market and Mydei and Hyacine became her great companions in the kitchen.

It was… nice. Nicer than she had expected, when Phainon had offered for them to stay at the Palace. Audata had been hesitant – they came from a humble farming village in the middle of nowhere, after all – and intimidated, but the longer she stayed and the more she saw, it became abundantly clear that her son had opened the door for them to meet and get to know his new family.

And, for all the exaggerated stories and new legends that talked of golden-blooded heroes, Audata was starting to understand just how– human all the Chrysos Heirs were.
