She had already noticed it during that first speech, in which Castorice’s hands shook and in which Lady Aglaea huffed at a slight imperfection in her dress, but now… Now, she could see Hyacine scolding Little Ica when the pegasus tried to snack on the ingredients she had been preparing for twenty minutes. Now she could see Hysilens practice her music outside the window and get frustrated when she couldn’t get the piece just right. Now she could see the three Tribios yelling at Professor Anaxa to stay away from the kitchen – “He will make something explode, I just know it! The kitchen is not a lab, Naxy!” – and then push him away like a torrent of red hair and wings. 

Now, she could see Phainon – who had dropped by later, clearly tired but glowing with the satisfaction of a job well done – bicker with Mydei as they argued about how to best prepare the meat.

(Mydei ended up pushing him out of the kitchen, just like Professor Anaxa had been, while Phainon laughed loudly and almost ended up slamming into the door. Audata’s heart sang.)

Now, she could see Cyrene hovering by the door, hands clasped behind her, eyes amused but a bit distant, only for Hyacine to find her and hand her a bowl of what would be the dessert – Cyrene froze it within seconds, and both pink-haired girls laughed together. “Efficiency”, called it Hyacine.

(Cyrene stayed for a bit longer, so Audata gave her some fruit to slice. She, as always, jumped to the chance to help, and Audata kept an eye on her as Cyrene tried to cut the fruits without freezing them in the process. The answering smile was rueful but bright with pride.)

Audata watched each show of genuine care between them, each familiar touch, with a small smile and a weight that had been her most loyal companion for months – ever since she woke up alone in her home – finally… lifted off her chest.

By the time dinner came around, Audata was a bit tired, but the excitement kept her from plopping down on her bed. Instead, she took a short bath – and squinted at all the oils and soaps available – and agonized over her too cheap clothes, before Hieronymus finally found her and dragged her off to the official dining room: a large room, bordered by tall columns of alabaster, golden-linned windows that showed the beautiful dusk and a long table now piled with the food they had spent all day preparing.

“You really went all out, huh?” came Phainon’s voice from behind them, and Audata turned to smile at him. His eyes were a bit distant – which seemed to be… more common than she would have liked – but he still looked down at her and returned her smile. “Thank you.”

“There’s no need to thank me,” she pointed out, but Phainon huffed out a soft laugh, shook his head and then walked to the table – he sat down to Aglaea’s right in a practiced motion, which seemed meaningful, somehow, just like his sudden thankfulness.

The other Chrysos Heirs trickled into the room slowly, but each of them made themselves known, anyway, be it from talking between them or arguing or rushing inside after a race.

When everyone was finally seated and already looking at all the food with hungry and interested eyes, Imperator Cerydra – and Audata still had a difficult time processing the fact that they were sharing space with such a legendary, uh… monarch – stood up and tapped her cup. Immediately, all conversation died down and all eyes were on her, expectant.

“We gather here today to welcome a fellow Chrysos Heir’s parents,” she announced, severe and heavy. Aduata felt her cheeks flush. Hieronymus grabbed her hand, probably even more obvious than her. “They have braved Amphoreus’ current stormy situation and arduous paths to come here, to the Holy City, and they have also faced their own situation with honor and bravery. Thus, they deserve all our respect and collaboration.”

There was a moment of silence, in which Phainon sent them an amused smile and Cyrene clapped her hands once in a clear show of support – and just how red were their faces, then? – before Lady Aglaea stood up as well and opened her arms.

“Now, please, dig in,” she said, firm and elegant like her golden dress and the light that glinted off her jewelry. “Let’s make this a night to remember.”

And somehow, that last word felt terribly significant to all of them – a few of the Chrysos Heirs raised their cups and nodded, small smiles on their faces and shooting knowing glances at each other.

After that, dinner was much less stiff. Conversation flowed between everyone, some louder than others, but every word left it clear just how close they all were with each other.

Imperator Cerydra, Lady Aglaea and Mydei got tangled in a heated discussion about systems of governance and which regimes were doomed from the start – the third bottle of wine they had taken hostage passed from one hand to the other, until Lady Aglaea discreetly passed it off to Phainon with a pointed glance and Phainon innocently passed it off to both Hieronymus and Audata, who in turn tried to pass it off to Hyacine and Professor Anaxa and– paused, because the Professor was just throwing back his cup and taking a long gulp of his own drink in the middle of his argument with Hyacine, who alternated between arguing back good-naturedly and pushing Little Ica back when the pegasus tried to eat her food. 

By their side, the Tribios sisters seemed to be arguing about who would eat what so they could taste every single dish, and said argument veered off into loud complaints between two, while the third expertly moved the plates out of the way when a flash of lightning passed by them and tried to steal their food. Cipher appeared on her seat, cackling, before she shifted targets and tried to steal from Phainon, Cyrene and Castorice, who were now talking over a very old scroll that shouldn’t be on top of a dining table full of food. Audata sent an unimpressed stare at her son, but Phainon only smiled and resumed his long-winded defense, only to be cut off again when Cipher tried to sweep a bowl of vegetable soup from him and he had to slam his hand on the table, almost knocking over half the plates in the process.

“Not a chance!” hissed Phainon, steely with resolve as he watched Cipher. Cyrene and Castorice made sure that the scroll was untouched, sending reproachful glances at Phainon.

“Ah, right, right,” nodded Cipher, and something in her eyes spelt trouble. “You need to eat your veggies to outrun the sun, after all!”

Phainon fell silent at that, eyes wide and mouth slightly agape as he stared at Cipher, speechless and leaving his food unsupervised.

“How…?” he asked, a bit strangled, but Cipher took the chance to dive in again and managed to snatch away the chicken he had set aside for later. He gaped at her, offended, but then his surprise turned into a familiar shine of competitiveness and challenge in his eyes. “Cipher!”

Audata had to hide her laughter behind her hand. And it was then that she could finally put words to the feeling bubbling in her chest: chaotic and joyous… like a family dinner.

There was something in that loud room that reminded her of home, of loud family gatherings during the festivities and during the harvest. The warmth emanating from the group was like the sun, gentle and bright and all-encompassing. From time to time, Audata heard someone laughing, and when she turned to look, it was like seeing someone for the first time again – they all looked younger, lighter.

“They don’t look like living legends now, do they?” whispered Hieronymus next to her, eyes bright as he looked around, hand relaxed around his own cup of wine.

“They look like a family,” muttered back Audata. Hieronymus crossed a knowing glance at her and they shared a secret smile.

Even after eating most of the food, the group of Chrysos Heirs – plus two farmers, which was still wild – remained around the table, only now, they exchanged places with each other, talking with different people. Audata and Hieronymus tried to follow their rhythm, moving with them and finding themselves talking with each Chrysos Heir at least once. 

Their lost bottle of wine finally found its place next to Hysilens’ never-ending pile of empty plates, and so Audata asked her about her music and favorite songs.

During her conversation with Castorice about the care of plants and flowers – the girl seemed terribly paranoid about hurting the plants in her care, for some reason – Audata caught Mydei’s eye and gave him a thumbs-up to celebrate the success of their joint menu. He awkwardly returned it.

At some point, Cerydra yelled at Anaxa and pushed away the plates and cups and cutlery away from her corner of the table, placing instead a... a chess board. She then pointed at the professor and challenged him to a match. And then another. And then another.

And soon, the entire table had chosen sides and cheered for their favorite, treating it like some kind of sport. Audata and Hieronymus hovered in the middle, a bit nervous about getting on the bad side of a talented and – maybe? – dangerous professor and the literal Imperator. They tried to seek some kind of guidance from their son, who was now hiding a wide grin behind his hand as he watched the match and whispered with Aglaea about the movements. When they couldn’t get Phainon’s attention, they tried Cyrene, but they also found a wall, because said girl was scribbling with the Tribios sisters into a notebook that she then showed to everyone: the tally, decorated with caricatures of the two challengers.

And Audata couldn’t quite contain her laughter at that, trying to stifle it behind a hand as her shoulders shook and the entire group complimented the drawings loudly, so loudly that the two challengers had to look up and stare at the drawing and its proud creators. Something was shared between the two, then, before the professor smirked and–

“Checkmate,” he said, smugness pouring out of his voice.

Cerydra’s answering glare was fiery.

She cleared the board and started replacing the pieces.

“Again,” she said, and it was mostly an order. Not that Anaxa seemed to mind, because his smirk only grew and he followed her lead, placing his pieces back into the starter position.

“Oh, this is going to take forever!” complained Cipher, throwing her hands up and almost dropping her piece of cake.

Trianne gasped, offended, and jumped at her, but Cipher yelped and dodged just in time.

“That’s my cake!” she yelled, before throwing herself into the fray again.

Cipher cackled and took another bite of cake just to spite her.

Audata and Hieronymus fell back, then. Hieronymus nursed another cup of wine – and Audata wondered if she should cut him off before he could say something stupid in front of all these important people – and Audata leaned her elbows on the table, watching as Cerydra and Anaxa started muttering dramatic one-liners at each other, much to Cyrene, Castorice and Hyacine’s amusement as they all cheered exaggeratedly at each word and insult like children.

She smiled softly. This dinner had been the perfect way to mix them all together. It had let them meet and know these people as people, not as figures on top of a pedestal. But it also seemed to have helped the Chrysos Heirs too. It was in the little things, she thought; in how relaxed the leaders of the group were, in how mischief could run rampant at a moment’s notice, in how discussions rose in volume and how laughter echoed around the room.

Phainon’s usually distant and tired eyes were now bright like the sun. Maybe not quite as much as when he was a kid, unburdened by whatever he had gone through, but he smiled, he tried to talk circles around the other Chrysos Heirs – and failed, because they knew him too well to fall for his tricks – and, more importantly, he laughed, loud and light.

Cyrene, who had been a bit too similar to a ghost before, from what Audata had been able to see, was now in the middle of it all, cheering and narrating the match with her usual dramatic flair and a wide grin and bright eyes. She still jumped a bit when Hyacine touched her arm or when Castorice whispered something in her ear, but her smile was genuine.

And Audata finally understood what Hieronymus had mentioned, about this being Phainon and Cyrene’s second family and how they could make it their own, too, in their own way.

Audata tried to imagine all these people – with their grander-than-life presence, their glittering clothes, their cautious and tired eyes – back in Aedes Elysiae, and… She could see them. She could see them running or walking through the golden fields of wheat, she could see them sitting at the dock, looking out at the sea, she could see them sitting at the Courtyard and chatting, she could…

She could see this new life working. Because– Audata was seeing them, not as Chrysos Heirs, but as what was after. 

Scarred, exhausted, haunted by too many ghosts and bad choices and suffering, just like all heroes in the stories would have been, had their stories covered this ‘after’. But they were still hopeful, still willing to step forward and continue living – and that alone was enough to make Audata respect them more than anyone else in her life.

She could see how comfortable Phainon and Cyrene were with these people, and really, why would they even separate them? Why should they, when they could just accept them all into their own not-quite-normal family?

Audata closed her eyes and the loud cheers and laughter transported her to the past, to when Phainon and Cyrene and the other children in Aedes Elysiae were the fresh air their little coastal village needed to be alive.

Yes, Aedes Elysiae was nothing if not accepting, especially when it came to kind-hearted people – Little Ely, mysterious baby under a tree, was proof of that.

“Hey, no, no kissing in here!” yelled Cipher, far too amused to be serious. Audata’s eyes snapped open, anyway, frowning at the woman and then following her gaze to… “No PDA! There are children present!”

“Ciphy! We’re not a child!” yelled back Trianne, as Cipher covered Trinnon’s eyes with her hands and a wide, wide grin. "We're literally older than you!"

Audata, though, was too busy staring as Phainon and Mydei – who had been innocently talking with each other in soft words… maybe a bit too close to each other? – startled and looked at Cipher with wide eyes and flushed cheeks and–

Oh. Wait.

What?

“Cipher!” hissed Phainon, and oh, his quick glance at both Hieronymus and Audata was as damning as ever, just like when he had been a kid trying to hide anything from his parents. Audata’s mind went blank. “We– I haven’t–”

“Oh, that’s a you problem!” chirped Cipher, far too amused for her own good.

Mydei rubbed his eyes and then left his fingers pressing the bridge of his nose.

“I’m going to crystallize her stupid coin,” he muttered under his breath.

Phainon sighed, a bit defeated, glancing at their immobile figures at the table. He shook his head, he sent a pointed glance at Cipher – who just cackled and rushed off, chased by Trianne and Tribbie – and then grabbed Mydei’s hand and dragged him to Hieronymus and Audata’s seats, a determined set to his jaw and a sharp shine to his eyes. 

Oh, this was serious. Audata took a deep breath, tried to shake off the surprise and then met Phainon’s gaze head-on. It reminded her of how he had come to them days– no, years before, firm on his decision to leave the village and find his own path.

“I’m sorry. I was going to tell you when the time presented itself, but…” he sighed, sent another pointed glance at Cipher’s retreating back, and then he smiled ruefully. “Yes. Mydei and I are… an item.”

“A couple,” cleared up Mydei with a roll of his eyes, but even then, Audata could see the tension on his shoulders, how he tightened his grip around her son’s hand, how his face seemed a bit too pinched.

Phainon, too, rolled his eyes, but he nodded.

“Yes. A couple,” he said, putting a bit too much amused emphasis on the word and getting an unimpressed stare for his trouble. That amusement didn’t last long, though, as Phainon, for once, stumbled on his tongue. “We uh–”

Audata didn’t let him continue. She stood up, eyes firm and a hand on Hieronymus’ shoulder.

She met Mydei’s eyes, and for a moment, she tried to think back to all the times she had seen this man interacting with her son and– how hadn’t she seen it before? When she thought back, it was clear as day. These two had a bond as firm as steel, as unbreakable as the earth. She still didn’t know what they had gone through to make their eyes have such an ancient shine to them, but– she was sure that they had gone through it together.

And that was more than enough for her.

So, she smiled softly, saw Mydei’s eyes widen with surprise – and why would he be surprised? – and then she was hugging him. It didn’t matter that she was much smaller than him, that he seemed tense and frozen under her arms, that she could feel his breath hitch for a second. She hugged him and smiled and said:

“Welcome to the family.”

And Mydei took a moment to process her words, but when he did, he finally let out a long breath, his shoulders dropped and– He hugged her back, careful, so careful, and so, so warm.

Hieronymus stood up, a bit unsteady on his feet, and clapped Mydei on the shoulder. Audata didn’t need to see him to imagine the lopsided grin he most definitely had in his face.

“Welcome to the family, indeed,” he said, amused. “I don’t know what you’ve seen in our son–”

“Dad!” cut Phainon, mildly offended and embarrassed, and Audata–

Audata laughed and stepped back and looked at Mydei again and decided: yes, Aedes Elysiae had enough room for all these beautiful and bright people.

—

The next morning, Audata took the time to relish in the private bath. She tried at least six oils, three soaps, and by the time she came out, her hair smelled the most fresh it ever had and her skin was wrinkled.

Hieronymus squinted at her from the bed, clearly suffering the effects of a hangover.

“Did I dream that Phainon was dating the former Kremnoan king or was that real?” he asked, confused and lost.

“It’s real,” answered Audata, unbothered, as she frowned at her everyday clothes and once again felt the spikes of inadequacy poke at her previous assuredness.

“Oh,” was Hieronymus’ flat response.

He spent the next few minutes staring at the ceiling, mind sluggish and lost. Audata stifled a laugh behind her hand, but she waited for Hieronymus to get ready to start their day anyway, looking out to the distant clump of buildings. Marmoreal Palace stood like a haven of peace, empty of the countless visitors that filled the streets and mostly quiet, with no protests and no chaos. Audata could understand why the Chrysos Heirs had decided to close their gates if it meant that they could work in peace.

The journey to the kitchen was still a bit unfamiliar, but fortunately, they remembered enough between the both of them to find their way and they managed to not get lost on the way. Even then, the last stretch of their walk was guided by the voices of who they soon recognized as their son talking with Aglaea and Cerydra.

“... You don’t have to do it if you really don’t want to,” was saying Aglaea, and something in her heavy tone made Audata stop in the middle of the hallway and grab Hieronymus’ arm before they could walk into a conversation that didn’t seem to involve them in any way.

“But it would be a good idea, right?” came Phainon’s answer, a bit bitter, a lot tired, and Audata’s heart squeezed. She had almost forgotten, in the excitement and cheerfulness from the previous day, that Phainon was technically recovering from an arduous battle that had left more scars than warmth.

“It… would,” replied Aglaea, a bit reluctant. Phainon hummed, unsurprised.

“Most people still remember you as the Deliverer. They know you, and when the official announcement about the Era Nova and the thirteen official demigods sees the light, they will recognize you as the original Worldbearer, Kephale, Throne of Worlds,” continued Cerydra, voice as firm as ever, as if she was constantly talking in front of an audience.

Hieronymus turned to her, eyes wide, and Audata felt her mouth go dry. The Worldbearer? She couldn’t help but think back to her old lectures in school, the scrolls that always depicted Kephale – enormous and strong, crowned in light – with the world on their shoulders. And now– 

She thought back to the mural, to the wings, the halo, the shared center he shared with who must have been the other Deliverer and Cyrene herself.

She thought back to Phainon’s own words – “don’t underestimate the pull I have around here” – and the clear reverence most of the Council members and guards showed him as he passed, the myths and rumors about him flowing around the streets.

And if the title of Worldbearing meant anything, then Audata was terrified of learning what exactly Phainon had gone through to reach the prophesied Era Nova. She took Hieronymus’ hand, squeezed tight, and pushed her tears back. She had promised, after all – no more tears, only hope and determination to stay.

“I…” Phainon trailed off with a conflicted sigh.

“Like I said, you don’t need to put on airs and play the role of Deliverer anymore if you don’t want to,” came Aglaea’s softer reassurances. Audata heard her dress swish through the air as she moved, weightless like the nymphs fluttering around the gardens. “You only need to… show yourself. Talk with the people, make them feel heard. You’re good at that.”

“I… don’t think I’ll be able to offer much hope, Aglaea,” muttered Phainon, his voice echoing slightly through the hallway. “Not anymore. Not after…”

His words floated in the air between them, heavy and bearing too much for Audata to make sense of the tangle of emotions – but she could hear the shared history there, the suffering, the exhaustion. 

He had never shown this part of himself to them, she realized painfully. He had hidden it away like one of his childhood treasures. A part of her wondered why he felt the need to do that, to hide this from them, to keep himself from leaning on them at all. Another part of her could guess, but the resulting ideas that cascaded from her guesses were heartbreaking. And so, her heart ached, again, and again, and she had to cling to Hieronymus to avoid rushing into the conversation and make a fool of herself.

“You don’t need to,” reiterated Aglaea, pointed and a bit amused, in a half-hearted kind of way. “Just– go out. Show your parents the best spots in the city. Take a walk through Marmoreal Market. Believe me, it will be as if you never left.”

“Well, he never did, right?” pointed out Cerydra, and Audata frowned, a bit lost. Why would Phainon have… left? “At least, not in the Recurrence that this Era Nova is based on.” A sharp step, firm and sure. “In this new era, you are the Worldbearer, as it was originally. So, go and walk into the future you sacrificed yourself to build, Dux Solaris.”

Audata’s grip tightened even more around Hieronymus’ hand at that, feeling her legs shake at the confirmation that, indeed, her stupidly selfless son had chosen to suffer and – probably – bear the world, to give their world a future. She didn't understand what that meant for Phainon, but- She bit her lip, heart aching and tears prickling at her eyes. She had to take a deep breath to keep herself from crumbling down.

The more she learnt about what their children had gone through, the less she wanted to know – but was that really helpful? Would them knowing help them, or would it hurt them more? Audata now doubted that Phainon could open up to them in that regard, doubted that Phainon could even put everything that had happened to him into words, no matter how good he was with them. And Audata would be remiss to force him to, even if every little detail that floated through the air stabbed her heart with more ice.

“I’ll… think about it,” was Phainon’s final answer, soft and a bit distant.

“I’ll leave the choice to you,” said Aglaea.

A couple of seconds later, they heard their steps getting further and further away, in the opposite direction from Hieronymus and Audata’s spot. The sudden silence was deafening, but Audata took the opportunity to wipe her face and take a deep breath. Hieronymus took a moment to gather himself, leaning against the wall.

They crossed a red-rimmed glance and then chuckled – it was familiar, reminiscent of all those days when bad news never stopped coming their way. Audata didn’t miss it, but she acknowledged that it was inevitable. Even now, they continued being too naive, thinking that a family reunion and a cheerful dinner all together would be able to cure all the existing scars.

(Even so, all of these little ideas, these spots of light– they had to mean something, right? They had to help, somehow.)

When they were feeling more human and less like tear-shaped globs, they turned the corner and Audata immediately jumped and yelped.

Phainon, who had been looking out the window, blinked, but he didn't quite turn to them. He seemed– not quite present. His eyes were unfocused. Audata's heart squeezed again, and even though she took a step forward to get to him, she couldn't quite bring herself to take another.

“We didn’t see you there, son,” tried to joke Hieronymus, a bit rattled – they had thought that Phainon had left with the other two, but instead, there he was, lost in thought – or just lost? – in the middle of the hallway.

Phainon’s eyes were a bit strange when he finally seemed to realize that he wasn't as alone as he had thought. His gaze passed over them at first, as if they were mere furniture – and Audata felt cold worry climb up her spine – but then he blinked slowly and tilted his head and finally, he focused on them. But his eyes– they were a bit too old, a bit too empty. It only made Audata’s lingering worry flare up again, so she steeled herself and walked over to him, careful and unsure. This was still her son, no matter how changed he was.

Aedes Elysiae was a small village, where people were usually… similar, at least when it came to their experiences. And now, she had a definitely-traumatized son with too old eyes that couldn’t stop – not that it was his fault – worrying her and giving her miniature heart attacks.

“Phainon?” she asked, careful, reaching out with a hand. "Khaslana?"

Phainon tracked her hand, silent, a wall between his gaze and his feelings. He seemed terribly ancient, then, and it made Audata’s skin itch. It was like– like standing too long under the sun, like facing something not-quite-human, but Titan-adjacent.

The Worldbearer, they had called him. Kephale.

Audata pressed her lips into a thin line and finally touched Phainon’s arm. He was warm, as always, but that fact seemed more poignant than ever now, for some reason she couldn't quite understand.

And then Hieronymus moved to follow her lead, and–

Phainon blinked again and suddenly, he was back, humming under his breath in consideration and thought, but something in the sound seemed half-hearted, still distant. He placed his hand on Audata’s wrist, careful and gentle, and the next time their eyes met, Phainon managed to pull up a smile that seemed far too empty.

“Say, do you want to go visit the city with Cyrene and me in a few days? I still owe you a tour,” he asked, voice a bit too flat.

But Audata gulped down her worry, squeezed Phainon’s arm, and felt a wave of relief when the next time he blinked, he seemed more present. She smiled then, because she had always had a hard time saying no to her son.

“Of course.”

Chapter End Notes

The parents are learning shit.

chapters.title: Chapter 16: Hieronymus
chapters.html:
Phainon ran off after that, citing something or other he had to do – not that either of them believed him, anyway, after years of countering his half-truths. And still, they let him escape, still reeling from yet another revelation, yet another knife to the chest – they were becoming experts at enduring them by now, joked Hieronymus in his mind, even as he stared after his son’s tense back with anxiety rolling in his gut.

Little by little, he reminded himself, and then he reminded Audata too, when she kept biting her lip, even during a much more relaxed breakfast.

They drifted around the Palace for the rest of the day, peeking into rooms and finding a myriad of treasures, staring out the windows at the beautiful landscape around them and running into hurried Council members and overworked Chrysos Heirs. The Palace was immense, and even after a tour guided by the Tribios sisters and a couple of days of individual exploration, Hieronymus still felt as if they had just scratched the surface of just how many secrets it hid. It would have been exciting, if they hadn’t been brimming with worry. Again.

These kids. Always getting into trouble.

Or, well– that was a bit unfair, in hindsight.

Still, they waited. And waited. Because Phainon would approach them, sooner or later, and apologize for maybe scaring them or acting strange or– Hieronymus knew his son, knew how he thought, and no matter how much he had changed, some things never did.

So, after an early dinner accompanied by the ever-calm Castorice and the ever-mischievous Cipher, they both climbed up to the Garden of Life to watch as the stars slowly took over the skies above their heads.

And a few minutes later, Phainon appeared like a ghost, silent and yet felt, as the world itself seemed to rearrange itself for him. He hesitated for a moment; Hieronymus felt him pausing at the edge of the grass, almost as if he was worried about touching it and– what? Setting it on fire?

Hieronymus turned and waved at him, patting the grass next to them in a clear invitation to sit side by side.

Phainon seemed to take a deep breath before approaching them, but soon enough he was sitting by their side, arms folded on top of his legs.

“I’m sorry I scared you,” he muttered, as predictable as always.

“It’s alright,” assured Audata, her soft smile back in place. She reached out, but stilled her hand before she could touch Phainon’s shoulder. “We’re just… worried. About you and Cyrene.”

Phainon opened his mouth, but the words died in his throat, and Hieronymus shook his head and placed his own hand on his son’s shoulder, grounding and tangible. If he was understanding things correctly, then that seemed like something Phainon would appreciate, something that would help.

“You don’t need to tell us anything if you’re not ready,” he said, a bit pointed, before Phainon could even begin to force himself to tear his wounds open just for them. His grip tightened on his shoulder and Phainon finally turned to him, eyes so, so tired it hurt. 

“We’re here with you, now,” added Audata, twisting and getting grass stains on her pants, but she didn’t care. Instead, she grabbed Phainon’s hands and met his gaze. “We’re sorry about what happened when Aedes Elysiae… fell, but–”

“Don’t. Please.” Audata immediately closed her mouth at Phainon’s ragged whisper, the crack in his voice, the absolutely devastated shine to his eyes. At that moment, he seemed the most present he had ever been since their reunion, and in turn, it was all the more painful. “What happened then… It wasn’t your fault. Please, never apologize for it.”

Audata squeezed his hands, nodding slightly. Phainon sighed, then, soft and yet terribly loud in the silence of the garden. He bit his lip, looked out at the distant silhouette of Okhema, at the mountains around them, at the starry sky. He swallowed, probably steeling himself.

“I… don’t think I can tell you what this Flame-Chase Journey has been like for me,” he admitted, voice strangled, almost painful. Then, he huffed out a humorless laugh. “I don’t know if I’ll ever be able to, if I’m being honest.”

“And that’s alright, Khaslana,” said Hieronymus. “But at least… let us be here for you, now.”

(“Let us be here, when we couldn't before.”)

And Phainon understood. He understood everything: the guilt, the bitterness and frustration they felt. The hurt. The want to fix everything, leave it just like it was before the world ripped it all apart and left the pieces behind. But that was impossible, wasn’t it?

Maybe that was why Phainon’s shoulders dropped with a soft sigh, why he squeezed Audata’s hands and why he closed his eyes.

“I will… try,” he said in the end. “And I know that Cyrene will, too. Just… be patient with us. We’re… not used to this, anymore.”

And wasn’t that heartbreaking, that they hadn’t been able to find support before? Hieronymus thought back to how close the Chrysos Heirs were, and then frowned slightly, because that made no sense, then. They were definitely close, tight-knit, like a group of people that had gone through hell and back, so why–?

“We’ll be with you every step of the way,” said Audata, soft and yet firm like a promise, like a vow.

Phainon’s answering smile was small and tired, but genuine. Hieronymus threw an arm over his shoulders – which was a bit weird, because his son was now taller and broader – and rubbed his arm, feeling the ever-present warmth of Phainon by his side. It was strange, because in the past, he would have checked if Phainon had a fever when he was this warm, but now… Well, Hieronymus was learning that a lot of things that once made sense didn’t anymore.

“For now… what happened back there? At the hallway?” he asked, careful and soft. He left it clear that Phainon didn’t have to answer his questions if he didn’t want to, but he hoped that he would, anyway. He kept doing that, after all – staring off into nothing, eyes distant, as if he wasn’t really… there.

Phainon sighed again and rubbed his eyes. Audata moved to sit closer beside them, but she didn’t interject or push Phainon to answer. The worry in her eyes was obvious, though.

“Hyacine calls them… dissociative episodes,” he explained, a bit stilted, as if he was trying to look for words that wouldn’t worry them unnecessarily – not that it would work, because if there was one thing that parents excelled at, Hieronymus had found, it was worrying about their children’s wellbeing. “It’s like… my body remains, while my mind… 'flies away' is the best way I can describe it. I mean, I am there, but I feel like I’m not.” Phainon paused and grimaced, not really satisfied with his explanation but struggling to come up with something better. “It’s… a new development, anyway. A little… souvenir from the Flame-Chase Journey and Era Nova.”

Hieronymus thought about it for a moment, and then felt a chill climb down his spine – to be a ghost in your own body, that had to be pretty strange and maybe even scary. But Phainon explained it with a resignation born out of knowing that it could be worse. So much worse. Honestly, Phainon seemed almost relieved that these dissociative episodes were his most pressing worries. Or maybe– maybe he was just surprised about it.

(And why, oh why, did that logic make it sound all the more horrifying?)

“Can we do anything to help?” asked Audata, eyes searching Phainon’s eyes for any tries at playing down the situation.

“Not really,” admitted Phainon with a smile that was too close to a grimace. “But– honestly, it’s not that bad.”

There it was.

Hieronymus hid a sight that he was sure that Phainon could feel, pressed against each other as they were. Audata bit her lip, not really happy with his answer.

“We probably don’t want to know what you’ve all gone through, do we?” he asked, bitterness bleeding into his voice.

Phainon’s answering smile was bigger than the last, but there was no glint of humor or happiness in his eyes.

“You definitely do not,” he answered, and oh, how tired he sounded. Hieronymus felt a bit helpless, then – the only comfort he could offer was to tighten his half-hug and rub his son’s arm. “But… we’ll be fine, I think. Amphoreus finally has a tomorrow – a tomorrow that we can all be a part of. I think that’s enough.” And his next mumble was so soft that Hieronymus was quite sure that Phainon was mostly telling it to himself. “It has to be enough.”

Hieronymus sent a glance at Phainon and then crossed another with Audata.

(Why did that ‘finally’ make Hieronymus think that the Chrysos Heirs had tried to get Amphoreus a tomorrow more than once–?)

“We’ll hold you to that,” was Audata’s answer, trying to lighten up the mood.

It seemed to work, because Phainon huffed out a soft laugh and let himself fall back to lie down on the grass with a sigh. Hieronymus leaned back on his hands too, feeling a knot of tension come undone in his chest. Even if getting Phainon – and Cyrene, who seemed to keep her distance most days for some reason – to open up and rely on them again was a work in progress only in its beginning stages, they had taken the first step. And if they wanted this to work…

“So, the Worldbearer, huh?” he threw to the wind, relaxed and yet pointed. Audata turned to him with wide eyes, a complaint on her tongue and a frown pulling her eyebrows down, but Hieronymus arched an eyebrow and nodded at their son.

Their son, who didn’t seem all that surprised about the fact that they had overheard his conversation. Instead, he smiled a bit, crooked and a bit nostalgic. Not quite pained, which Hieronymus had feared.

“You were listening, then,” he didn’t ask, but Hieronymus nodded slightly nonetheless. Phainon took a deep breath and nodded, too. “Yes. I was– or I am, the Worldbearer.”

“What does that really mean…” asked Hieronymus, and he tilted his head down to look his son right in the eye. “... for you?”

Phainon endured his gaze unflinchingly, but then again, why would he cower from it? Hieronymus had always been a pretty laid-back type of father, which had once annoyed Galba and some of Phainon’s teachers at some point – and his own parents, most of all. They had tried to push him – and Audata, too – to be more heavy-handed to avoid their son getting into more trouble, citing that Phainon had always been too smart, too mischievous, with too many stories and dreams in his head. But they had refused profusely in turn. Now, he was grateful and relieved that they had approached parenthood that way, when it meant that Phainon would have the door open for any and all kinds of conversations with them.

“In previous Era Novas, it would have meant that I would become Kephale in the new world,” said Phainon, and Hieronymus frowned and straightened out at that, feeling a spark of– he didn’t know what exactly, but it felt like electricity, like worry, like a strangeness that made his skin itch. Phainon’s next smile was crooked, though, and he even folded his arms behind his head. “In this one… Well, it means that I retain some of my power. If anyone out there dares to mess with Amphoreus, I am more than capable of dealing with them.”

Hieronymus didn’t know much about whatever laid ‘out there’ – didn’t even know there was an ‘out there’ before – but he could feel the heaviness in Phainon’s words, the fiery power that lapped at their skin as a consequence or an answer to it, like the sun, but stronger, all-comsumming–

Hieronymus blinked, thought back to a certain mural, and arched an eyebrow at Phainon.

“Wait. Do you actually have wings?” he asked, and his eyes flew wide when Phainon nodded absentmindedly, lost in thought.

“Yes, but how…?” he started to ask, confused and maybe a bit sheepish.

“There’s a mural depicting all of you,” explained Audata, still smiling, but she seemed just as surprised as Hieronymus.

“Oh. I didn’t know that,” muttered Phainon, and it was then that Hieronymus noticed the slight flush on his cheeks. “But, yes. I do have wings and...”

He trailed off with a wave of his hand, a bit awkward, very clearly embarrassed.

“And I suppose you also have a broadsword,” poked Hieronymus, just out of curiosity. In a now-distant past, he had imagined that the Phainon who would return from wherever the wind had carried him would show them his sword of choice with a proud smile, shoulders thrown back and standing tall.

“Ah, Dawnmaker.” And yet, Phainon said the name of his sword with softness, almost hesitatingly.

Phainon clearly debated with himself for a moment. And then, he was standing up, grass sticking to his dark pants and boots and shirt, coat left behind in his room – and that simple act of leaving behind something that seemed to be his ‘Deliverer’ armor was relieving in a bittersweet sort of way, because it felt as if he was making an effort to open up, if only subconsciously. He hadn’t worn his coat during their reunion at the gardens, either, noticed Hieronymus, and his chest felt warm.

Phainon made a move in front of him with his hand, practiced and fluid, and suddenly, Hieronymus had a broadsword right in front of his face, almost as long as he was tall, decorated with sun motifs.

Hieronymus felt a bit breathless. He could see his own reflection on the blade, wide-eyed and open-mouthed. Phainon moved it around as if it was second nature, an extension of his arm – and Hieronymus tried not to think too much about how exactly he had become so dexterous with such a big broadsword – until he was sitting down again, with Dawnmaker on his lap. His hands brushed over it almost reverently, eyes gaining that distant shine that Hieronymus was starting to dread the longer Phainon stared at the few scratches on the blade, small scars and echoes of a past better left in the dust.

“... Wow,” breathed Hieronymus, just because he had to. Audata definitely sent him a look, both amused and unsurprised about his eternal fascination with swords and anything remotely foreign or hero-adjacent. He turned to her, frowning. “What? It’s a mighty blade!”

“It is,” nodded Phainon, smile small, shining with clear nostalgia. “A friend of mine crafted it for me. It has been my eternal companion.”

And something in Phainon’s words felt terribly heavy. It seemed to appear mostly when he – and the other Chrysos Heirs, really – talked about the so-called Flame-Chase Journey and the time it had taken, which was weird, but Hieronymus found that he didn’t like where his thoughts took him when he tried to dig more into it – he would call those guesses impossible, but a lot of what he thought impossible was now possible, so… It would be better to keep his mouth shut, just in case.

“It looks well cared for,” he commented, reminded of their little village’s knife-sharpener’s complaints about dull sickles and knives.

“It’s not a good idea to neglect one’s weapon, after all,” pointed out Phainon and– right, his son had pretty much fought in a world-ending war. That made sense. But then Phainon hummed and tilted his head to the side. “Then again… I think it’s time to lay Dawnmaker to rest.”

“Huh? Lay it to rest?” repeated Hieronymus, frowning at his son with clear confusion.

Phainon’s eyes looked ancient again, tired.

“Dawnmaker has served its purpose,” he said, terribly heavy and a bit too emotionless for Hieronymus’ taste. But when Phainon looked up at the sky, his eyes were mostly clear, if only too old and burdened for someone his age. “The next time I raise a sword, it won’t be this one.”

The air was dense again, full of bittersweet memories and feelings foreign to the two parents. And yet, Phainon needed to feel it, to accept it, and live with it– At least, for a couple of minutes, before Hieronymus felt like he was choking on it all and reached out with a hand and a crooked smile.

“So, before it turns into an antique… can I try to wield it?” he asked, knowing that he would look like a fool and not caring one bit.

Phainon blinked, returning to the present, and then he arched an eyebrow at him, a glint of amusement sparking in his eye– and that was much better than the choking air, the heavy words and the distant eyes. Even if Hieronymus would end up paying the price with his own dignity, it would be worth it.

“Are you sure?” asked Phainon, but when Hieronymus stood up, he followed suit, expertly moving his sword. “It is quite heavy.”

Hieronymus huffed in mock offense and stretched out a hand, just like how he had done back in the day, when he had to make repairs at their house or hut, asking for the tools that Phainon would pass to him.

“Gimme,” he said, simply.

Phainon stared at him for a moment, then he shrugged, and offered Dawnmaker, hilt first.

His son had handled it as if it weighted nothing more than a stick, but as soon as Hieronymus closed his fingers around the hilt and Phainon let go of it, letting Hieronymus bear the full weight of it– Hieronymus fell forward, hurriedly clutching the sword with both hands and still finding himself leaning forward, unable to keep it straight for even a second.

“Wha–? How can you hold it so–?” he gasped, trying – and failing – to raise the sword upright.

Audata laughed heartily behind him, light and terribly amused, and Hieronymus knew that he would never live it down. Especially seeing the glint of amusement in Phainon’s eyes, the wide grin he tried to hide behind his hand, the slight shake of his shoulders.

(This stupid idea was worth it. It was so worth it.)

“I’ve been training for years now, Dad,” said Phainon, when he could open his mouth without bursting out laughing. “And I’m quite sure that we Chrysos Heirs are… a bit different.”

Hieronymus huffed and heaved the sword up anyway, even as Phainon side-stepped quickly to avoid getting hit by the blade, and even as Audata cackled.

Something in Hieronymus’ eyes sparked something like curiosity in Phainon’s eyes, because he was soon advising him on how to best hold the sword and how to distribute his weight and how to put his feet, and soon, Hieronymus could at least hold the sword straight in front of him in a messy starting position that he had seen Phainon practice over and over again at the old rickety dock by the river, eyes determined and firm like steel, Cyrene nodding off on her swing after cheering him on for probably too long.

Now, Phainon smiled wide and congratulated him on not cutting his feet off or tumbling down with the sword, and it sounded a bit condescending and a bit too amused for it to be honest and pure-hearted, but Hieronymus had always let his son get away with too much shit, and this time wasn’t any different.

So, now sweaty and with aching muscles, he sat down next to Audata, who smiled softly at him with a knowing smile. Phainon sat down again, too, looking much more relaxed, shoulders lighter, eyes softer and with some of that past spark of mischief back.

It was enough.

“I can make a swordsman out of you yet,” commented Phainon, smile a bit too amused, but Hieronymus still thought the offer over for all of two minutes, before he remembered how now his back cracked after crouching for too long.

“I’m too old for that, kid,” he said, with a rueful smile.

Phainon only hummed with a slight shrug.

They moved on to a much more relaxed and light conversation, after that. They tried to guess when would be a good time for their long-overdue tour of the city – and tip-toed over the matter of Phainon letting himself be seen to boost morale – and they soon talked Phainon into telling them some funny anecdotes and stories from the other Chrysos Heirs – which he had a lot of, apparently, most of them of his time as a student at the Grove, where he became close friends with Castorice and Hyacine and where he got to know just how crazy his Professor was.

The stars watched over them as they laid on the grass and it reminded Hieronymus of those nights when they would stay with Phainon after one of his infamous nightmares, out in the open, where the breeze could bring some peace to restless minds and where the sound of waves in the distance could drag away any bad thoughts.

And so, they talked and talked and talked, as if no time had ever passed.

(But it had.)

(But it was fine.)

—

Hieronymus woke up the next morning with a sharp ache on his lower back and a crick in his neck.

He groaned, annoyed at the fact that suddenly his body got sore easier than ever before – he had been able to sleep on a tree and not wake up feeling like an abandoned wooden plank when he was a kid, why not now?

But then again, maybe falling asleep on the grass, in the middle of the Garden of Life, hadn’t been the smartest idea. It wasn’t as if they had done it consciously, but maybe they should have acted like the responsible adults they were and gone back to their rooms after the first round of yawns and when their eyelids had become too heavy to keep up. Still, Hieronymus had slept– surprisingly well. No nightmares, no waking up in a panic, no–

There was no sun in his face, either, which was nice, but really weird when he thought about it.

He frowned, raised a hand to rub at his face, preparing himself to open his eyes and face yet another day when they would inevitably get wrecked by yet another revelation about their son or his childhood friend, but his hand brushed over something soft and really warm and–

Hieronymus opened his eyes with a choked gasp. He found that, instead of the blue sky and sun, he could only see– something dark. Something… suspiciously feathery.

Audata was curled up on his right, so that was good, and he could hear someone else’s deep breath on his left, which was probably his son, but then, what–?

His half-asleep brain screeched to a halt.

Feathers. Dark feathers. Phainon. A mural that had haunted his nightmares for at least a month. Wings.

Oh. Wait. Were these…?

He wormed his way out of Audata’s steely embrace – and wow was it obvious that she worked in the fields and also chased after the chimeras, her grip was relentless – and dragged himself through the grass until he could escape from the feathery cocoon he had been under.

He had known that Phainon had wings, his son had even confirmed it for him the previous day, even, but he had known it only on an abstract and conceptual level. Now, seeing those wings out and physical and real was… another thing entirely.

For one, they were big. Bigger than the mural would want you to believe, but maybe it was only logical, because the cost of so much paint and the space that would be occupied by only the wings would be– But wow, were they huge.

Phainon’s wings were as long as he was tall – probably – and they were asymmetrical, one dark and one golden, with thick feathers that gleamed under the dawn, and they acted as some sort of overgrown blanket that Phainon had used to cover both himself and his parents, like a hug, like a shield. A feathery shield.

The Worldbearer. Would have become a literal Titan in the new world, if things had gone as usual. Was powerful enough to deal with ‘anyone out there that dared mess with Amphoreus’. Had wings and a halo and a sword that weighed as much as a loaded cart.

Sure. Okay.

This was Hieronymus’ life now. Every once in a while, the reality of just how important and powerful his son had become smacked him in the face and he had to take a minute to just breathe, stare and then get his shit together and continue on with his life.

This time was no different. So, he sat there in the grass like an idiot for probably too long, staring at the wings that didn’t quite sprout from his son’s back – which was… handy, he supposed, no need to wreck his clothes – and just how relaxed and unbothered Phainon was with the whole thing and– He took a deep breath, let it out, and then stood up, filing this new image with the rest of totally-normal stuff he had learned during his stay at the Holy City.

He needed coffee, he decided.

So, he walked off, rubbing sleep and shock out of his eyes, trying to brush grass off his clothes and failing and then making a face at the green and mud sticking to his tunic. He probably should change clothes, before he turned up at the kitchen looking like a kid that had been frolicking in the fields for too long. He veered off the vague path he had been following, hoping that it would bring him to the kitchen, and instead, he headed in the direction he remembered the living quarters were in.

This area of the Palace was usually peaceful and quiet, devoid of almost anyone other than the few guards that made sure that no one sneaked into the Palace and bothered the overworked Chrysos Heirs and Council members. It was that simple fact which made Hieronymus stop in the middle of the hallway when he heard a loud thud and a stifled curse in a too-familiar voice.

Hieronymus grimaced at his grass-stained tunic and pants and then veered off the path again, this time towards a dimly-lit room where a familiar pink-haired girl was sitting on the floor with a thick tome on her lap and a few other scrolls spread around her – she had been definitely organizing her extensive collection of scrolls and they had tumbled down to the floor after maybe kicking the shelves or the desk or–

“That’s a pretty thick book,” he commented, leaning on the door and praying that Cyrene was too preoccupied with being annoyed at her collection of scrolls to pay much mind to the messy appearance of his clothes. She would laugh at him, he knew, and then she would remind him of it again and again in the future – her memory was too good.

“Ah– it is, isn’t it?” she said, but her voice sounded a bit weird. Her smile was also weird. “I’m trying to find the best place for it, but… I can’t seem to make up my mind.” Cyrene looked up at him, then, and her eyes were heavy, a bit too similar to how Phainon’s had been the previous night. “I’ve already given the original to a friend of mine, you see. This is just… a copy. For… safekeeping.”

“Wouldn’t the library be the best place, then?” he asked, a bit wrong-footed.

Cyrene’s hands were ink-stained, he noticed, which in any other moment would have made Hieronymus sigh with relief. But this Era Nova was weird, it had turned everything upside-down, and suddenly, what was normal wasn’t normal anymore, and what had once been wholesome now made him nervous in an uncomfortable way.

Maybe it was the fact that Cyrene’s hands were also shaking slightly around the book, clutching it with a bit too much force for it to be a normal and not-at-all special book. Maybe it was the way she hugged it to her chest as soon as the words left Hieronymus’ mouth.

“Ah… I’m afraid this book is my creation, you see,” said Cyrene, and her smile was painfully pinched. “I can’t bring myself to part from it.”

It reminded Hieronymus of finding this same girl at the Courtyard, laid back on the mountain of cushions, with her cards strewn around her, hands stained with ink and with a small pile of paper by her side, her familiar feather in her hand. He would always sit down next to her, then, maybe steal some of her grapes and laugh when she tried to stop him and she would have to decide whether she wanted to mess up her manuscript or slap his hands away – she always chose the second option, and she always complained about how messy her drafts were, but she always smiled. She always smiled.

Now, years later, with this kind-hearted girl looking so different but also not, Hieronymus did the same; he sat down on the floor, because his clothes were already ruined, anyway, and he eyed a few of the scrolls around them and he arched an eyebrow at her.

“What is it about?” he asked, nodding to the book in her embrace.

Cyrene blinked, maybe a bit surprised, but then she smiled again and she looked down at the book with a complicated shine to her eyes that Hieronymus couldn’t quite put a name to.

“It’s a story about heroes,” she said, voice soft, fond, but also sad. “Heroes that challenged fate, sacrificed themselves for a tomorrow they might not see, and when all was said and done– they embraced hope and managed to get a happy ending.”

“You were always fond of happy endings,” said Hieronymus.

“I still am,” admitted Cyrene, smile trembling slightly. “If a story full of tragedy and suffering doesn’t get a happy ending… Well, that would be too sad, right?”

“It would,” nodded Hieronymus. He paused, feeling a too-familiar knot in his throat the longer he watched Cyrene brush her finger over the pages like one would caress a chimera. “So… what happens now?”

Cyrene blinked, dragged away from her thoughts. She frowned at him, her usual smile falling into something hesitant and a bit lost, maybe.

“What do you mean?” she asked, just like she had when she was a simple kid starting to write her little ideas in a messy notebook, at the margins of her homework, small dreams and short stories told to her childhood friend as they ran through wheat fields.

Hieronymus bit his tongue again, letting himself have this final chance to back out– but he couldn’t, right? Because Cyrene had always tried to find the words and the way to end her stories, but when they were done, she always looked a bit bitter, a bit sad, like letting a beautiful flower fly away with the wind into the sea.

“I mean… the story is done and the heroes have their happy ending, so… What’s next?” he asked, terribly obvious, and Cyrene probably saw through his half-hearted attempt at asking the deepest questions that he’d had to swallow down for too long. 

But she still smiled, a bit brittle, and lowered her head to look at the book on her lap.

“Well… that’s not exactly the writer’s job, is it?” she said, just as half-hearted, slightly distant, and it reminded Hieronymus of Phainon, in a way. 

They really were similar in this way, both of them – self-sacrificing, kind, bright, willing to take the world on their shoulders. But when all was said and done, and when they could finally lower the weight at the end of the journey… What was left? 

In the past, Hieronymus had wondered how the heroes of those legendary stories would have fared after their adventures were done and they – in some cases – got to return home. When he was a kid, those questions hadn’t been important; the heroes had gotten a happy ending, and that was enough. But when he got older and he could understand how cruel life could be and how humanity’s fate was always to gain something and then lose it, he had wondered what that question meant for the heroes of those stories.

Of course, most of them were pure fiction. The more realistic legends, those based on real events and real people, usually had sad or tragic fates, or maybe a bittersweet end. But Hieronymus had wondered, anyway.

And now, faced with a too-real example of those same wonderings, he could see what the shadows of optimistic writing and embellished endings hid – the exhaustion, the doubts, the scars, the trauma. As exciting and emotive as those stories were, when one saw them through the lens of reality, they twisted easily into something more akin to nightmares and a hard life full of pain and tears.

The Chrysos Heirs knew that, Phainon knew that, Cyrene knew that – they had lived through it. And now they had their happy ending, and while the world was saved and okay – or getting there – they had sacrificed too much to get to where they were, they had lost something on the way, something they would never get to reclaim, and yet– they were expected to keep going, even as their long journey ended, even as they stood in front of a field with no roads, directionless. Lost.

He could see Cyrene’s smile with everything that she hid behind it – the pain, the loss. He could see the young girl standing in a field, still and frozen, lost, with no new roads she could take. A character – or a writer? – with no plot to move her forward.

(And wasn’t that good? She was free, after all. But humans were nothing if not creatures wed to routines and self-imposed aims, and feeling lost was akin to drowning for most people.)

“Let’s say that it is the writer’s job, then,” he poked, pushed. He smiled reassuringly at Cyrene when she looked up at him with a slight frown. “The long road is over. They stand in a field; no more crossroads, no more duties. No more roads. What will the heroes do?” And before Cyrene could answer, because she was nothing if not creative and boiling with millions of ideas at any given time, Hieronymus hurried to cut her off and looked her right in the eye. “What will the writer do? What does she want to do?”

Cyrene closed her mouth slowly. Her eyes were wide, but not surprised. Thrown off-guard, probably. It was as if she was tying everything they had talked about in the last few minutes together, as if she was realizing a few things, maybe, he hoped – she had always been too smart for her own good. 

He could reach a hand and try to guide the girl away from the field, from the overwhelming choices laid out before her.. but where would the fun be in that? Where was the freedom they had suffered so much to gain?

“I… don’t know,” she admitted, and at that moment she seemed terribly small in her puffy dress, her multicolored hair, her glittering eyes and frosty nails and high heels.

“... Yet,” he added, and when Cyrene blinked at him, looking so lost it hurt his soul. Still, he smiled and huffed out a laugh and he reached out to put a hand on Cyrene’s shoulder. “You don’t know yet. But you will. You all will.”

It took Cyrene a moment, but after a few seconds, her eyes glistened, her smile widened and trembled in equal measure, and so, she left the book on the floor reverently, before she was throwing her arms around Hieronymus and giving him a tight hurt with countless unsaid words and doubts and–

And so, Hieronymus could only hold her tightly and hope that whatever words had left his mouth would mean something for this lost girl.

Chapter End Notes
