Maybe he could bring himself to tell them in a (probably distant) future, but for now... I don't see it happening. Sorry if you were looking forward to that!

chapters.title: Chapter 17: Audata
chapters.html:
They fell into a kind of routine after that.

As Phainon recovered, he stubbornly carved a place for himself into the overworked Council of Chrysos Heirs and other politicians, and soon, he was just as busy as them, looking through correspondence, writing speeches, looking over petitions and deciding what to do about them. Cyrene soon found her place there, too, after one too many times of Phainon himself “accidentally” leaving paperwork on her desk.

With those two – and the other Chrysos Heirs – too busy to spend much time with them anymore, Hieronymus and Audata soon fell into a restless kind of routine that left them wandering the Palace and helping with whatever they could, which… wasn’t that much, seeing as they were simple farmers and not politicians.

Maybe they should just… leave? Return to Aedes Elysiae, no matter how hard it would be to part ways with Phainon – who was making a clear effort to get closer to them, to not isolate himself – and with Cyrene – who still struggled to leave her room, to talk and be noticed and be included – and with the rest of the Chrysos Heirs – who had turned into, as Hieronymus had guessed, a second family?

It was a bit demoralizing, in Audata’s opinion, but it wasn’t as if they had much reason to linger in Okhema any longer. After all, they had already reunited with their son and his childhood friend, they had cleared the air between them and managed to get the both of them to lean on them as much as they could bring themselves to, currently. They had even managed to practically adopt all the Chrysos Heirs into their small family – not that said Chrysos Heirs even noticed, with how stumped with work they were.

But Audata had regular cooking sessions with Mydei – where she managed to gather some confusing and worrying information about his past and a few Kremnoan words here and there – and Hieronymus usually helped Hyacine and – surprisingly – Professor Anaxa to look after the Dromases and chimeras in Okhema and soon, all of their interactions with the Chrysos Heirs reminded Audata of how things were back in Aedes Elysiae, where everyone greeted each other with wide smiles and joked around with no problem.

And yet, they missed the golden wheat fields, the chilly morning air, the sound of the waves lapping at the coast, the sound of children running around the houses, the smell of wheat and fruit and grass and…

And that thought brought forth a nagging question that had never left Audata’s lips: a hopeful wish that she was ready to part with, cradled in her hands like precious fruit, like a risky present for someone she was only now beginning to understand better.

“Say, Phainon,” she said one day, while their little cooking team of Phainon, Mydei and Audata were working together on an Aidonian dessert that Castorice had once mentioned missing. She tried to make her voice soft and light, but Phainon had always been too perceptive when reading people, and she was no exception, so her son turned to her with a slightly pinched expression. And in spite of it all, she managed to smile up at him anyway. “Don’t look at me like that, it’s nothing bad. It’s just…” Audata bit her lip for a moment, saw how Mydei turned around discreetly to focus on his task and give them more privacy. She saw Phainon’s frown. “Will you two ever return to Aedes Elysiae?”

That made Phainon pause, she noticed. His hands, which had been stirring the mix, slowed to a crawl as his gaze lowered to the flour-stained counter. The air around him did that thing that Audata was starting to hate; it became heavier, with a thousand unsaid words, with too many memories to count, and so, she reached out with a hand and placed it on Phainon’s arm.

“Don’t misunderstand. I’m not telling you to return,” she pointed out, still soft, still careful. “I’m just asking. You don’t even need to answer right now.”

Phainon’s face did something strange, then – a grimace, but not exactly. He scrunched up his nose, his eyes glinted with something she couldn’t quite name. But he ended up taking her hand, anyway, and looking up at her with his usual sharp eyes that spoke of unbreaking will.

“I’ll… We’ll think about it,” he said, and his voice contrasted with his gaze, but that was alright.

(Something in that gaze left it quite clear that he wanted to say “yes”, and yet… the word got stuck in his throat. Was it the same worry that had made him fear that his own parents would see him differently? Or was it… something else? 

Audata didn’t know, but she hoped that Phainon would be able to see that Aedes Elysiae would welcome him and Cyrene with open arms and a big banquet.)

“That’s all I’m asking for,” she said, smiling and squeezing Phainon’s hand. Then, she paused and her smile widened. “Well… maybe not all. After all, it is getting a bit boring standing around here all day doing nothing…”

“It’s a nice vacation, right?” pointed out Phainon, knowing perfectly well that the restlessness he was known for had come from his parents to start with. Audata sent an unimpressed glance at him and managed to get a huff of laughter for her trouble. “Yes, I’ve noticed. I’m sorry, we’re pretty busy–”

“It’s not your fault,” said Audata, a bit hurried, but she knew where Phainon’s words would lead him. “We’re just– thinking of, you know, going back.”

Phainon faltered for a moment, but he didn’t look particularly surprised about it.

“To Aedes Elysiae?” he asked, soft.

“To Aedes Elysiae,” she nodded, just as soft. “As nice as Okhema is and– as welcoming and hospitable as you have all been, this… isn’t our home. We miss the fields and the sea. And it’s not like we’re of any use here–”

“You’re not useless,” cut in Phainon, face disgruntled and a bit offended. Audata laughed softly and rubbed his arm placatingly, shaking her head.

“I didn’t mean it like that,” she said, and only when Phainon’s shoulders finally relaxed did she continue. “But… We’re not made for the big cities, Khaslana. And that’s okay. We’ve already found what we came here for, after all.”

She looked up and smiled and she could see Phainon searching her eyes, attentive and lost in thought, in a very reminiscent way to his child-self – it still surprised Audata from time to time, how much he had changed and yet how little. She could see echoes of little Phainon and then those echoes turned into a new person, a strong and important Chrysos Heir, and then– but it was all Phainon, it was all Khaslana. Always.

“If that’s what you want,” answered Phainon, in the end, with a soft sigh. The shine in his eyes wasn’t quite resignation, but it was close, and so Audata frowned up at him and pinned him under her most powerful Mom Stare.

“Is that what you want?” she asked back, pointed.

Phainon faltered once again and– he kept doing that. He kept biting his tongue, kept pushing back what he wanted, kept stifling his preferences and wishes. Before, when he was a kid, he had been so stubborn and decisive about everything he put his mind to, but now–

(What had he gone through? Audata wondered and wondered and wondered and she always, always decided that she was better off not knowing, because she would definitely break down and she couldn’t have that.)

Phainon let out a sigh, louder and longer, and he resumed his task of stirring the mix as he glared down at the bowl.

“It’s… nice to have you back, is all,” he said, more similar to a mumble, really. As if it was a secret. “Still, you’re free to go back home whenever you want. I wasn’t trying to keep you here or anything– And I do understand that Okhema and Marmoreal Palace are intimidating and overwhelming and a total chaos right now, too. Really, escaping back to the countryside sounds really good, and–”

He cut himself off with another sigh, shoulders dropping when he couldn’t quite word his thoughts better. But Audata understood – she understood the unsaid, the hidden, the too-raw emotions under the surface.

“That’s why I asked if you would be willing to return to Aedes Elysiae,” she admitted, just as soft as him. “When we leave… I’m just trying to think of how to organize our reunion. I mean– if you don’t want to return to the village, we can always come back to Okhema again or… or maybe we could meet up somewhere in the middle…”

Phainon’s hands had stilled again, so Audata looked up again with a spark of worry – had she overstepped? Maybe it was a bit too early to start talking about their next reunion, when they hadn’t even left Okhema yet.

But Phainon’s eyes were a bit wide, a bit surprised, and then it changed into a more relaxed look, fondness clear in his gaze as he smiled.

“We’ll figure it out,” he said. The next time he opened his mouth, his voice had that strange tint back, that shadow of doubt and disbelief every time they talked about a possible future, that distance from the present. “After all, we have time.”

“That we do,” nodded Audata, cementing it, making it something certain and true.

“When would you leave?” asked Phainon, trying to sound nonchalant but ending up as nervous instead.

“Ah– we haven’t thought of any dates yet, actually.” She smiled, a bit self-deprecating, and it only made it all the more clear that leaving this pace would be one of the hardest things they’d done in their lives. She only hoped Phainon would see that.

“Aren’t you forgetting anything?” asked Mydei, turning to them for the first time since Audata started this conversation. He also raised his own bowl, showing the creamy paste that gleamed under the sun. “The cream is ready too.”

“Ah– right,” Phainon returned to his own mix, looking a bit flustered. Mydei rolled his eyes.

“Not that, HKS. I meant the tour around Okhema,” he said, as if it was the most obvious thing in the world.

At that, Phainon paused and stared forward to the wall, cold realization spreading through his gaze until he grimaced and lowered his head.

“Oh. Right,” he mumbled to himself. When he turned to Audata, his flush had climbed up his cheeks and his smile was crooked. “I did promise you that, didn’t I?”

To be quite fair, he hadn’t been in his best moment during that conversation and he had been pretty busy ever since, so it wasn’t as if Audata and Hieronymus would blame him if he had forgotten about it – and he had, apparently. 

Audata opened her mouth to reassure him that it was alright, that they could go on with their lives even without the promised tour around the Holy City, but her son was nothing if not stubborn, so when his eyes took that familiar shine again, she closed her mouth with a soft exhale and a gentle smile.

“Let's do it tomorrow, then,” he said, and it sounded like a promise, something heavier than this simple invitation to go for a walk together. 

It was a strange dichotomy, she had noticed; what seemed simple was treated with a surprising amount of gravitas and seriousness now, and what could be a groundbreaking revelation was treated like something normal and unimportant. It made her mind reel every time, but it also made her get that urge to wonder and guess and walk down a terrible, terrible path that would lead her to horrible ideas and heartbreaking answers.

So, not for the first time, she pushed it all away and smiled.

“Let’s do it,” she nodded, trying to match Phainon’s gravitas with her own. She fell a bit short, but then again, she guessed that it would be pretty difficult to match a would-be-Titan’s aura, right?

Her smile turned a bit bitter at that thought, but Phainon’s satisfied and relieved glint in his eyes and his widening grin brought the warmth back with no trouble.

“Let’s invite Cyrene, too. And Mydei.” Phainon nodded to Mydei, who startled slightly and then sent a confused glance back at him. Phainon simply grinned wider and tilted his head to Audata in a very pointed way, to which Mydei answered with a sigh. “C’mon. You said you wanted to check on the Kremnoan merchants at Marmoreal Market, right? This would be the best time to do so.”

“We would be delighted to have you,” added Audata, just because she had quickly figured out that Mydei’s past hadn’t been… pretty, either.

(And it broke her heart that all Chrysos Heirs had that in common. 

She could see that same darkness in their eyes, that exhaustion, that sadness – but also that drive to continue onwards, that strength, that wish for connection and those hopeful eyes that looked out to tomorrow.)

Mydei caved almost instantly with another sigh.

—

Just as promised, they met up the very next morning at the entrance to Marmoreal Palace. By the time Hieronymus and Audata made it to the meeting spot, the three Chrysos Heirs had already arrived and were now chatting with each other, restlessness and sparks of nervousness obvious to whoever dared look underneath their calm expressions and straight backs.

They were all dressed more intricately, with various layers of cloth and more expensive accessories. They looked like important people, untouchable, tied to the Titans in a way that not even the venerated priests could. Phainon himself, standing with his back towards them, looked the very image of a hero or a high-ranking general, imposing and intimidating – until he turned and he saw them, his stiff gaze relaxing into a fond smile.

“Do you have any preference for where we should start?” he asked, mostly cheerful, maybe a bit too cheerful to be believable– but Audata would let him have it, this time.

“We don’t know that much about the city, anyway,” shrugged Hieronymus with a crooked smile. “We’ll leave it to the experts.”

“Funny that the ones you call ‘the experts’ are all technically outsiders in this city,” commented Cyrene, hands behind her back like always. She was wearing that dress that reminded Audata of a kaleidoscope of colored glass again, and it threw her back to that first meeting – and how disastrous it had been. She only hoped this adventure would go well.

“Oh, well. We do know of a few nooks and crannies," shrugged Phainon, shooting twin knowing glances at both of his companions. “So… market first and then we go around?”

“Sounds good,” nodded Mydei, arms crossed but relaxed. He arched an eyebrow at Phainon, pointed and yet amused. “I suppose you won’t drag me into any of your insane competitions?”

“What? I don’t know what you’re talking about.” But Phainon was already walking out of the Palace, hesitating only for a second before he took a deep breath and took the first step outside.

And it hit Audata, then, that Phainon... had probably stayed at the Palace for more than a few months. Probably since the beginning of this so-called Era Nova, in fact. That– that was a long time, she realized, but then she looked out to the city, saw the streets – still bustling with people but nowhere near as bad as they once were, when Hieronymus and Audata had been stumbling around searching for any clues that would lead them to their son – and she understood. For someone still struggling under the weight of a future they hadn’t expected to have – because Audata had pieced together that much, at least – the thought of going out into the world and grappling with that reality while everyone could see them tear apart at the seams… 

Now things were different, she thought. When they crossed over to the other side, the streets were crowded and people moved from one place to another, talking loudly with each other, hurrying through the corners, laughing. But most of the visitors from outside the Holy City had already left after dealing with their problems – or at least informing the authorities about them. They could walk without stumbling on other people, they could talk with each other without needing to yell into each other’s ears.

And so, the three Chrysos Heirs guided them through the streets and buildings. They pointed out stores that Hieronymus and Audata had missed during their hurried visits in the past, they used the alleys and courtyards and side-streets and sometimes even the roofs as shortcuts.

Through all of it, the people of Okhema slowly came to realize that the little group of colorful people was, in fact, a group of Chrysos Heirs – and two nobodies that most people looked past, every time they realized who they were walking side by side with. Audata didn’t mind – in fact, she was grateful for the lack of care. Something about having so many gazes on her all the time made her extremely uncomfortable; she didn’t know how the three Chrysos Heirs could stand them.

Only… they, too, struggled with them, she could see. 

Mydei usually dealt with them with grace, standing proud and tall, a bastion of strength and royalty – no matter how many times he pointed out that he was no longer a king, he still wore the cloak of authority around his shoulders like a second skin. And still, he always chose to remain behind a corner, to the side, where people wouldn’t get to see his face, where only the eyecatching red and gold of his clothes could be seen.

Cyrene remained cheerful and joked with Hieronymus as if nothing was wrong, but she still startled every time someone so much as bumped into her. She always seemed a bit confused when someone addressed her, complimenting her hair or her dress. She recovered quickly, all things considered – really, if Audata hadn’t been checking on them all periodically, she would have missed the strange glint in Cyrene’s eyes and the slight tremble of her hands behind her back.

(No one seemed to recognize her – at least, not personally. Everyone in the city seemed to know that she was a Chrysos Heir, but no one asked about how her latest story was coming along, no one asked more than surface-level questions – not like with Phainon and Mydei, who people asked about their hobbies or their health or…

Why? Why why why?)

Phainon seemed to be the people’s favorite, in that everyone – or, at least, most people – flocked to him from time to time and inquired on his health, thanked him for his help, confessed their admiration or simply handed him gifts. Phainon dealt with it all with grace, gentleness and clear experience, sending warm smiles this way and that, chuckling and thanking the people back for their support, their gifts, the hope they entrusted to him.

And yet– Audata could see the slowly growing uneasiness, the tense set of his shoulders, the clenched jaw even as he smiled wide with tired eyes. After an entire hour of going around and people flocking to their little group like birds to freshly-made bread, his hands clutched the few gifts he had received with white-knuckled hands and his eyes had a sharpness that made Audata want to yell and push everyone away.

Mydei beat her to it, though – and it was a good thing that he did, because his intimidating stare made quick work of the cloud of people still getting too close, too loud, too excited. He pushed against the most daring, he thanked the elderly while scaring them off at the same time – he grabbed Phainon’s arm and pushed him behind his body.

“I think you’ve shown yourself long enough,” grumbled Mydei, when the troupe of excited people had scattered at last.

Hieronymus, who had grabbed both Audata and Cyrene’s arms to avoid losing them in the sudden thick crowd, sighed in relief and finally let them go. Still, Audata could see that he seemed just as on-edge as she felt. They really weren’t used to so many people at once. The biggest crowd that they had been a part of in Aedes Elysiae was during the festivals, and even then, the fields were calm enough for them all to talk in normal volumes and big enough that bumping elbows was unnecessary.

“It’s okay,” sighed Phainon, but even now, his voice sounded tired and a bit overwhelmed. “They were just… excited. I didn’t think–”

“Once a Deliverer, always a Deliverer,” pointed out Mydei, strangely heavy.

Audata was reminded of the tarot card that Phainon had shown her what seemed like a century before – the Deliverer, the hero.

From the thoughtful look that Hieronymus was sending to their son, he was probably reminded of the usual hero stories he had always loved so much – of how villages and cities welcomed the heroes with cheers and raised hands and gifts when their adventures were over and the big evil villain had been dealt with. Seeing it first-hand, though, only brought to light how extreme and overwhelming that simple show of gratefulness could become.

“Let’s continue the tour around the outskirts of the city, shall we?” offered Cyrene, appearing at Phainon’s side like a ghost, meeting his gaze and searching for something in his eyes.

Phainon sighed softly, but he nodded.

Before they took the side-streets that would take them to the districts close to where Hieronymus and Audata had once stayed, Phainon dragged them to an antique store in Marmoreal Market – “To leave these gifts” he said, nodding to the small assortment of sweets and accessories the various citizens had dropped into his hands. A man greeted them warmly when they arrived, and from how he checked on Phainon, it was clear that they knew each other.

“I’m glad to see you around again, Phainon,” said the man with a small smile. “This place has been far too quiet without you.”

“Ah– sorry, Theodoros. We’ve been… quite busy,” admitted Phainon with a crooked smile.

“Well, no worries. I’ve already stored a few interesting trinkets… They’ll be waiting for you until you have time to fetch them and take a look at them,” nodded the man, Theodoros, smile widening into a fond grin when Phainon’s eyes glinted in interest at his words.

Hieronymus smirked as soon as they left the store, amused and fond as he slung an arm around Phainon’s shoulders.

“So… antique appraisal?” he poked. Phainon rolled his eyes with a small smile.

“Of course. But I have to say– grandpa lied. This method has cost me more money than I’ve gotten back from it,” complained Phainon, and Audata could breathe out a sigh of relief – he sounded more like himself now. Less tired, more amused.

Hieronymus continued ribbing him as their group snaked through the streets, and at some point, even Cyrene joined them, telling Hieronymus about Phainon’s biggest moments of bad luck when acquiring antiques and appraising them. Audata, for her part, fell back and watched, letting herself relish in the moment – after all, they would leave sooner rather than later.

Mydei fell in step beside her, silent but calm, a steady presence by her side. She could already see and understand why Mydei and her son had gravitated to one another: they were far too similar in some things, and far too different in others. But most of all, she was starting to realize, was that they were ready to entrust their back to the other, no questions asked, no hesitation. That simple act spoke volumes – and it settled something in Audata’s heart. Even if Hieronymus and her left, Phainon wouldn’t be alone. He would be taken care of. He would be fine.

“Thank you, for looking after him,” she mumbled to the man beside her, because it was only fair.

Mydei sent her a glance, heavy but peaceful, before he looked back to the trio of loud talkers in front of them and he sighed with nothing but warm fondness.

“No thanks needed,” he muttered back.

Audata smiled widely, anyway.

“I asked Phainon if he would return to Aedes Elysiae, but… I want you to know that you’re also invited, if you ever want to come visit,” she said, letting a sliver of amusement bleed into her voice, pointed and meaningful. She saw the slight change in Mydei’s calm expression – that almost nervous glint in his eyes, that twist of his lips.

“I’ll… think about it,” he said, after clearing his throat. There was a slight flush to his cheeks now, and he kept avoiding her gaze, but this was enough. More than enough, really.

The outskirts of the Holy City were calmer, empty of the bustling crowd, alight with groups of children that played in the gardens and climbed onto roofs of buildings that looked far too important to be touched. People approached the Chrysos Heirs again, but this time, it was in a calmer manner – a kind grandma that offered them fresh bread, a shy child offering handmade flower crowns, a smiling woman that talked of rambunctious children, a teasing man that got along with Hieronymus a bit too well.

Audata felt like she could breathe again. The atmosphere here was more relaxed, quieter, in a way that reminded her of home. The children playing, the small stores run by kind-hearted and welcoming people, the colorful gardens, the blue sky over their heads, the smell of freshly-baked bread and colorful fruits.

It made her heart ache, so much so that she made up an excuse to sit down at one of the benches as Phainon, Cyrene and Mydei eyed a clothing stall and chatted with the young woman that kept up with Phainon’s haggle with ease.

“Even after all this time, your fashion sense still sucks,” she could hear Mydei poking at Phainon, voice gruff but amusement clear for all to see.

“Oh, really? As if yours is any better,” shot back Phainon, swift as the wind that ruffled the leaves over Audata’s head.

“It is, actually. I didn’t need Aglaea to give me lessons.”

Phainon turned to him, gaping slightly with a betrayed expression.

“That– there’s nothing wrong with my fashion sense!”

“Oh, I’m sure.” Mydei’s grin was unabashedly wide, this time.

“My style is just… colorful! There’s nothing wrong with trying to find some cheer in colorful clothes!” yelled Phainon and to prove his point, he shook a bright orange chlamys under Mydei’s nose.

“There’s a lot of wrong in blinding people with all those clashing colors, though,” grumbled Mydei, pushing Phainon’s hand away.

“Oh, don’t exaggerate. It’s not that bad!” huffed Phainon.

“Keep telling yourself that,” huffed back Mydei.

“Children, children. Let’s not fight,” placated Cyrene, but her grin was wide and terribly amused as she placed a hand on each man’s arm.

“Cyrene, you’re supposed to be on my side–” huffed Phainon, offended.

“Hey, why would I? As your childhood friend, the logical course of action would be to be against you!” shot back Cyrene, far too smug. “But seeing as I’m so great, I’ll be neutral this time. Aren’t I gracious?”

And so, the Chrysos Heirs soon devolved into another pointless argument. Audata watched on from her bench, smile never leaving her lips. It must have been freeing, she thought, to get to argue about such a stupid matter, instead of the probably-heavy and important issues that they surely addressed during their long meetings at Marmoreal Palace.

If she closed her eyes and she tilted back until her back brushed the rough bark of the tree behind the bench and she let her mind drift, she could even fool herself into thinking that she was back in Aedes Elysiae, listening to the children argue about something or other, smelling the results of hard work from the bakers up the hill, hearing the distant murmur of the sea…

“It sure takes me back,” mumbled Hieronymus, sitting down beside her. She knew what he meant; there was no need for words.

“I miss our home, Hieronymus,” she mumbled, so soft that the light breeze carried her words away.

“I do, too,” he answered, just as soft.

At some point, Hieronymus left, citing something about wanting to try some of that delicious bread. At some point, the three Chrysos Heirs’ argument trailed off into silence. At some point, Phainon sat down next to her and offered a handful of grapes.

“What do you think of Okhema now?” he asked, mostly curious. There was something else there, though.

It made sense – after all, Okhema had become Phainon’s second home. The complete opposite of Aedes Elysiae, and yet, her son still regarded this sprawling forest of buildings and towers with fondness.

“I can see why you’d like it,” she admitted with a small smile. And yet, she looked around and munched on her grapes and sighed. “But… I much prefer this safe little haven you’ve found.” She sent a pointed look at her son, but Phainon only tilted his head innocently. “You’ve brought us here on purpose, haven’t you?”

Sly and too smart for his own good, that was her son. His lips twitched up and he looked up at the green leaves dancing with the breeze over their heads.

“When I first came to Okhema, I felt so overwhelmed I didn’t leave Marmoreal Palace for a month,” he started, voice soft and a bit distant, but not the bad kind of distant. Still, Audata placed a hand on his arm, just in case. “Lady Tribbie noticed, of course. She guided me around the streets and Marmoreal Market, but it didn’t really help – if nothing else, it actually overwhelmed me even more. So… the next time she managed to get me out of the Palace, she brought me here, to this district.” Phainon paused, as if he was organizing his thoughts. He tended to do that, as if he was parsing through his countless memories, trying to figure out where they all fit together. “It was peaceful and full of kind people that reminded me of… back home. It was painful, at first, but… I kept coming back.”

Audata waited for him to continue, but he didn’t. Her hand moved to his wrist, his sleeve hiding the pale scars underneath.

“Have you thought about what I asked?” she mumbled, once again soft enough for him to ignore if he so wished.

Once again, he didn’t.

“Yes.” Phainon took a moment to breathe, to gulp down the hesitation he definitely felt scratching at his chest. “I… I think I do want to return at some point.”

Audata looked around them again, at the colorful garden, at the blue sky, at this artisanal district, at the laughing children. She could see home here, she could recognize the warmth in her chest. And so, she squeezed Phainon’s wrist and smiled.

“Then, we’ll be waiting,” she mumbled, and it was a promise.

Chapter End Notes
