chapters.title: Chapter 18: Hieronymus
chapters.html:
There was nothing left for them to do in Okhema.

Three days after their long-awaited tour of the Holy City, they decided to return to Aedes Elysiae.

A week later, they woke up bright and early, tried to fit everything they had been gifted into their measly bags – and failed, until Aglaea gave them their last gift in the form of bigger and more expensive-looking bags – and stood at the gates of the Holy city, feeling a knot in their chest and tears in their eyes as they hugged their son and who could very well be their adoptive daughter for the last time in a while.

“I promise I’ll visit,” was mumbling Phainon into Audata’s hair, arms tight around her.

“We’ll visit,” corrected Cyrene, hugging Hieronymus in turn. She was as cold as always, but they had gotten used to it by now, so when they parted, Hieronymus simply shook his hands to force some feeling back into them and grinned at Cyrene.

“When that day comes, I expect you to have that story ready for revision, young lady,” he said, arching an eyebrow for good measure and shooting a pointed glance at Cyrene’s ink-stained hands.

Something about his comment seemed to be particularly funny to Cyrene, because she stifled a laugh behind her hand. Hieronymus, as expected, didn’t get his answer, because Phainon and Audata finally parted from each other slowly, as if it was the hardest thing they had both done in their lives – which it could be, really.

“Don’t forget to write,” said Audata, for what had to be the twentieth time. “And… tell us when you’ll visit ahead of time, okay?”

“No reason,” added Hieronymus, making their plans all too obvious.

Phainon and Cyrene shared a look and a knowing smile, but they didn’t call them out on it. Good. Otherwise– well, Hieronymus wouldn’t have cancelled the banquet, but he would have made it a point to avoid including their favorite dishes.

Audata took his hand, squeezed tightly and took a deep breath. She was looking at Phainon and Cyrene as if she was branding their image into her mind – as if she didn’t have a pile of photos in her bag of all Chrysos Heirs that she would definitely frame as soon as they got back – and making sure that she wouldn’t forget any details. Hieronymus was tempted to do the same, but… They would meet again. Phainon had promised, Cyrene had promised, Audata and Hieronymus had promised, too.

He trusted them. And so, he grinned at them, pushed back the stubborn tears and the paranoia that twisted at the back of his mind – the one reminding him that things could still go to shit, that this could very well be the last true time he saw them – and nodded at the group of Chrysos Heirs behind them.

“It was truly a pleasure and a real honor to meet and get to know all of you,” he said, with as much respect and fondness as he could. With that out of the way, he allowed some of his amusement to leak out. “And… please know that you’re all welcome in Aedes Elysiae. I must say, we do have great bakers.”

“We will keep that in mind,” came Aglaea’s as always elegant answer, but something in her smile and glinting eyes left it clear that she would, indeed, keep it in mind.

Hieronymus couldn’t wait until the day when all these eccentric and heroic people would follow up on this light deal and Aedes Elysiae would fill with their presence.

“Now, then… We’ll be off,” he said, gentle and warm, meeting Phainon’s gaze one last time, before he swung one of their heavy bags onto his shoulder and he turned away from him, from Cyrene, from the Chrysos Heirs, from Okhema. Tinted with as many bittersweet memories as it was, he had to admit that Okhema was still a breathtaking and beautiful city. If only they could have visited in better circumstances… “We’ll see each other again.”

“We will,” was Phainon and Cyrene’s joint answer, firm like a vow and light as the breeze.

Trianne – the Tribios sister lucky enough to have been chosen as their guard and chaperone – cheered and waved back to the other Chrysos Heirs and followed as Audata and Hieronymus walked down the worn path that led to and from the Holy City, back to Amphoreus’ roads and other city estates and…

Back home.

—

Dear Audata and Hieronymus,

It seems I'm following up on our promise to write sooner than expected. So soon, in fact, that I'm quite sure you're still en-route for Aedes Elysiae. But well, writing is my thing isn't it?

I just wanted to let you know that you've left behind that scroll that talks about soils and farming techniques from other city estates. It's fine, we'll bring it to you when the time comes. On that note, we will probably also bring you more scrolls about other techniques and some… experimental stuff? Professor Anaxa has – apparently – found out a new interest in gardening and farming, so he’s started doing what he does best, which is: experimenting.

(Don’t worry, we’ll make sure those new inventions of his are safe.)

(Also, you can just– not use them at all. His methods can be a bit… hit-or-miss, sometimes. Don’t feel pressured to try them out, okay? We’ll figure something out.)

We hope your journey is going well and with no trouble. The roads are still a bit of a mess, so we hope Trianne has been able to help you.

Sending our love and regards,

Cyrene (and Phainon)

—

The journey back to Aedes Elysiae was much quicker than the journey they had taken once upon a time to Okhema. It was to be expected, though, seeing as they were making a pretty straight line to it, instead of wandering around listening to rumors and panicked people left and right. 

Trianne also seemed to know plenty of shortcuts, cutting through remote villages and using the opportunity to check up on them. Hieronymus found himself making fleeting friends at each rural village they visited. Or maybe fans, he wasn’t quite sure. He only knew that coming into these villages side by side with a Chrysos Heir meant that they were treated like celebrities or respected idols. It made them awkward and uncomfortable, but it wasn’t as if they could simply refuse the free food and lodging that the villagers offered them as they passed.

“It’s just– we’re simple farmers, Trianne,” he commented to Trianne, as they finally walked away from the smiling crowd and waving hands, back to the roads.

Trianne arched an eyebrow at him with a crooked grin.

“You’re the Deliverer’s parents, though,” she pointed out, terribly amused as Hieronymus sighed and tried to hide the redness of his ears. Trianne laughed. “C’mon. Embrace the title!”

Easy for her to say, he had thought in the moment. But they still tried to stay by Trianne’s side, still tried to help as many people as they could when they passed and they accepted the offerings with polite smiles and careful hands.

Still, when the rolling hills of golden wheat finally surrounded them and the dark roofs of the Aedes Elysiae houses glinted under the sun in the horizon, Hieronymus finally felt some of the tension that had nested in his shoulders finally lift off. From the dusty road, he could still hear the sound of waves breaking against the rickety old dock, he could hear distant childish laughter, he could see the silhouette of the Sacrament Courtyard – it looked strangely small, compared to the marvels they had seen during those past months.

Both Hieronymus and Audata picked up their pace, heavy steps turning light as they followed the snaking path down to Aedes Elysiae proper. Trianne followed, eyes wide and curious as they got closer and closer to her dear students’ home.

The first one to see them was, of course, Galba, who looked up from his trusty bow, only to almost fall down from his post at the stone fence around the border of their little village in his haste to hurry to them.

“You’re back!” he greeted, relief and surprise clear as day in his voice. He patted Hieronymus’ back and smiled at Audata. “You were gone for months! We almost thought that–”

That they wouldn’t make it. That something horrible had happened to them. That the children were lost and Hieronymus and Audata couldn’t bring themselves to return to a place where every corner would remind them of the kids. Hieronymys could see it in Galba’s eyes – the relief turning into slowly dawning realization that there were no white and pink haired kids running behind the two parents, the cold spreading through his expression, the glint of something sad and horrified in his eyes. 

Hieronymus smiled as wide as he could and placed a heavy hand on the hunter’s shoulder.

“We have much to tell you,” he said, as cheery as he could. “And… we also have a guest.”

With those simple words, Galba’s eyes widened as he followed Hieronymus’ gaze down to the red-haired girl now grinning up at them. Her delicate and expensive clothes stood out between their humble and coarse tunics, as did the old shine to her eyes.

Galba cleared his throat, nodding stiffly, gesturing for them to enter the village.

“I’ll… tell everyone that you’re back,” he said, voice rough and lost, before he hurried off, leaving his hunting bow forgotten on the fence.

Hieronymus wanted nothing but to plop down on his bed and sleep for at least a day, but… well, they had a lot to announce to their neighbors.

—

Dear Cyrene,

You just missed Trianne by a day, that was a shame. We could have sent this letter with her. It would have reached you much sooner than it will now. We’re sorry. Mail doesn’t really reach Aedes Elysiae that easily… But you already know that.

We’re already at Aedes Elysiae by now. The journey was shorter than last time and much calmer thanks to Trianne’s help. She was a godsend…  Um, maybe literally? Still, we’re not used to traveling this much and we’re already getting old and all… 

(Ignore him, he’s just complaining about nothing. We’re used to working the field, we’re plenty strong!)

Oh, don’t worry about the scroll. You can bring it whenever. I’ll simply have to start reading from the beginning again. And about those experimental ideas from your Professor… I mean, we can always try them out? As long as it won’t mess with the harvest, we can give it a chance. Who knows, if it works out, we can double the production in Aedes Elysiae! Or even triple it!

We hope you’re okay and dealing with the chaos in Okhema without running yourselves into the ground. Yes, we say this to all of the Chrysos Heirs. Take breaks, sleep early, eat when you need to and talk about something that isn’t work from time to time!

With much love,

Hieronymus and Audata

P.S.: We’ve told the people of Aedes Elysiae about what you’ve been up to all this time. I think you guys have a new fan club! When you come visit, prepare yourselves to have the kids pestering you for stories and cool poses all day. Good luck.

P.P.S: I seem to remember that Mydei mentioned something about wanting to use our wheat for a bread recipe he wanted to try. We’ve included a separate package with this letter, full of wheat. I hope it reaches you still in good condition…  Let us know how it turned out! We can send you more!

—

Going back to normal life in Aedes Elysiae after everything they had learned and after what they had seen was… strange. But not unwelcome.

They returned to their usual routines, only now with no children running around the house and eating their food and climbing their roof. Sure, Piso and Livia still swung by sometimes, asking about Phainon and Cyrene, usually, or fishing for more details about their stay in Okhema. But there was no Phainon offering to make salads with Audata during lunch hours, no Phainon helping Hieronymus with the fields, no Phainon and Cyrene ‘studying’ at the table after dinner.

It only reminded him of how much things had changed. The wound of what had happened to Phainon and Cyrene and why they weren’t by their side would probably haunt them for life, but… it was becoming more and more manageable as the days passed.

And it helped that Hieronymus had his memories of their stay in Okhema to fall back on, when his worry climbed up his throat and threatened to choke him. There was a firm wall between his paranoia and his reason – Phainon’s words had seemed unbreakable, his eyes fiery like a hearth. “I can deal with anyone that would dare mess with Amphoreus”, he had said, back then. And Hieronymus would always trust his son.

“It’s strange, right?” asked Audata one day, as they ate dinner together, windows open to let the sound of the fields and the crickets envelope them into their embrace. “Not having the kids here.”

“It is,” nodded Hieronymus, feeling some of the now-familiar melancholy strangle his voice. He hummed and tried to lighten up the air, before they both tumbled down a hole of worry and nostalgia. “But I don’t miss those loud arguments they always had at this hour. ‘That’s not the card you pulled out first’! Or… ‘Phainon, you’re cheating again’! Or…”

Audata’s laugh was soft, but genuine and light-hearted. Her eyes danced as her gaze moved to the wall, where the very obvious dent on it spoke of a very colorful anecdote.

“Do you remember when they both stayed up too late running around the fields and watching the stars, and then Phainon tried to sneak in through the window, only to push the window too far and knock over the table and–?” she started, huffing laughs between words.

“Ah, yes– he crashed the window, broke the table, and slammed the window into the wall. It really startled us– we thought it was a thief, right?” he said, grin wide. 

The idea of a thief trying to break into their humble home was laughable now, but in the moment, it had been the only thing that Hieronymus’ half-asleep mind had been able to think of. Then, he had opened the door of their room and saw the mess in the main room, with a flustered Phainon in the middle and Cyrene with her head on the windowsill, groaning.

“You scolded them for almost twenty minutes,” laughed Audata, and Hieronymus rubbed the back of his head. He had, indeed. He had sat the two children on the chairs – with no table, because it was broken – and ranted at them for almost twenty minutes about missed curfews and bad ideas and responsibility.

“And the next day, I made them help me fix the table and the window,” he said, smile crooked and yet amused. “That was fun. I also had Phainon helping me with the field for a while after that.”

“You went a bit overboard with that, I think.” But Audata was smiling widely, now, amused and with warm eyes.

Hieronymus laughed.

“Yes. I think I did.”

—

Dear Mom and Dad,

We’re happy to hear that you’re back home safe and sound. Trianne came back a few weeks ago, too. She said that everyone in the village seemed to be okay, too, and that the food is very good. Glad to know that our habit of overfeeding our guests hasn’t faded yet.

Sorry for taking so long to write back. We’re finishing up on some new treaties to improve communication between the city estates and– I won’t bore you with work-talk. I can see Mom glaring at me from all the way over there. In any case, the end of this long crisis cabinet is in sight. Finally. With some luck, we’ll be able to go visit before the year is over.

We received the wheat. It was a bit damaged after such a long journey, but we managed to make use of most of it, anyway. Mydei decided to make corn-and-seed bread with it – it turned out pretty good! We feared it would end up like my first attempt at bread. Remember? It was hard as a rock. Luckily, Mydei is better at baking than my six-year-old self.

I helped Professor Anaxa the other day and he mentioned that he would need a sample of the soil from our fields to figure out the composition of his new invention. Just a bit should be enough. He gave me a vial to send you, you can just put it in there.

(And really, if you don’t want to try it out, you don’t have to. It’s fine. Don’t do it just because he intimidates you or out of politeness. I can make something up to get the idea out of his head.)

Oh! Castorice has been getting better and better at crocheting, so she’s thinking of trying out new projects like… scarves? Also plushies? She’s open to ideas. She also wants to make something for you two, so she would really appreciate it if you chose a pair of colors for her to work with. She won’t tell me what it is she’s making, though.

Hope the harvest is going well. The cabbage and spinach should be about ready to be harvested by now, right?

Love and regards,

Phainon

P.S.: How are Piso and Livia? Are they giving you much trouble? I don’t know if I have many stories to tell, if I’m being honest. Mm… I’ll probably ask Cyrene for any ideas, even if I have to come up with fake stories myself.

—

The sun was already climbing down the sky when Hieronymus stepped outside their home with the vial in hand, frowning down at the earth beneath his sandals. The Professor had asked for samples, but would a simple pinch of dirt suffice? Should he take it from the surface or should he dig down a bit?

With a slight shrug, he crouched down and dug his fingers into the earth, brushing some leaves and rocks away. He put some of the resulting earth into the vial, squinting at the few blades of grass that sneaked in. Would this be enough? Oh, well. They were only a letter away – if the Professor deemed it necessary for them to be more thorough with their samples, he could always ask again.

“Um, Hieronymus?” came the hesitant voice of Pythias from behind their fence. Hieronymus turned to her, back cracking after a long day of work at the fields, and he tried to smile without it seeming more like a grimace. “Uh, what are you doing?”

“Ah, Phainon’s teacher, he… asked us for some soil samples. He wants to help us with the harvest, I think,” he tried to explain, even though he wasn’t an expert researcher and he didn’t really know what Professor Anaxagoras’ help would end up looking like. “So…”

He shook the vial in the air with a slight shrug. Pythias, always curious to a fault, jumped over the fence so she could look at the vial as if it was the most interesting thing she had ever seen. 

Hieronymus had once thought that Pythias would end up leaving the village, take the road up to the Grove of Epiphany and become a great scholar. That ended up not being the case; death got their hands on her family too soon, and so she had to leave her dreams aside to become the village teacher and bring money to the reduced table in her home. Hieronymus had always thought that it was a shame – Pythias was clearly smart, with a drive not seen in many people. But she was also a very good teacher, and as the years passed and she found a new place in their village, Hieronymus supposed that this was enough for her.

Still, he wondered if Pythias would ever want to follow up on her past dreams and finally leave Aedes Elysiae for some time, now that Amphoreus was healing and the roads were safer than they’d ever been.

“You mentioned that the Professor was from the Grove of Epiphany?” asked Pythias, even though she definitely knew that by heart. Hieronymus had seen the spark in her eyes when he had mentioned it during the banquet the villagers had thrown in their honor after their return with good news. “Professor… Anaxagoras?”

“Yes. He’s… a bit strange, but from what I was able to see, he seemed like a true genius,” commented Hieronymus, thinking back to wide grins, a glinting red eye and a dangerous chuckle.

“Will he ever visit Aedes Elysiae?” asked Pythias, and the interest and hope in her voice was clear as the sky over their heads.

“I have no idea,” admitted Hieronymus, because as much as they had pretty much accepted all the Chrysos Heirs into their little family, they were a group of very important adults, each with their own duties and desires. And maybe those desires would lead them in the opposite direction of their small village by the sea. So, he arched an eyebrow at Pythias. “Why don’t you visit him at the Grove instead?”

“Oh– oh! I couldn’t!” Pythias waved her hands in the air, cheeks flushed. “I’m just– a teacher from the countryside. I couldn’t possibly…”

“Think about it, anyway,” he shrugged again, standing up on cracking knees and longing for a good cup of tea after a day of hard work. “Amphoreus has changed a lot. The children would cheer for you to get a vacation.”

“Oh, I’m sure they would love to have the chance to miss classes,” chuckled Pythias. She looked out, to the roads leading away, and hummed. “I’ll… think about it.”

Hieronymus grinned and patted her on the shoulder. 

Who knew? Maybe he could open up Aedes Elysiae to the outside. The village of origin of the Deliverer and the 13th Titan… Then he shook his head, finally sealing the vial and entering his warm home. No, it would be best if Aedes Elysiae remained as a haven of peace and tranquility. A shelter. A place where two certain demigods could simply retreat and breathe and be themselves, without the heavy weight of expectations and titles.

Yes, he decided. That would be best.

—

Dear Phainon,

You seem awfully insistent on getting us to abandon the idea of letting Professor Anaxagoras help us with the harvest. Why? No matter, I’ve taken a sample of our soil; is it enough? I took it mostly from the surface, but if he needs more samples he need only ask. And do give this to him, Khaslana, I’m serious. He has offered his help, the least we can do is collaborate.

Pythias has asked me if the Professor would ever come here. I told her to go to the Grove herself. She says that she’ll think about it, but… you know how she is. When you come visit, do try to get her to open her mind a bit about the idea – the children from the school would treat you as their hero. Hero times two, actually.

Speaking of, don’t break your head trying to come up with stories. I’m sure those two - and the rest of the children - will listen to anything you have to say. Titans, I think they revere you as one of their favorite heroes, like those legends you and Cyrene liked to tell them sometimes.

So, how’s work treating you? Has the paperwork finally given you ink-poisoning? Are you sleeping well? Eating well? Do you go take walks from time to time? (These are Audata’s questions, actually – I’d like to think that our son, a responsible adult that has been living on his own for a while, knows how to take care of himself, huh? Right?)

I found some of Cyrene’s old drafts under that old bedside table – remember? You stuck a knife to its side once. We honestly had no idea she used to hide them here. We can give them to her when you come, for safekeeping. Tell her not to worry, we haven’t read anything written in there.

Audata insisted on sending you some of the spinach we harvested last week – we hope it survives the journey. You can always ask for any other cravings you might have – now, whether they survive the trip to Okhema… well.

With much love,

Hieronymus and Audata

P.S.: Please tell Castorice that we don’t really have a preference when it comes to colors, actually. Some gold and green would be nice, I suppose? Maybe purple? Tell her to send us letters directly, it’s perfectly fine.

P.P.S.: Actually, you can tell the other Chrysos Heirs to send us letters whenever they want. They’ll have a pretty long journey until they reach Aedes Elysiae, but they will reach us eventually. Remember that we’re now family! You can’t get rid of us that easily!

—

Now that Amphoreus had a real sun, Hieronymus had thought that winter would be easier to deal with. Something about the sun being a star and stars being giant balls of fire, from Professor Anaxagoras’ rants as they ate lunch together a few times. 

But actually, winter was as merciless as always – though, it probably was much gentler than it would be up north, in Aidonia and the northern city estates. Just being side by side with the sea made it so that their winters were less overbearing. Still just as humid, though.

Their homes were small and easy to heat up. Hieronymus liked to fire up the brazier after a long day in the fields, if only to try to get the clinging sensation of humidity and cold off their bodies. Once upon a time, Hieronymus had left the task to Phainon as soon as he could be sure that his son wouldn’t end up lighting his hair on fire as soon as he looked away. Now, he wondered if Phainon would even need the matches to light it up. What kind of powers did he have, exactly? He had never told them.

Audata had taken up crocheting and knitting again. It was probably a consequence of her correspondence with Castorice – they had become crafting buddies, liked to joke Audata as she moved the needle in a practiced motion. Soon, their little home would be infested with hand-knit blankets and scarves and gloves and little nick-nacks that Castorice introduced to Audata.

It wasn’t as if they were pressed for money, anyway – not anymore. Not since Phainon and then later Cyrene and then pretty much all the Chrysos Heirs – including Imperator Cerydra herself – had made it a point to give them part of their allowance. They had refused at first, of course. They couldn’t simply… take the money.

But then Phainon had done his usual thing of bringing up very good and convincing arguments, and Cyrene had smiled at them, and then Aglaea had said that it would be no trouble to give Phainon his due after his deeds during the Flame-Chase and well, Phainon could do whatever he wanted with his own money, right? And giving the money to his family and friends was just common sense, right?

“It’s either this or I spend most of it on antiques,” had pressed Phainon, jaw set in a familiar way that left it abundantly clear to Hieronymus that arguing with his son would be a waste of time.

And so, just like always, they had caved.

“That damn brat,” grumbled Hieronymus at the reminder, stoking the flames with a crooked smile and no glimmer of real anger.

Audata raised her gaze from her newest project and frowned at him.

He simply smiled wider and shook his head.

—

Dear Mom and Dad,

I have good news! Seeing as things have – finally! – calmed down enough around here, Cyrene and I have decided to go visit Aedes Elysiae. It will still take us some time, though; we do want to leave everything settled here so we can stay longer, instead of having to run back only a few days later. For now, we’re thinking… The beginning of spring? Before the full harvest starts. Let us know what you think, we can work from there.

And I’m not telling you not to work with Professor Anaxa. It’s just… well, he can be a bit… I just want our home to stand in one piece, is all I’m saying. Still, I’ve given the sample to him. He’s disappeared back into his lab, so I can’t tell you much more, but I suppose we’ll be able to give a try to his invention when we go visit.

We received the spinach. It was… usable. Don’t worry about it. Still, maybe next time we send something more delicate, we can ask the Tribios sisters for help. They’re already done dealing with urgent correspondence, so we can probably use the Century Gate for more… personal matters. I’ll ask Tribbie.

Sorry for the short letter, but hopefully we can reunite soon.

Love and regards,

Phainon

P.S.: Cyrene is already fluttering about everywhere, asking me what she should bring on the journey. I sometimes forget that she’s not used to traveling. I just hope she doesn’t bring her entire scroll collection with her.

—

Hieronymus and Audata crossed a glance, a wide smile, and squeezed their hands tightly, overcome with emotion and excitement.

Hieronymus laughed loudly, grabbed the letter and slammed the door of their home open, startling Livia and Piso, who had been playing nearby. Hieronymus’ grin was wide and his eyes bright.

“We have good news!” he announced loudly down the road.

—

Dear Phainon,

We’re so happy to hear that! When you finally settle on a date, please tell us. No reason why. None at all.

But, hey, you’re Professor Anaxagoras’ student, shouldn’t you trust him more than that? I know he’s a bit… eccentric, but c’mon. Blowing up the house? We’ll try his invention when you come by. I’m sure it’ll be fine.

And there’s no need to rope Tribios into this. It’s fine. I’m sure we can think of another way to send some of our produce to you without it being damaged in the process. There’s a nice merchant family in a nearby village, maybe we can ask them for a favor? Your mother knows just about everyone there, too.

In any case, don’t use this possible visit to overwork yourselves more than you already are. Pace yourselves and rest when you need to. We’re not going anywhere.

Looking forward to more news,

Hieronymus and Audata

P.S.: Tell Cyrene to calm down. This is still her home. We have everything she might need.

—

Dear Hieronymus and Audata,

It’s settled, we’ll set off at the start of the Month of Freedom. We’ll be going by foot and stopping by some towns and cities, so we’re not sure when we’ll arrive exactly. Aglaea and Cerydra say that it would be good for all of us Chrysos Heirs to make some tours around the city estates, let ourselves be seen and mingle with the crowds. We’ll try to send you letters during our journey, just in case.

(I won rock-paper-scissors against Phainon, so I get to tell you the good news! He’s sulking right now as I write this. He’ll probably write something to you as well, just because he always needs to have the last word.)

Thank you for what you told me, too. I think I really needed to hear that. Sorry for forgetting it. Haha, my head is still a bit of a mess, but hopefully the smell of wheat and the sea can help me see things more clearly.

Sending love and regards,

Cyrene

P.S.: I have a few stories ready for Livia and Piso. I’ve worked hard on them, so I hope they’ll like them!

—

Dear Mom and Dad,

Read Cyrene’s letter first. She won rock-paper-scissors, so it’s her right to tell you first, as much as I hate it.

But, it is also my right to tattle on her and tell you her bad ideas. Who would be crazy enough to think that making the journey wearing high heels is a good idea? Her, apparently. When I told her that the roads aren’t in good condition, she just huffed and told me ‘a girl like me knows how to walk with heels in any terrain’. She will end up twisting her ankle, and I will not be responsible for it. Please, mom, tell her that she’s being too stubborn.

By the way, Professor Anaxa has given me a bottle of fertilizer of his own making. We only need to test it on a patch and wait to see how it develops. Don’t worry, I’ve already tried it at the gardens and there were no explosions, so it should be safe to use it at home.

Do you need anything from Okhema? Or maybe some other town? Just tell me and I can go fetch it.

Love and regards,

Phainon

—

Dear children,

You’ll always be welcome at home. We’ll be waiting for you.

P.S.: Elysiae, dear girl, please don’t be stubborn and wear some travel-safe shoes. As pretty as those high heels are, a twisted ankle is not worth it.

P.P.S.: Phainon, Khaslana, my boy, what do you mean ‘there were no explosions’?

Chapter End Notes

In honor of my mother, who is now going jam with crocheting stuff for everyone.
Only one chapter left!

chapters.title: Chapter 19: Khaslana and Elysiae
chapters.html:
They left Okhema at the start of the Month of Freedom.

They reached Aedes Elysiae a few weeks later, after a somewhat hurried tour through a few of the city estates where the citizens cheered and asked for their help and regaled them with gifts and exaggerated banquets.

When Khaslana finally laid eyes on the rolling hills of gold, his breath stuttered and his feet stopped, leaving him immobile in the middle of the road. For a moment, all he could see was fire and all he could hear were screams... before it all faded away just a second later, leaving him in the peaceful silence of the countryside once again.

This was what they had feared: their memories, twisted after cycles of suffering and the same cruel end, forcing their way to the front of their minds, drowning out reality and making them drown in a past that should be left behind.

But no matter. This was their beginning. Their first and true home, a little pocket of peace and love. This was where they had grown up, where they had embraced their destinies, where they had lost everything, where they started over and over and…

This was their home.

And no amount of tangled memories had the right to ruin it for them.

Not anymore.

So Khaslana took a deep breath, tightened his grip around his bag and resumed his walk down the road. And when Elysiae bit her lip and faltered in her steps as well, he tapped her shoulder and dragged her away from ‘yesterday’ and back to ‘today’. Back to the rolling fields of gold, back to the seaside, back to where they began.

“Ready?” asked Elysiae when they reached the highest hill over Aedes Elysiae, eyes locked on the few houses scattered around the seaside.

Khaslana counted the houses, had to riffle through his memories to remember which house was whose, squinted at how small the Sacrament Courtyard looked now compared to the grand buildings he was familiar with.

He saw in the distance those who had once been his neighbors, his friends, his teachers. His world.

“Let’s go,” he said, even though his voice trembled slightly.

He wound his arm around Elysiae’s, just like old times, and their gazes met and so, they both trudged down the hill, listing to the side because of their difference in height, stumbling on each other’s feet. They almost fell more than once, but they still laughed, and that managed to make some of the weight lift off their chests.

By the time they finally made it to his parents’ lands, Khaslana had stopped breathing in smoke and fire and Elysiae’s hands weren’t hand-shaped ice cubes.

His mother was the first to notice them, looking around as she had been. Her eyes lit up immediately, and she hurriedly left her basket on the ground to run to their side, smile wide and arms already open for a hug.

“You made it!” she cheered softly, before she wound her arms around the both of them, not caring how lopsided they looked.

“Sorry, we took a while to get here,” he apologized half-heartedly.

His mother shook her head and leant back, enough to press her forehead against his and wipe her tears away. Khaslana himself had to bite down a bit harder than usual to keep his jaw from trembling – and how strange it still was, to feel everything this strongly again, to feel this human.

“None of that,” mumbled Audata, making a point of looking him right in the eye. “You’re here. That’s enough for me. For us.”

“Honestly, with how overexcited people seem to be, it’s a wonder you haven’t been held back for a month, if not longer,” came his father’s amused voice, but Khaslana could hear the very real and very heavy relief and happiness pouring from his voice.

Audata finally let them go, only to caress Elysiae’s hair – now tied into a high ponytail for the trip – and smile warmly at her. Hieronymus didn’t waste time and hugged Khaslana too, patting his back and ruffling his hair, and Khaslana found himself overwhelmed with warmth – but not the raging inferno of Destruction. No, this was all love and affection and a wave of nostalgia so tall it threatened to drag him under. His father only hugged him tighter, as if he could hear the storm in Khaslana’s head.

“We’re home,” he mumbled against his father’s shoulder, and it sounded a bit too hesitant, too dreamy, like a kid asking their parents if they were back in reality after a bad dream.

“Welcome home,” answered Hieronymus, solid like a rock he could cling to. Just like always.

Their lands connected straight to their house, which was handy, because Khaslana didn’t really want to deal with any more old faces at that moment. Not yet. Not when simply walking into his old home already had him on edge, expecting monsters from the Black Tide to suddenly jump up at him, attack him, tear everything away from him–

He ran his hand over the dinning table, the window he had once broken, the kitchen counter, the door.

His parents left him to it, leaving him space as they moved around the house, placing the basket in the kitchen and making space for his and Elysiae’s bags. He was thankful for it, even though it felt a bit embarrassing to fall back on that distance that he knew freaked them out – he just couldn’t help it. So many memories clambered up to gain his attention, some good, some bad, some terrible.

His father left the basket in the kitchen with too much force and his head whipped around at the sound, shoulders tense and hands ready to summon Dawnmaker like so many times in the past.

His mother called from one of the rooms – his, he recognized – and he stiffened, thrown back to a terrible, terrible day where his mother had called for him to hurry, to hide under that very same table, as she–

“Ah,” came Elysiae’s soft whisper from behind him. He turned, taking a deep and slow breath and blinking bright flames out of his sight. She was staring down at something on the table, a hand hovering in the air. “This is…”

Khaslana walked over to her, a bit curious. The fogginess scattered with every step he took, every surface his hand ran over, like a blind man relearning his home once again. When he followed Elysiae’s gaze, he came face to face with a messily-made book, pages crumpled, letters crooked and hurried.

“Those are the drafts we mentioned,” explained Hieronymus, appearing at their backs carefully. He didn’t touch them – not yet. Not when the past seemed so present in their eyes. “We bound them into a book, just in case. So we wouldn’t lose anything.”

“I remember,” was Elysiae’s distant answer, as her hand finally lowered to pass the pages, slowly, reverently, as if she was afraid that her simple touch would make the pages crumble away. “I hid it under your nightside table. I thought… Well. It was stupid.” And then, she finally raised her head to smile at Hieronymus. “Thank you.”

“No thanks needed, dear,” came his mother’s voice, just as soft as always. She gestured to the doors that Khaslana knew led to the two bedrooms. “Now, we’ve readied your bedroom… Ah– You know we don’t have any more bedrooms, so…”

“It’s fine,” shook her head Elysiae, with her usual smile that soon turned amused and teasing. “It’ll be just like the old days.”

“Do I have to check on you two in the middle of the night to make sure that you’re sleeping?” joked his father, grin wide.

Khaslana huffed out a laugh and moved to his childhood bedroom, careful and maybe even hesitant. Once again, he couldn’t help but run his hand over the door frame, the door, the wall.

Everything was as he remembered it: his practice sword, the pile of scrolls and books he had ‘borrowed’ from the Courtyard, his bed, the extra cot wedged between his bed and the wall, even the few drawings he had made during classes stuck to the wall.

He approached them now, steps heavy, Elysiae’s teasing laughter feeling more and more distant the deeper he ventured into his small bedroom. He recognized some of the drawings – most of them were of characters from legends he had read or heard, but one of them… Dark cloak, dark pants, a mask, a heavy broadsword. His lips twitched up as he took the drawing into his hand. How funny, that the hero he had drawn – had dreamed of becoming – had ended up twisting himself into the villain of the story.

He saw movement out of the corner of his eye, but he couldn’t quite bring himself to look away from the drawing his childish self had made what seemed like millenia ago.

“You haven’t changed anything in here,” he muttered, a bit choked up.

His father hummed, leaning against the doorframe with his arms crossed over his chest.

“Well, there was no need. After all, you’d return,” pointed out Hieronymus, terribly knowing.

Khaslana looked this noble hero in the eye, feeling something twist in his chest, before he sighed softly and lowered the drawing to smile up at his father.

“Mm. Well, I did promise,” he said with a slightly crooked smile.

“That you did.” His father’s eyes were as soft as the green grass, as the gentle waves, as he looked at him. And then, his grin returned. He patted his arm and nodded to the main room. “Now, c’mon. I’m sure you’re hungry after such a long journey. And… you can tell us how you managed to convince little Ely to wear travel-appropriate clothes instead of those high heels.”

He hesitated for a moment, but in the end, he left his drawing on the desk carefully, a corner under one of the worn books to avoid it being dragged away by the wind. Just like that, it was as if he had dropped a weight off his chest.

“Oh, that was my hardest battle yet,” he managed to joke, as he followed his father back to the main room, just in time for Elysiae and his mother to hear him.

Immediately, Elysiae turned to him and stuck her tongue out.

“Oh, shut up,” she shot back, but her grin was wide, and her new-old book rested under her cold hands.

Khaslana finally grinned back for the first time since he stepped foot into Aedes Elysiae.

—

The celebratory banquet came as no surprise.

Still, it made nervousness churn in her chest; once again, it was no surprise. After all, they had both changed a lot. They weren’t those playful and cheerful children anymore.

And yet, she shouldn’t have worried that much.

When night started blanketing the small village under a starry sky, Audata and Hieronymus led them to the dock, to the rickety shed where most banquets took place. And just like always, everything was decorated with lanterns and tables full of food, people smiling and children running around and music and–

And Elysiae felt that familiar warmth spread from her chest, felt a genuine smile tilt her lips up, felt her eyes tear up, because… everyone recognized her, smiled at her, greeted her with tight hugs and gentle hands.

Soon, the crowd had absorbed them into their chaos and cheer. Soon, Elysiae lost sight of Khaslana and his parents– but it was alright. She was home, right? She was…

She was happy, she realized. More than she’d ever been, ever since opening her eyes in her ‘tomorrow’. She felt so happy she could float away, she thought, but with so many hands grabbing her own, patting her back, placing gentle touches on her arms and shoulders… she stayed with her feet firmly placed on land.

“Ely!” called Piso, running to her with shining eyes. She turned away from the table, where she had been standing frozen, trying to choose between all her childhood comfort foods. “Tell us a story!”

“Oh? I thought you’d ask Khaslana for some of his?” she asked, feeling a familiar kind of amusement spark in her chest. Once upon a time, she had been just a head taller than this kid – her dear friend, with whom she had climbed trees and who she had helped study math. Now, even without her trusty high heels, she towered over him.

“But! He’s busy talking with Prof Pythias!” complained Piso, waving a hand to the corner where, indeed, Khaslana was talking with a doubtful-looking Pythias.

“Ah, so I’m your plan B. I see how it is,” she sniffed, sprinkling some fake-offense onto her voice. She pointedly grabbed a plate of puff pastry filled with grapes and other fruits and turned to leave, but Piso’s hand predictably grabbed the edge of her tunic.

“No, no! You’re our plan A!” he corrected, nervousness clear in his voice.

Elysiae pretended to think it over, humming loudly to be heard above the cheerful music coming from the other side of the area.

“I guess... I have a few stories I could tell you,” she said. Piso’s answering grin was wide as he jumped up and waved back to the small group of children that had been waiting for Piso to convince her to step into her usual role of storyteller. The group of children cheered. “But! Only a few. You have a curfew, right?”

That seemed to surprise Piso, because he turned to her with wide eyes and a dimmed smile, and Elysiae felt some of the now-familiar cold threaten to spread through her. But then Piso pouted, grabbing her hand and dragging her off to a quieter place.

“C’mon, Ely! You’re supposed to be on our side!” he complained, and he was definitely referencing the many times she and Khaslana had stayed up past curfew themselves, getting into trouble or exploring.

As strange and unsettling as it was to be reminded that she was suddenly much, much older than her childhood friends, she could hear no trace of awkwardness or accusation in his voice. The children had taken everything in stride, had mentioned Hieronymus during lunch. Now, the adults… had been much more confused and worried, but– Well, it wasn’t as if Audata and Hieronymus had told them everything.

“That’s not our story to tell,” had said Audata, winking at Elysiae.

“You don’t have to tell anything to anyone,” had added Hieronymus. “You’re home. Aedes Elysiae should be… your safe haven. A place where there are no expectations pushed on you, a place where… you can be yourselves.”

‘Be themselves’... Elysiae wasn’t sure if she remembered how that felt like, but she was sure that she could get there, someday. And being surrounded by laughing people, playing children, endless fields of golden wheat and the sound of the sea… Maybe she was closer to it than she had thought.

Khaslana met her gaze and he smiled, raising his cup, watching and laughing as she was dragged off by Piso, with no intent of helping her. She sniffed, lips twitching up – what kind of hero didn’t help a damsel in distress?

But he wasn’t a hero now, was he? He was simply Khaslana, son of Audata and Hieronymus. He was no Worldbearer, no Deliverer, no Chrysos Heir. He simply… was.

And the same could be said about her, then, right? In this small village in the middle of nowhere, she was no Demiurge, no 13th Titan, no Heart of Amphoreus, no Pure Child of Anasarava. She was simply Elysiae, Cyrene, daughter of Aedes Elysiae. And she, too, simply… was.

Piso finally stopped by the side of the shack, facing the sea, terribly proud of himself as the other children cheered at her appearance, because that meant…

Elysiae smiled wide, took a bite of her dish – and had to close her eyes for a moment when infinite memories sprung up in her mind – and then nodded to herself.

“Now, where should I begin…?” she asked the wind, or the haggle of children in front of her. “The thief that stole the heart of a Titan? A priestess that touched the sky? A mighty warrior that guarded a mysterious crown?” She tapped a finger to her chin as the children around her raised their hands, making their choice and trying to talk over the others. “Or maybe… a boy who traveled through time and a girl that created an archive of all the dreams in the world?”

And as the children cheered and asked for that tale, Elysiae smiled and sat down on one of the haystacks littering the place – just like old times – and in her hands appeared a very familiar book.

“Well, then. It’ll be As I’ve Written…”

—

The festivities went on until late at night – or the early hours of the morning, even.

Khaslana had stumbled his way back home with his mother when the sky was already changing colors, drunk not on alcohol but on warmth and happiness and relief.

Some part of himself had expected the people of the village to regard them like strangers, like too-important people, like– not monsters, because they probably didn’t know what they had done to get Amphoreus this future they now lived in, but… Well, Khaslana could admit that he hadn’t been in the best place mentally for… a while.

Instead of dubious and mistrustful glances, they were met with warm hugs and fond pats on their backs and cheerful reminders of their stupid ideas from their past and careful questions about life in Okhema and gentle inquiries about his health.

“You’ve both changed a lot,” had mentioned every person at least once. And when that had made Khaslana’s smile dim slightly, they all backtracked or clarified. “You’re now all grown up, all big and strong! Why, I still remember when you…”

It was… nice. Really nice. And as the night went on, the tension he had been harboring for days, weeks, months, finally– dissipated like storm clouds.

For these people, he wasn’t the Deliverer, the Worldbearer, the–

(Executioner, vessel of Destruction, Flame Reaver–)

He was simply… Khaslana. And there was a simple freedom in that, in knowing that these people didn’t know how he was made to fight, how he had needed to be grander than life, how he had taken up the sword over and over and over–

He could breathe, here.

He could think without being weighted down with “what-if”s or paranoia or the feeling of detachment that had haunted him like a ghost for the best part of a year now. 

He could wake up with the early morning sun in his face, with Elysiae swatting away his wings as she rolled away in bed grumbling curses under her breath, with the sweet smell of his mother's pancakes and the sound of his father readying himself for another day of hard work in the fields.

He could simply… exist. As himself, as that kid that once dreamed of seeing the world. As a hero returning home and being able to rest.

And so, he helped his mother with breakfast. He threw a pillow at Elysiae’s nest of pink hair to wake her up and threatened her with eating her share of pancakes if she didn't get out of bed in time. He dodged the ball of ice to his head that he got as an answer. He sidestepped Piso’s questions and requests to see his broadsword and ‘cool powers’. He followed his father to the fields, Professor Anaxa’s new invention held carefully in his hand.

“What did you mean with ‘explosions’?” asked his father as Khaslana poured the liquid over a patch of soil next to their fence. Khaslana kept quiet. His father crossed his arms, like always, and stared down at him. “Khaslana.”

Khaslana sighed, shook the vial to get all the liquid out and then stood up with a slight grimace.

“I just meant– Professor Anaxa’s area of expertise is Alchemy, alright? And I know for a fact that sometimes experiments can go wrong and– Look, Professor Anaxa is not really a ‘believer’ in lab safety and…” he trailed off, avoiding his father’s unimpressed gaze. “Sometimes, things just go ‘boom’ during his experiments.”

His father remained silent for a moment, thinking over his words.

“... And you said there were no explosions with this, right?” he asked in the end, neutral.

“... Not in Okheman soil, no,” admitted Khaslana, keeping an eye on the patch that was now absorbing the new liquefied fertilizer. It didn’t seem to be smoking or showing any signs of a sudden explosion or fire, so… that was good. “That’s why I told you to stay away.”

Hieronymus grimaced slightly, rubbing his eyes. It was probably too early in the morning to realize that, if Professor Anaxa had somehow messed up, they could have very well blown up part of the field. Not that Khaslana would have let it come to that – he had enough faith in his reflexes to be able to block anything before it could get out of hand.

“Let’s just… get to work,” was his father’s last word on the matter.

Working on the field was familiar and soothing, in a way. He fell back on old habits soon, following his father around the field and checking what could be harvested and what needed some more time. At some point, his mother also joined them, with her trusty basket at her back.

“Ely?” he asked, arching an eyebrow.

Audata smiled softly and nodded to the Sacrament Courtyard.

“She said that she wanted to talk with some of the priests and… reminisce, I think,” she explained and– ah. Of course. There was no more Oronyx, not really. And the demigod of Time was…

Working on the fields was hard – though, not as hard as having to fight everyday – but it was the perfect moment for reflection, to think about anything and everything. To make a decision that had been banging around his mind for a while.

Elysiae was making peace with a past she had finally left behind – he knew about the book ‘As I’ve Written’, about her now-frequent trips to the Library of Philia and the Marmoreal Palace archives. He should do the same.

And so, when the Parting Hour was finally upon them and his parents started tidying everything up after a long day of work, he slipped away with a promise to get some good meat from Galba. But not before…

Even after all this time, he still remembered the exact place. The waves lapped gently at the shore, the dock cracking and groaning with each movement of the waters.

There was no grave, now. No withered flowers, no scorched earth. Yet, he stopped at the exact place where there had been, once upon a time. The sky was painted with oranges and yellows, and it reminded him of endless fire and flames consuming his skin, his insides, his heart. He could almost hear it, too – a melody of suffering he would never be able to truly leave behind, no matter how much he ran.

He took out Dawnmaker and gazed at its blade, at his own reflection, and saw everything it had witnessed. All the failures, all the deaths, all the pain, all the futility.

He couldn’t continue to wield this blade. Not anymore. Not after it had become too heavy with everything it encompassed, every memory it contained.

Maybe like this, he could finally take the first step into a hopeful future, instead of lingering at the starting line.

So, he gripped the hilt with both hands, took a deep breath and– stabbed Dawnmaker where, at some point in time that didn’t exist anymore, there once rested the grave of his best friend.

Taking his hands off the hilt was more difficult than he could have imagined – it would be the last time he touched this sword. His fingers lingered, just like his mind liked to linger too long in a horrible past, before he let out a long breath and finally… let go.

Somehow, he felt… lighter. As if he had let go of a heavy weight, both literally and metaphorically.

He would never take up that sword again.

And that was… alright.

If there ever came a day when he would need to fight again – which, knowing his luck and how chaotic this universe was, would be sooner rather than later – then he would find another sword to raise to the sun. But Dawnmaker had seen far too much pain, too much blood, too many failures.

He hadn’t realized how long he had been standing there, staring at the sword with a distant gaze, until he heard footsteps behind him and he blinked, coming face to face with a darkening sky.

“Are you okay?” asked his father, cautious and worried.

Khaslana was tempted to laugh – he had scared them, once again.

“Yes,” he said, trying to sound as present as he could. Not lost. He wouldn’t let himself become lost. Not anymore. “I was just closing a… cycle, I guess you could say.”

His father walked closer to him, coming to a stop next to him and looking at his sword with a knowing glint in his eye. His father’s hand was gentle on his shoulder, grounding, and Khaslana let himself close his eyes for a moment.

“You don’t need it anymore?” asked his father in a soft whisper.

“No,” he answered. When he opened his eyes, he turned to the sea, to the horizon, and smiled. “After all, the dawn is already here.”

—

The Sacrament Courtyard was just as she remembered it. Just like Aedes Elysiae itself. And why wouldn’t it? After all, she usually ‘died’ during the Black Tide attack, when Khaslana returned to the starting point to fulfill his promise.

Elysiae gazed at the statue of Oronyx and thought back to March, sweet March, who could be said to be her sister. And who was, technically speaking, the Titan of Time. Only… Titans didn’t exist anymore. And in this case, there wasn’t even a respective demigod to handle the power vacuum.

Only… there could be? Elysiae had once been the demigod of Time, after all. Did she still count as it? It wasn’t as if the 13th Titan was even really known around Amphoreus – it was usually treated as an old legend, a conspiracy theory that madmen or rebel priests clung to when the Titans turned their backs on them.

“Elysiae,” called one of the few priests that still lingered around Aedes Elysiae.

“I’ve just come to tell you that there is no more Oronyx to answer your prayers,” she said, smiling ruefully. She kept her hands folded in front of her, just as they had taught her to do during meetings, rituals, celebrations. “There isn’t a demigod of Time, either, technically speaking.”

“We know,” admitted the old man. He looked just the same as always, just as stern, if only more… tired. More weathered. Once upon a time, Elysiae had thought him to be ancient – now, she would be the most ancient one between them by a landslide. “We talked with the main temple a while ago. Still… that is what faith is, right? Knowing that there might not be an answer, and yet calling out anyway.”

Elysiae’s smile twitched, but she lowered her head in clear deference, a simple bow of respect. Even now, old habits die hard.

“I… know I’m not really under your care anymore, but… I did want to announce my official departure from this order,” she added, careful and heavy.

“It’s okay, child,” sighed the old man, voice rough. He approached her, paused, and then patted her hands. “For what it’s worth… It’s good to have you back.”

And ah, how frustrating, that every time someone mentioned how happy and glad they were that she was back home, her lips and jaw would tremble and her eyes would tear up.

Having said that, the old priest walked off, wooden cane tapping the stone under their feet.

Elysiae took a moment to compose herself, taking soft breaths and rubbing her eyes from time to time. She let her gaze rove around this patio, this place where she had spent so much of her time in the past – reading, writing, doing readings with her cards, napping, playing. This was also the place where she landed, after walking backwards through time – back to the beginning, where she would then…

She reached down to take the book that contained a lot of her old drafts – the one she had naively hidden inside Khaslana’s parents’ house, thinking that it was the perfect hiding spot – and hurried out of the Courtyard.

Predictably, she found her way to the swing. 

It swayed in the wind peacefully, inviting and familiar in a way that made Elysiae’s heart squeeze painfully. She approached it like someone would approach a nervous chimera, book pressed tightly to her chest. She ran her hand through the weathered rope, finding it as firm as always. And with a trembling breath, she sat down on the swing.

Her feet reached the ground, now. For some reason, that fact made her chuckle, as she kicked her legs up and started rocking herself in the swing.

The wind caressed her long hair, the rope was tense and firm under her palms, and the book stayed on her lap as she went up and down, up and down, up and–

The sky changed around her, turning blue and then yellow and then orange.

And she went up and down, up and down.

She saw Livia and Piso running around, she saw Galba return from the forest after a good hunt, she saw Pythias talking with some of the neighbors.

She saw Khaslana leave home with a determined set to his jaw and shoulders.

It was then that she stopped and finally opened the book. Her messy scrawl greeted her like a punch to the gut, and as she read the few first pages, she could feel her chest tight with emotion.

She remembered these drafts, and she remembered what inspired them in the first place.

She remembered waking up with a choked cry that night, sneaking away out her window, seeking refuge in the trees, writing the idea with shaky hands and tear-streaked cheeks. She remembered staying awake all night, unable to put down her pen, getting cramps in her hands. She remembered the after, the impulse to set these pages on fire and then deciding to hide them away in a safe place. And what safer place than Khaslana’s home?

She read over this messy story again, now, and a bitter smile twisted her face.

It talked of a group of heroes doomed to failure, doomed to a world without a future, doomed to a never-ending loop of suffering and death. It talked of pain and loneliness, so much loneliness, and “what if there really is no tomorrow?” and–

Her writing cut off abruptly, as if she had escaped from a trance and had suddenly forgotten where she had been headed.

Elysiae caressed the page, now, in the ‘tomorrow’ the heroes hadn’t been able to reach.

She raised her gaze when she heard Hieronymus talking with Khaslana, both of them returning home. Somehow, Khaslana looked lighter. More alive. As if he had let go of something too heavy to carry anymore.

And so, Elysiae thought back to that conversation she’d had with Hieronymus, about what happened after a story was done. She thought of a wide field with no roads, no tale, no prose to act as her guiding signs. What direction should she take, then?

Elysiae took out her trusty pen, a gift from the Chrysos Heirs that would always wait for their return in Okhema, and placed it on the page. She hesitated for a moment, biting her lip, but– Writing had always come naturally to her. And now was no exception.

And so, she wrote the happy ending this story that had haunted her dreams for eons deserved:

“... And so, the heroes stepped into a golden tomorrow, where hope enveloped them in warmth and where the stars sang of their deeds.

And they were happy.”

– Written by: Cyrene

Chapter End Notes

And it's done! This got... so long...
Man, I don't think I've ever written this much for a single fandom in less than a year.... As Cyrene would say, I think this is a good place to put down my pen for a while. I need a break from HSR hahaha
